"images/e5/e52c421785b646c83ea29542a02e05c5f460ae8dab3b4e97d8148fe84704063a.png" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158543 :tutorial/content "Given the graph of a curve $y= f(x),$ there are two types of reflections we can apply to it:

1\. Reflection across the $y$-axis. This is a transformation of the form 

  $$
  y=f(-x).
  $$

2\. Reflection across the $x$-axis. This is a transformation of the form 

  $$
  y=-f(x).
  $$

For example, let's consider the function $y=f(x)$ below. 

![](images/69/6931216dd63985631394e3f3f2fe59246ddd810ecce5af0f0c7ad18b8634133b.png)

The graph of $y=f(-x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the $y$-axis, and it looks as follows:

![](images/e2/e2274a68c25ed14ba93410fe87d672f85b839b7214b30e80d34a3ae28f47ef03.png)

 

The graph of $y=-f(x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the $x$-axis, and it looks as follows:

![](images/ee/eee560bdd17899d55cdaea35204e9963ae9f0148f0ef897173e6250a3eb874b3.png)

  

We can also combine reflections with other graph transformations. Let's see how." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157496 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186129528 :question/answer-fields 17592186126667] [:db/retract 17592186126620 :answer-field/choices 17592186126624] [:db/retract 17592186126620 :answer-field/choices 17592186126625] [:db/retract 17592186126620 :answer-field/choices 17592186126621] [:db/retract 17592186126620 :answer-field/choices 17592186126622] [:db/retract 17592186126620 :answer-field/choices 17592186126623] {:db/id 17592186129277 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-31b80dba-d43f-591d-b1ec-e6cb3d1597c2" "question-ac81bb63-6896-5260-96a8-5a88cb11f40d" "question-fff4e417-ea88-59e6-bd63-239378f4d2c6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129279 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7da71e9d-63e8-5f19-957f-ca4c328a0eb6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128857 :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as

$$
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)}  f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integrals, we see that the domain of integration $R = R_1\cup R_2,$ where $R_1$ and $R_2$ are type I regions, is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{1} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 1,\,\,x-1\le z\le {y}^{2}\}, \\ {R}_{2} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,y\le x\le 1,\,\,x-1\le z\le {y}^{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{x-1}^{y^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/c8/c8bfd933472e1944f63b1295bda7fc324311ea2ca2ada3636e9f5ab82e4e5fc5.png)

The region $D$ consists of two type II regions in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D =
\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq y \leq 0, \quad y^2 \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
\:\cup\:
\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad y \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the lower boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=y^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
y = -\sqrt{x}
$$

and the upper boundary of the region is

$$
x=y
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
y =x.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad -\sqrt{x} \leq y \leq  x \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/c7/c73a0e30d6996490f9f41bf3e8777c14d542755387f643ad464bd1dd6cab2839.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\int_0^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{1}} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{-\sqrt{x}}}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{x}} \int_{x-1}^{y^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129280 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f35d7c5d-0e2d-5ee0-b1c5-16c26213b1d0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-31b80dba-d43f-591d-b1ec-e6cb3d1597c2" :question/id #uuid "31b80dba-d43f-591d-b1ec-e6cb3d1597c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-162327" :question/problem "![](images/d4/d4573a2e3c7b220ac363c996c5332a3db93cc48b5b941e46a529b6912804f0c6.png)

The triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over the region $R$ (shown above) can be expressed as the following repeated integral:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2-y-z}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y
$$

Rewrite this repeated integral by integrating first with respect to $x,$ then $y,$ and then $z.$" :question/worked-solution "From the given repeated integral, we see that $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le x\le 2-y-z\}
$$

We wish to rewrite our triple integral as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

Since both repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{0}^{2-y-z}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/8d/8d1db6e886f00596814900ca0c4113590a37a407b65c800eb1f9926328ade50c.png)

The region $D$ is a type I region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1-{y}^{2}\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we write $D$ as a type II region.

Notice that the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(z),$ is 

$$
z=1-{y}^{2}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt{1-z}.
$$

and the left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

Then, the type II representation of the region $D$ is

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{1-z}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/1f/1fe8a810a7e98c8a40739d5019ff9054a5375c0a12ae7fd1b17f8b6c8bb19f75.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}{\int }_{0}^{2-y-z}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e8f2f208-bfdf-5d7a-b0b7-7f94fe8a16ae"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Since both repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}+y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

$$

Determine whether the sequence is convergent or divergent. If it converges, find the limit." :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

The given sequence is a geometric sequence with the common ratio 

$$

"![](images/dc/dcddc9ee6fe49965ea4f261fcb43c6f7ccd14193910e864b950745ef513e67a6.png)

The sets $X = \{ 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 \}$ and $Y = \{ 1, 2, 4, 8 \}$ are shown in the Venn diagram above. Find $X\cup Y.$" :question/worked-solution "The union $X \cup Y$ consists of all the elements that are in $X$ or $Y,$ or both. To represent $X \cup Y,$ we will shade in all the area that is contained within either $X$ or $Y,$ or both.

![](images/c9/c94cfc38872dfe0673e112e09feec7781ab4f247f08932d1d8ecd167b4a99d32.png)

The elements $1,2,3,4,5,8$ are in either $X$ or $Y,$ or both. Therefore, the union of $X$ and $Y$ is

$$
X \cup Y = \{ 1,2,3,4,5,8 \}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157280 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3ece29a0-cc0f-5be6-9001-b8cc96566290" "question-e3ebe755-cc28-56a9-a6f9-b3ea716cdfc2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157084 :question/problem "Given the sets $X = \{2, 5, 7, 8\},$ $Y = \{1, 3, 5\},$ and $Z = \{2, 4, 6, 8\},$ find $X \cup Y,$ $Y \cup Z,$ and $Z \cup X.$" :question/worked-solution "The union $X \cup Y$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $X$ or $Y,$ or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}X\cup Y & =\{2,5,7,8\}\cup \{1,3,5\} \\  & =\{1,2,3,5,7,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

The union $Y \cup Z$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $Y$ or $Z,$ or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Y\cup Z & =\{1,3,5\}\cup \{2,4,6,8\} \\  & =\{1,2,3,4,5,6,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

The union $Z \cup X$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $Z$ or $X,$ or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Z\cup X & =\{2,4,6,8\}\cup \{2,5,7,8\} \\  & =\{2,4,5,6,7,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157281 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b7be71bb-2a94-5959-b6e1-bd279930afab"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157085 :question/problem "Let $A$ and $B$ be the set of all multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ and the set of all multiples of $6$ that are greater than $0,$ respectively. What is $A \cup B?$" :question/worked-solution "The multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
A = \{ 4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32, 36 \ldots \}.
$$

Likewise, multiples of $6$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
B = \{ 6,12,18,24,30,36,\ldots \}.
$$

Now, $A \cup B$ is the *union* of $A$ and $B,$ which means that we want to find the elements that are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cup B & =\{4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,…\}\cup \{6,12,18,24,30,36,…\} \\  & =\{4,6,8,12,16,18,20,24,28,30,32,36,…\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233058 :question/problem "![](images/1f/1f3d0b514bc4ec701b6ac755b82cec7246a7a819400108e1733759eb0a2fec86.png)

Given the sets $A=\{o,p,q,r\}$ and $B=\{q,r,v,w\},$ find $A\cup B.$" :question/worked-solution "The union $A\cup B$ consists of all the elements that are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both. To represent $A\cup B,$ we will shade in all the area that is contained in either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

![](images/79/7984b0cb81df816388aa0d5cbf860fc4bdad9f7e871e8671d4616ded02bcaf5b.png)

The elements $o,p,q,r,v,w$ are in either $A$ or $B$, or both. Therefore, the union of $A$ and $B$ is

:question/math-academy-id "q-102147" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be the set of all non-negative integer powers of $3$ and the set of all multiples of $4$ greater than $0,$ respectively. What is $X\cup Y?$" :question/worked-solution "The non-negative integer powers of $3$ are

$$
X=\{1,3,9,27,…\}.
$$

Likewise, multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
Y=\{4,8,12,16,20,24,…\}.
$$

Now, $X\cup Y$ is the *union* of $X$ and $Y,$ which means that we want to find the elements that are in either $X$ or $Y,$ or both. In other words, $X\cup Y$ denotes the set of natural numbers that are either powers of $3$ or multiples of  $4.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}X\cup Y & =\{1,3,9,27,…\}\cup \{4,8,12,16,20,24,…\} \\  & =\{1,3,4,8,9,12,16,20,24,27,…\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a097d8b4-61d7-5c24-b4fc-50630068161e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a097d8b4-61d7-5c24-b4fc-50630068161e" :answer-field/id #uuid "a097d8b4-61d7-5c24-b4fc-50630068161e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2f3ce74f-3cd9-5ddc-870f-ba877c7553c2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fdbc25d6-14b6-50fd-a0ba-7e894e123ebf" "answer-2f3ce74f-3cd9-5ddc-870f-ba877c7553c2" "answer-d79beda6-776f-5231-b900-195a05c1e7fa" "answer-6d532b24-3d74-5a1e-9f87-6c1093e9a0ab" "answer-69419d5e-cec8-59b3-9be5-476325804ea8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fdbc25d6-14b6-50fd-a0ba-7e894e123ebf" :answer/id #uuid "fdbc25d6-14b6-50fd-a0ba-7e894e123ebf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{1,3,4,6,8,9,12,15,18,20,21,25,…\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2f3ce74f-3cd9-5ddc-870f-ba877c7553c2" :answer/id #uuid "2f3ce74f-3cd9-5ddc-870f-ba877c7553c2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{1,3,4,8,9,12,16,20,24,27,…\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d79beda6-776f-5231-b900-195a05c1e7fa" :answer/id #uuid "d79beda6-776f-5231-b900-195a05c1e7fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{1,3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,…\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d532b24-3d74-5a1e-9f87-6c1093e9a0ab" :answer/id #uuid "6d532b24-3d74-5a1e-9f87-6c1093e9a0ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{1,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,…\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-69419d5e-cec8-59b3-9be5-476325804ea8" :answer/id #uuid "69419d5e-cec8-59b3-9be5-476325804ea8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{3,4,6,8,9,12,15,16,18,20,…\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186234433 :question/worked-solution "The multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

Notice that ![](images/a7/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) belongs to both ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) and ![](images/65/65ada9c919fe5c4bee19fb4cafff28ed46a36bf6fc90b4cecf70e0fa02386ce0.svg) but we list it only once in ![](images/bb/bbb285be6a3e138649aa4a514c34823a6b39d094dca3427eb34eb4a326854fcf.svg) In a set, each distinct element is written only once." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158478 :tutorial/content "Although Venn diagrams can be useful to visualize unions, we do not have to draw a Venn diagram every time we wish to compute a union.

For example, let's again consider the sets $A = \{ a,b,c \}$ and $B = \{ b, d, e \}.$ This time, we will compute the union $A \cup B$ without using a Venn diagram. We just need to find all the elements that are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

So, we will start with the elements of $A,$ and then go through the elements of $B$ to look for any elements that we do not already have. Remember that we are looking for elements that we do *not* already have in $A.$

- For the element $b \in B,$ we have $b \in A. \quad \color{red}\times$

- For the element $e \in B,$ we have $e \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

So, to get the union, we need to take the elements of $A$ and also include $d$ and $e.$

$$
x=2{e}^{t/2},\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡3].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t/2})={e}^{t/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t/2})}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}(1+{e}^{t})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t/2}\cdot {e}^{t/2}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{e}^{t}.$ Then, $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi \cdot {\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}({4}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}(8-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}(4-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c5e8aa5a-ac76-5fe7-8cbb-d1e2111d6174"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{5} & = \\ 3\cdot y\cdot \sqrt{5} & = \\ 3y\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}

#uuid "e6203f86-9cf0-5174-84bf-8575e36ffa78" :question/math-academy-id "q-127310" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{2y}+4x,\,{x}^{7}-{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 0,-1\le y\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/09/09acd3df62b333bdaeb7553599507d4dbad7412ef2770b00e8fc8855b38a774e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{2y}+4x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}-{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,dy \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-64fabadb-f80e-5526-b940-02e3d7342ff0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192387 :question/problem "Let $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7  x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $(x_1,y_1), \: \ldots, \: (x_{8},y_{8})$ of $n=8$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overline{x}=2.4,$ the mean square error of the model is $1.25,$ and $S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2 = 42,$ find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $6$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for $\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is given by 

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE} \cdot \bigg( \dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}} \bigg) }
$$

*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{\widehat{\,\beta}_0}_{\:\: \textrm{point} \ \textrm{estimate}} \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0,$ given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

where we have:

- $\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

- $S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=1.6+0.7x,$ our point estimate is

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 = 1.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.90=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{6,0.05} = 1.943.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]  = 1.943 \cdot \sqrt{1.25 \cdot \bigg( \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{2.4^2}{42} \bigg)} \approx 1.1
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 \: \pm \: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] =  1.6 \pm 1.1
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192683 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" "question-14b7fe25-0e56-53c7-82f0-cba7c7a1a3e7" "question-a77fcdca-ce6d-5371-a7a2-e886bf8d2462" "question-4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" "question-8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192388 :question/problem "| **Hours ($x$)** | **$4$** | **$4.5$** | **$5.5$** | **$6$** |

The table above shows the ages, in years, and the number of hours each of four randomly selected adults slept last night. The corresponding linear regression line fitted using this sample is $\overset{^}{\,y}=0.6+0.2x.$
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=38,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.0125,$ find an $80%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line. 

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>1.886)=0.1,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is* 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=0.6+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=0.6+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=0.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $80%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.8=0.2\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.1.
$$

We are given that $P(T>1.886)=0.1.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.1}=1.886.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(34-38)^{2}+(36-38)^{2}+(40-38)^{2}+(42-38)^{2} \\  & =16+4+4+16 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=1.886\cdot \sqrt{0.0125\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{38}^{2}}{40})}≈1.3
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=0.6\pm 1.3
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178" :answer-field/id #uuid "67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" "answer-6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" "answer-94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" "answer-62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" "answer-7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" :answer/id #uuid "b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 0.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" :answer/id #uuid "6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer/id #uuid "94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" :answer/id #uuid "62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37" :answer/id #uuid "7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57" :question/id #uuid "8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57" :question/math-academy-id "q-159590" :question/problem "| **Height ($x$)** | **$64$** | **$68$** | **$72$** | **$76$** |

$$

$$

$$

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=-165+4.6x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=-165.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.920)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.05}=2.920.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(64-70)^{2}+(68-70)^{2}+(72-70)^{2}+(76-70)^{2} \\  & =36+4+4+36 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.920\cdot \sqrt{3.6\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{70}^{2}}{80})}≈43.4
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=-165\pm 43.4
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a" :answer-field/id #uuid "fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" "answer-c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" "answer-8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" "answer-5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" "answer-2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" :answer/id #uuid "91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 41.7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" :answer/id #uuid "c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 42.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" :answer/id #uuid "8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 43.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer/id #uuid "5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 43.4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3" :answer/id #uuid "2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 44.7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population. 

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x.
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$  are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} -  \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x},
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i,$ and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}).
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following: 

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as 

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize, 

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,$

- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1,$ and

- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0.$

In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the intercept parameter $\beta_0.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193892 :tutorial/content "Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{\widehat{\,\beta}_0}_{\:\: \textrm{point} \ \textrm{estimate}} \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}_{\textrm{standard} \ \,\:\: \textrm{error}}}^{\textrm{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0,$ given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

where we have:

- $\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

- $S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2
$$

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by 

$$
(y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i).
$$

- The expression $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$ gives the sum of the squared residuals of our regression model.

- Even considering the entire population, the data points will not fall on a perfectly straight line. Thus, errors are present even in the "true" regression model. These errors have some (unknown) variance, which we'll denote as $\sigma^2.$

- It can be shown that the $\textrm{MSE}$ is an *unbiased* estimator of $\sigma^2.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193900 :tutorial/content "We'll now derive our expression for the confidence interval for our intercept parameter estimate $\widehat{\beta_0}.$

Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i).$

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Let's assume that our "global" regression line (i.e., the line that best fits the entire population) is given by

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

For each $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ let

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i,
$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and 

$$
\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2.$ The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/69/69135b6cdc4d34f5422da39bac5d15624d16f4817e91f282974507c711953796.png)

This means that each $y_i$ is a normally distributed random variable with

$$
y_i \sim N\left( \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i , \sigma^2\right).
$$

It can be shown that 

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0,
\qquad
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] =  \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right).
$$

We'll derive these results separately in a while. But for now, we'll simply state them.

Using these results, we can express the distribution of $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as

$$
\widehat{\beta}_0 \sim N\left(\beta_0, \: \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \right).
$$

We do not know $\sigma^2,$ the variance of the error terms. However, it can be shown that the mean squared error, given by

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2,
$$

is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2.$

Our estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_0$ is now given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \sqrt{\textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)} .
$$

Since this is an *estimate* of the standard error, it can be shown that the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_0 -\beta_0}{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta_0}] }
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom. 

Finally, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] }^{\textrm{margin of error}}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193893 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we made use of the following results:

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0,
\qquad
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] = \sigma^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)
$$

Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i.
$$

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$

The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$

Now, recall that

We can rewrite our expression for $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as follows:

$$

We're now in a position to compute $\textrm{E}[{\widehat{\beta_0} }]$ and $\textrm{Var}[{\widehat{\beta_0} }].$

- For the mean, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{0}}] & =\frac{1}{n}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i}{y}_{i}]-\overset{―}{x}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}\text{E}[{y}_{i}]-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i}\text{E}[{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}[{\beta }_{0}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}+{\beta }_{1}{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{x}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}[{\beta }_{0}{\cancel{{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}}}^{0}+{\beta }_{1}{\cancel{{\sum }_{i}{k}_{i}{x}_{i}}}^{1}] \\  & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i})-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\  & =\frac{{\beta }_{0}}{n}{\sum }_{i}1+\frac{{\beta }_{1}}{n}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\  & =\frac{{\beta }_{0}}{n}\cdot n+\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1}-\overset{―}{x}{\beta }_{1} \\  & ={\beta }_{0}.\end{aligned}

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}.
$$

Applying this formula with $n=4$ and $n=9,$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{4-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{3}, \\ {a}_{9} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{9-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $a_4 = 6$ and $a_9 = 192,$ we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{r}^{3}=6 \\ {a}_{1}{r}^{8}=192\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{r}^{8}}{{a}_{1}{r}^{3}} & =\frac{192}{6} \\ \frac{\cancel{\,{a}_{1}\,}{r}^{8}}{\cancel{\,{a}_{1}\,}{r}^{3}} & =\frac{192}{6} \\ \frac{{r}^{8}}{{r}^{3}} & =32 \\ {r}^{5} & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the common ratio satisfies $r^5 = 32.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147462 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7794f339-0fd4-50d9-a0ab-1ce4d82318cb" "question-a5c77383-51aa-56e3-a7b4-492c5c358798"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147226 :question/problem "Find the common ratio of the geometric sequence whose fourth term is $2$ and whose seventh term is $-686.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

$$

In this case, we're given $a_7 = -686$ and $a_4 = 2.$ Substituting $n=7$ and $m=4$ into the formula, we have

$$

Finally, by solving the equation for $r,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =-343 \\ {r}^{3} & =(-7)^{3} \\ r & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147463 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e964bcbb-bd9b-5437-9046-a26f2773d2b6" "question-5abf554f-7e7b-567c-9a3f-c62e189188a5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147229 :question/problem "The third term of a geometric sequence is $80$ and its fifth term is $20.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive." :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

is $3$ and its fourth term is $27.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive." :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms ${a}_{m}$ and ${a}_{n},$ we use the formula

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}.
$$

In this case, we're given ${a}_{4}=27$ and ${a}_{2}=3.$ Substituting $n=4$ and $m=2$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{4-2} & =\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{27}{3} \\ {r}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, solving the equation for $r$ and considering that $r$ is positive, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2} & ={3}^{2} \\ r & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7642a863-35ca-5b78-ad8e-1abd8f1a804b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7642a863-35ca-5b78-ad8e-1abd8f1a804b" :answer-field/id #uuid "7642a863-35ca-5b78-ad8e-1abd8f1a804b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d001064d-a7b9-5252-ae9d-6a2f9bf8b5d3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fd3e4f46-d7a4-5d08-926a-46332f200d82" "answer-d001064d-a7b9-5252-ae9d-6a2f9bf8b5d3" "answer-82fdc835-0849-5692-9878-06b5cdcfa034" "answer-9ae7a74d-b582-5f2c-bdae-4e37c229e899" "answer-6486fb05-2c8e-59e9-a3f2-53960b0abd36"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd3e4f46-d7a4-5d08-926a-46332f200d82" :answer/id #uuid "fd3e4f46-d7a4-5d08-926a-46332f200d82" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d001064d-a7b9-5252-ae9d-6a2f9bf8b5d3" :answer/id #uuid "d001064d-a7b9-5252-ae9d-6a2f9bf8b5d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-82fdc835-0849-5692-9878-06b5cdcfa034" :answer/id #uuid "82fdc835-0849-5692-9878-06b5cdcfa034" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9ae7a74d-b582-5f2c-bdae-4e37c229e899" :answer/id #uuid "9ae7a74d-b582-5f2c-bdae-4e37c229e899" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6486fb05-2c8e-59e9-a3f2-53960b0abd36" :answer/id #uuid "6486fb05-2c8e-59e9-a3f2-53960b0abd36" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5abf554f-7e7b-567c-9a3f-c62e189188a5" :question/id #uuid "5abf554f-7e7b-567c-9a3f-c62e189188a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-250943" :question/problem "Find the common ratio $r$ of the geometric sequence whose tenth term is $-8$ and whose twelfth term is $-72.$ You're given that the common ratio is negative.

$r=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms ${a}_{m}$ and ${a}_{n},$ we use the formula

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}.
$$

In this case, we're given ${a}_{12}=-72$ and ${a}_{10}=-8.$ Substituting $n=12$ and $m=10$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{12-10} & =\frac{{a}_{12}}{{a}_{10}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{(-72)}{(-8)} \\ {r}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, solving the equation for $r$ and considering that $r$ is negative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2} & =(-3)^{2} \\ r & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f78565af-1ce0-5d78-bd24-bee276b6e56e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f78565af-1ce0-5d78-bd24-bee276b6e56e" :answer-field/id #uuid "f78565af-1ce0-5d78-bd24-bee276b6e56e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5" :answer/id #uuid "247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148692 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a *positive* geometric sequence where the second term is $4$ and the fourth term is $64.$  How do we find the common ratio $r?$

This is a little trickier than before because we're not given two consecutive terms, but let's try to figure it out. First, let's denote

$$
a_2 = 4, \qquad a_4 = 64.
$$

The $n$th term of a geometric sequence is given by:

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}
$$

Applying this formula with $n=2$ and $n=4$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{2-1}={a}_{1}r \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{4-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using that $a_2 = 4$ and $a_4 = 64$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}r & =4 \\ {a}_{1}{r}^{3} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

So now, we have a system of equations to solve. To solve this system, we *divide* the *second* equation above by the *first* equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{r}^{3}}{{a}_{1}r} & =\frac{64}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{{a}_{1}}{r}^{3}}{\cancel{{a}_{1}}r} & =\frac{64}{4} \\ \frac{{r}^{3}}{r} & =16 \\ {r}^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r.$ Note that $16 = 4^2,$ and so we can solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since our sequence must be positive.

Therefore, the common ratio $r=4.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148693 :tutorial/content "Finding the common ratio by solving a system of equations is quite a lot of work. Is there an easier way?

Indeed there is. Given two terms of a geometric sequence $a_n$ and $a_m,$ the formula for $r$ is as follows:

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}
$$

Let's demonstrate how this works. Suppose that we have a geometric sequence whose second term is $3$ and whose fifth term is $192.$ What is the common ratio?

Here, we're given $a_5 = 192$ and $a_2 = 3.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=2$ into the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-2} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{192}{3} \\ {r}^{3} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r$ by noting that $64 = 4^3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =64 \\ {r}^{3} & ={4}^{3} \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So the common ratio is $r=4.$ 

When dealing with an equation that is **cubic** in $r$ (i.e., contains an $r^3$), then there is only one possible answer, unlike the squared case ($r^2$) where we have to pick from either positive or negative." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147713 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

{"source" ":org/Math-Academy" "forms" [{:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/id #uuid "5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/math-academy-id "q-138860" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{({x}^{2}+2)(11{x}^{2}+24x-2)}{g(x)}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}}{\sqrt[3]{3x+6}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6/3}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{2}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{2}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((3x+6)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+6)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2}\cdot 2x-\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3x+6}\cdot 3 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6}) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{4x(3x+6)-({x}^{2}+2)}{({x}^{2}+2)(3x+6)}) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{11{x}^{2}+24x-2}{({x}^{2}+2)(3x+6)}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)(11{x}^{2}+24x-2)}{\sqrt[3]{(3x-6)^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=\sqrt[3]{(3x-6)^{4}}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8c497ffd-4cca-50b5-a7fc-dc93d720ea25"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5964ffcf-bc61-5cdb-8ce3-fe3d629e8c05" :question/id #uuid "5964ffcf-bc61-5cdb-8ce3-fe3d629e8c05" :question/math-academy-id "q-340513" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi $-periodicity:

$$
f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $2\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $2\pi $-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi )=f(\frac{3\pi }{2})=F(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2})=F(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5932e5d0-9d0c-54be-9a78-8ee0938071e4"] :db/ensure $$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{4-8}{4-2} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=-2$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach

$$
y=-2x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+b \\ 4 & =-2(4)+b \\ 4 & =-8+b \\ 4+8 & =b \\ 12 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

What is the residual after $5$ months if the actual height of the $5$-month old puppy is $15.5\,in?$" :question/worked-solution "The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{y} & =2.2x+3.5 \\  & =2.2(5)+3.5 \\  & =14.5\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y} \\  & =15.5-14.5 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "![](images/ae/ae6bc049d3bf3bbdf1a609b6cda4c3b4e9cc1699b387099d265e048a32be68d6.png)

The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data $(x,y).$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. When $x=2,$ the regression equation overestimates the value of $y.$

II. The residuals appear randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).

III. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 
From the plot, the residual at $x=2$ is positive. So, we have that $\text{Actual}>\text{Estimated},$ and therefore the model underestimates (*not* overestimates) this data point.

- Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as $x$ increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

![](images/2f/2f5f3a4dc75324a6ef415c987a62139e2dbd51c5b35a56d5a35f410781087c43.png)

  

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are *not* randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is *not* a good fit for the given data.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0a67e86b-e489-54d7-865b-2fc901ce36f3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0a67e86b-e489-54d7-865b-2fc901ce36f3" :answer-field/id #uuid "0a67e86b-e489-54d7-865b-2fc901ce36f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3c13437d-0881-5fe4-8a20-2ee35a2c1ddb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a8a52756-8d54-5488-b516-f0f46632e8a3" "answer-30cc2096-72bf-53ab-80cd-0e53283f4fe3" "answer-f1372349-8b30-54f1-9a67-58ef6c5b2f3d" "answer-8422f803-42bc-5dbd-9a9b-5c17b0bab74f" "answer-3c13437d-0881-5fe4-8a20-2ee35a2c1ddb"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a8a52756-8d54-5488-b516-f0f46632e8a3" :answer/id #uuid "a8a52756-8d54-5488-b516-f0f46632e8a3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-30cc2096-72bf-53ab-80cd-0e53283f4fe3" :answer/id #uuid "30cc2096-72bf-53ab-80cd-0e53283f4fe3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f1372349-8b30-54f1-9a67-58ef6c5b2f3d" :answer/id #uuid "f1372349-8b30-54f1-9a67-58ef6c5b2f3d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8422f803-42bc-5dbd-9a9b-5c17b0bab74f" :answer/id #uuid "8422f803-42bc-5dbd-9a9b-5c17b0bab74f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3c13437d-0881-5fe4-8a20-2ee35a2c1ddb" :answer/id #uuid "3c13437d-0881-5fe4-8a20-2ee35a2c1ddb" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177047 :tutorial/content "Given a dataset of paired numerical observations $(x,y)$ and the corresponding linear regression model $\widehat{y} =f(x),$ the **residual** for a particular observation $(x, y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-f(x) \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

We subtract the *estimated* value predicted by the model from the actual *observed* value.

To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature $x$ (measured in $^\circ \mathrm{F}$) and the resulting daily ice cream sales $y$ (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below. 

![](images/fc/fc149b8d911a7a9863df9cc25c635d6155accd676e83e335a65d9083596b779b.png)

Suppose the equation of the regression line is

$$
y= 2.5 x +165.
$$

Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates $\color{red}(82, 360)$ (shown in red on our graph). 

First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates ${\color{red}(82, 360)},$ our actual value is $y = {\color{red}360}.$

Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{y} & =2.5x+165 \\  & =2.5(82)+165 \\  & =370\end{aligned}
$$

 

![](images/38/3843c71b50251ae035378507ffb22cfade48dff8e1544d8e1317e4e6d611f7a1.png)

Finally, we compute the residual: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y} \\  & =360-370 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

     

The residual tells us that the linear model *overestimates* the true volume of ice cream sales by $\[math]10$ when the outside temperature is $82^\circ\,\textrm{F}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177048 :tutorial/content "A **residual plot** displays the values of the independent variable along the horizontal axis and the residuals along the vertical axis. 

The scatter plot below represents data from a four-day sample on the number of people visiting a swimming pool and the average daytime temperature, in degrees Celsius. The line $\ell$ is the corresponding linear regression line. 

![](images/62/6228578012fac7e42bedeb7ab7ad5fc9f42432aed8d5751b675df560bc867417.png)

    

These residuals for each of the four data points are highlighted below:

![](images/d7/d70c44fe7b8fce43a8962ac104651acced75e10598e865a3b3c80d09f16ce234.png)

    

If we calculate the numerical values for the residuals at each data point (from left to right), we get the following results:

$$
-4, \quad 8, \quad -8, \quad 4
$$

To compute our residual plot, we plot each $x$-value and its corresponding residual on some coordinate axes: 

![](images/ff/ff8e6da5489313f1f981c379505f9a72610dfd2a4b5dc0113685d647ba02a1f3.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177051 :tutorial/content "![](images/ff/ff8e6da5489313f1f981c379505f9a72610dfd2a4b5dc0113685d647ba02a1f3.png)

We should be aware of the following interpretations for residual plots:

- Any point *above* the horizontal axis represents a *positive* residual. A positive residual means that the regression model *underestimates* the observed value for $y$ at this point.

- Any point *below* the horizontal axis represents a *negative* residual. A negative residual means that the regression model *overestimates* the observed value for $y$ at this point.

Residual plots can also be used to assess whether a trend line is a "good" fit for the corresponding data:

- If a linear trend line is a good fit for the data, the residuals should be scattered randomly above and below the horizontal axis and be relatively close to zero.

- In cases where the residuals show some clear pattern, this usually indicates that the data has no linear trend.

The residuals are scattered randomly about the horizontal axis in our last example. However, they are not close to zero, indicating that the trend line is a weak fit for the data." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176138 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105808 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-29ae9066-cb5e-58ca-bc97-42812b49b53a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-29ae9066-cb5e-58ca-bc97-42812b49b53a" :question/id #uuid "29ae9066-cb5e-58ca-bc97-42812b49b53a" :question/math-academy-id "q-22657" :question/problem "![](images/6d/6d6009de9ef5df47144f36eb42393b7e9f77ab5c70e3606db09e48bf98289ecb.png)

"The function ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation $x{y}^{″}-(x+1){y}^{′}+y=0$ for $x>0.$ Use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation." :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x({u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})-(x+1)({u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})+u{e}^{x} & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux)-{e}^{x}{u}^{′}(x+1)-{e}^{x}u(x+1)+{e}^{x}u & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux-{u}^{′}(x+1)-u(x+1)+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(2x-x-1)+u(x-x-1+1)) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x+w(x-1)=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}\,⟹\,u=-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}(-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=(1+x).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f1e8ec1f-41ee-5320-b7b5-0129ea48c897"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Given the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,{e}^{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,-1,{e}^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }k \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\text{ }i-2yz\text{ }j-{y}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(1,-1,{e}^{2}) & =2{e}^{2}\text{ }i-2(-1)({e}^{2})\text{ }j-(-1)^{2}k \\  & =2{e}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{2}\,j-k \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2},2{e}^{2},-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,-1,{e}^{2})\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1,\,z-{e}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2{e}^{2},2{e}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1,\,z-{e}^{2}⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-69e14aac-1ab9-5ef1-86cb-e05f2514d2ec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-79a8ed53-1004-51ec-854e-1bc8377232da"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "39c46748-4786-53ad-a218-6f5fdd2db8c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-33453" :question/problem "Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,-8,-1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $2x+y-2z=-7.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=-3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z & =-7 \\ 2(1)+(-3)+7 & =2z \\ 6 & =2z \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,-3,3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-3,3⟩-⟨-2,-8,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,5,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨2,1,-2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|3\cdot 2+5\cdot 1+4\cdot (-2)|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|6+5-8|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\  & =\frac{|\,3\,|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b4a98275-e739-51cc-8112-6d634db0f987"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b4a98275-e739-51cc-8112-6d634db0f987" :answer-field/id #uuid "b4a98275-e739-51cc-8112-6d634db0f987" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4738641c-2dc2-53da-9d9a-b5f351c18c04" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d2870e0f-6294-5f82-8056-6334f7ab8f37" "answer-4738641c-2dc2-53da-9d9a-b5f351c18c04" "answer-3e48c6e1-979b-5319-ab3b-cf3af3e4ddf7" "answer-6020578e-6c29-5a90-8cfa-60aa1062193f" "answer-71da091c-aca1-5ad0-8e35-00a66ee352db"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2870e0f-6294-5f82-8056-6334f7ab8f37" :answer/id #uuid "d2870e0f-6294-5f82-8056-6334f7ab8f37" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4738641c-2dc2-53da-9d9a-b5f351c18c04" :answer/id #uuid "4738641c-2dc2-53da-9d9a-b5f351c18c04" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3e48c6e1-979b-5319-ab3b-cf3af3e4ddf7" :answer/id #uuid "3e48c6e1-979b-5319-ab3b-cf3af3e4ddf7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6020578e-6c29-5a90-8cfa-60aa1062193f" :answer/id #uuid "6020578e-6c29-5a90-8cfa-60aa1062193f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71da091c-aca1-5ad0-8e35-00a66ee352db" :answer/id #uuid "71da091c-aca1-5ad0-8e35-00a66ee352db" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119794 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-39a7d310-9046-5578-9f8d-31308eeefed9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-39a7d310-9046-5578-9f8d-31308eeefed9" :question/id #uuid "39a7d310-9046-5578-9f8d-31308eeefed9" :question/math-academy-id "q-75094" :question/problem "Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{23}=$" :question/worked-solution "To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=-4,{u}_{23}=3,$ and ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{23}=-12.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e485ffe4-c9b3-59e1-9725-0e402d6b690f"] $$

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}|=27.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find ${D}_{z}$, we replace the third column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$

$$

$$

\{\begin{aligned}kx+2y-4z=-4 \\ x-2y+5z=-6 \\ 10x+y+2z=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that  $x=-\frac{20}{3}$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $12-9k,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}k & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 & 5 \\ 10 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=12-9k\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & -4 \\ -6 & -2 & 5 \\ 8 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-6 & 5 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(-4-5)-2(-12-40)-4(-6+16) \\  & =36+104-40 \\  & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\frac{100}{12-9k}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $x=-\frac{20}{3}.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

In this lesson, we will practice applying Cramer's rule to solve $3 \times 3$ systems of equations.

Suppose we have a square system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y+{a}_{13}z={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y+{a}_{23}z={b}_{2} \\ {a}_{31}x+{a}_{32}y+{a}_{33}z={b}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

where ![](images/39/39c4a39573975acc249a4402799f40ef8d72666d4da03d6c4ed6cc299bc7fc52.svg). 
Then Cramer's rule states that

$$
\left< x,y,z \right> = \left\langle  \dfrac{D_x}{D}, \dfrac{D_y}{D}, \dfrac{D_z}{D} \right\rangle
$$

is the unique solution of the system, where

![](images/dc/dcda1374b4582e7978133bbf3cea0375b40095d353573f826a3bac7f212dfc03.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121047 :tutorial/content "To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z=9 \\ 2y+3z=7 \\ -8x+y+6z=0\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z=9 \\ 0x+2y+3z=7 \\ -8x+1y+6z=0\end{aligned}
$$

We start finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ -8 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(12-3)-2(0+24)+(0+16) \\  & =36-48+16 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $D_x,$ $D_y,$ and $D_z.$

- To find $D_x,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *first* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =9(12-3)-2(42-0)+(7-0) \\  & =81-84+7 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *second* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=|\begin{aligned}4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \\ -8 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(42)-9(0+24)+(0+56) \\  & =168-216+56 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_z,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *third* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 7 \\ -8 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 7 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}|+9\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(-7)-2(0+56)+9(0+16) \\  & =-28-112+144 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to the system is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩ & =⟨\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},\frac{{D}_{y}}{D},\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4}{4},\frac{8}{4},\frac{4}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119998 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "activity-80dffb9b-6686-5250-93b4-d26b471b47b4" :activity/id #uuid $f(x,y,z)=2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }k \\  & =2y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+2{e}^{x}\text{ }j-{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,-1) & =2(1)e\text{ }i+2e\text{ }j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =2e\,i+2e\,j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =⟨2e,2e,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2e,2e,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ 2ex+2ey-\frac{z}{e}-4e-\frac{1}{e} & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-102d43bf-f5e9-5d2c-bd0c-f23bbb64ece6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/id #uuid "d5913a4b-d974-52bc-82fc-74c4bb66f8ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-102710" :question/problem "Consider the surface ${e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}=e-3.$ Given that $n=⟨a,b,c⟩$ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(1,1,-1),$ what is the value of $\frac{a-b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define  $f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=e-3.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}))j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2})k \\  & =(y{e}^{xy}-2x)i+(x{e}^{xy})j+(-4z)k \\ ∇f(1,1,-1) & =((1){e}^{(1)(1)}-2(1))\text{ }i+(1){e}^{(1)(1)}\text{ }j+(-4)(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =(e-2)\text{ }i+e\text{ }j+4\text{ }k \\  & =⟨e-2,\,e,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨e-2,\,e,\,4⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{a-b}{c}=\frac{(e-2)-e}{4}=-\frac{1}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d777c8fd-8f4e-5ca8-a5be-b50636868cd0"] :db/ensure "Consider the surface ${z}^{2}y+16=4\sqrt{x}+y.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(4,-1,3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}y+16 & =4\sqrt{x}+y. \\ {z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-16.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,-1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y)\text{ }k \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\text{ }i+({z}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2zy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,-1,3) & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}\text{ }i+({3}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2(3)(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =-\,i+8\text{ }j-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,8,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,-1,3)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y+1,\,z-3⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-1,8,-6⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y+1,\,z-3⟩ & =0 \\ -(x-4)+8(y+1)-6(z-3) & =0 \\ -x+8y-6z+30 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-74e95cce-259a-58bc-a6dc-cf74c51c993b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
