#uuid "e6203f86-9cf0-5174-84bf-8575e36ffa78" :question/math-academy-id "q-127310" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{2y}+4x,\,{x}^{7}-{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 0,-1\le y\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/09/09acd3df62b333bdaeb7553599507d4dbad7412ef2770b00e8fc8855b38a774e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{2y}+4x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}-{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,dy \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-64fabadb-f80e-5526-b940-02e3d7342ff0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192387 :question/problem "Let $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7  x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $(x_1,y_1), \: \ldots, \: (x_{8},y_{8})$ of $n=8$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overline{x}=2.4,$ the mean square error of the model is $1.25,$ and $S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2 = 42,$ find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $6$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for $\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is given by 

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE} \cdot \bigg( \dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}} \bigg) }
$$

*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{\widehat{\,\beta}_0}_{\:\: \textrm{point} \ \textrm{estimate}} \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0,$ given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

where we have:

- $\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

- $S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=1.6+0.7x,$ our point estimate is

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 = 1.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.90=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{6,0.05} = 1.943.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]  = 1.943 \cdot \sqrt{1.25 \cdot \bigg( \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{2.4^2}{42} \bigg)} \approx 1.1
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 \: \pm \: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] =  1.6 \pm 1.1
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192683 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" "question-14b7fe25-0e56-53c7-82f0-cba7c7a1a3e7" "question-a77fcdca-ce6d-5371-a7a2-e886bf8d2462" "question-4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" "question-8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192388 :question/problem "| **Hours ($x$)** | **$4$** | **$4.5$** | **$5.5$** | **$6$** |

The table above shows the number of hours each of four students spent studying for a biology exam and the grades they obtained on the exam. The corresponding fitted linear regression line using this sample is $\widehat{\,y} = 21.3 + 10x.$
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overline{x}=5,$ and $\textrm{MSE}=1.375,$ find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 2.920) = 0.05,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is*

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE} \cdot \bigg( \dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}} \bigg) }.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x= 21.3 + 10x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\beta_0 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0,$ given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

where we have:

- $\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

- $S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=21.3 + 10x,$ our point estimate is

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 = 21.3.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T > 2.920) = 0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{2,0.005} = 2.920.
$$

- Computing $S_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(4-5)^{2}+(4.5-5)^{2}+(5.5-5)^{2}+(6-5)^{2} \\  & =1+0.25+0.25+1 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]  = 2.920 \cdot \sqrt{1.375\cdot \bigg( \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{5^2}{2.5} \bigg)} \approx 11.0
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

"question-812d00c8-ff0e-5dde-8e15-88d6aa199ddf" :question/id #uuid "812d00c8-ff0e-5dde-8e15-88d6aa199ddf" :question/math-academy-id "q-159561" :question/problem "Let $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.4+0.2x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $({x}_{1},{y}_{1}),\,…,\,({x}_{12},{y}_{12})$ of $n=12$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=1.2,$ the mean square error of the model is $0.7,$ and ${S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}=18.9,$ find a $95%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.228)=0.025,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $10$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is given by 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.4+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{{{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{⏟}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=2.4+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=2.4.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.228)=0.025.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{10,0.025}=2.228.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.228\cdot \sqrt{0.7\cdot (\frac{1}{12}+\frac{{1.2}^{2}}{18.9})}≈0.7
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.4\pm 0.7
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b86a25e5-3ce1-5477-9eb2-c277e7527b4c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b86a25e5-3ce1-5477-9eb2-c277e7527b4c" :answer-field/id #uuid "b86a25e5-3ce1-5477-9eb2-c277e7527b4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-93ebfe14-4c6e-5be6-8ef7-fc1066aec02c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e8c71797-2619-523f-998b-4dc9f5e6a269" "answer-b312c9b8-2b8a-552e-98f0-214625871779" "answer-93ebfe14-4c6e-5be6-8ef7-fc1066aec02c" "answer-489fcd75-9368-5e9b-acbf-94835400f3d5" "answer-92b0899f-5335-5dd0-a82e-12c93b11cd39"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e8c71797-2619-523f-998b-4dc9f5e6a269" :answer/id #uuid "e8c71797-2619-523f-998b-4dc9f5e6a269" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2\pm 0.1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b312c9b8-2b8a-552e-98f0-214625871779" :answer/id #uuid "b312c9b8-2b8a-552e-98f0-214625871779" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.4\pm 0.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93ebfe14-4c6e-5be6-8ef7-fc1066aec02c" :answer/id #uuid "93ebfe14-4c6e-5be6-8ef7-fc1066aec02c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.4\pm 0.7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-489fcd75-9368-5e9b-acbf-94835400f3d5" :answer/id #uuid "489fcd75-9368-5e9b-acbf-94835400f3d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.4\pm 0.9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92b0899f-5335-5dd0-a82e-12c93b11cd39" :answer/id #uuid "92b0899f-5335-5dd0-a82e-12c93b11cd39" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.4\pm 1.1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" :question/id #uuid "69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-159557" :question/problem "| **Height ($x$)** | **$67$** | **$70$** | **$73$** | **$76$** |

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=151.3-0.7x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=151.3.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $98%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.98=0.02\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.01.
$$

We are given that $P(T>6.965)=0.01.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.01}=6.965.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(60-64)^{2}+(62-64)^{2}+(66-64)^{2}+(68-64)^{2} \\  & =16+4+4+16 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=6.965\cdot \sqrt{7.7\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{64}^{2}}{40})}≈195.8
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=151.3\pm 195.8
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2fd0291-b761-5650-8e97-a72f4f5d21b5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b2fd0291-b761-5650-8e97-a72f4f5d21b5" :answer-field/id #uuid "b2fd0291-b761-5650-8e97-a72f4f5d21b5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9f303830-c78a-5b75-886c-4c70713deba0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e489115e-e8c1-5d14-a654-2c4be9ba3e26" "answer-ac8ab9d8-4875-5fd3-8eff-2b8511dc815e" "answer-4b209ccf-fac3-51cd-a24e-17d94342e720" "answer-7e50f150-1d03-5cdd-b228-0b83996b3433" "answer-9f303830-c78a-5b75-886c-4c70713deba0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e489115e-e8c1-5d14-a654-2c4be9ba3e26" :answer/id #uuid "e489115e-e8c1-5d14-a654-2c4be9ba3e26" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "151.3\pm 173.1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac8ab9d8-4875-5fd3-8eff-2b8511dc815e" :answer/id #uuid "ac8ab9d8-4875-5fd3-8eff-2b8511dc815e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "151.3\pm 175.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b209ccf-fac3-51cd-a24e-17d94342e720" :answer/id #uuid "4b209ccf-fac3-51cd-a24e-17d94342e720" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "151.3\pm 183.6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7e50f150-1d03-5cdd-b228-0b83996b3433" :answer/id #uuid "7e50f150-1d03-5cdd-b228-0b83996b3433" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "151.3\pm 193.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9f303830-c78a-5b75-886c-4c70713deba0" :answer/id #uuid "9f303830-c78a-5b75-886c-4c70713deba0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "151.3\pm 195.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" :question/id #uuid "4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-159556" :question/problem "| **Age ($x$)** | **$34$** | **$36$** | **$40$** | **$42$** |

Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=38,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.0125,$ find an $80%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line. 

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>1.886)=0.1,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is* 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=0.6+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=0.6+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=0.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $80%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.8=0.2\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.1.
$$

We are given that $P(T>1.886)=0.1.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.1}=1.886.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(34-38)^{2}+(36-38)^{2}+(40-38)^{2}+(42-38)^{2} \\  & =16+4+4+16 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=1.886\cdot \sqrt{0.0125\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{38}^{2}}{40})}≈1.3
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=0.6\pm 1.3
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178" :answer-field/id #uuid "67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" "answer-6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" "answer-94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" "answer-62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" "answer-7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" :answer/id #uuid "b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 0.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" :answer/id #uuid "6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer/id #uuid "94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" :answer/id #uuid "62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37" :answer/id #uuid "7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57" :question/id #uuid "8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57" :question/math-academy-id "q-159590" :question/problem "| **Height ($x$)** | **$64$** | **$68$** | **$72$** | **$76$** |

$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=-165+4.6x,$ our point estimate is

$$

$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.920)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.05}=2.920.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(64-70)^{2}+(68-70)^{2}+(72-70)^{2}+(76-70)^{2} \\  & =36+4+4+36 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a" :answer-field/id #uuid "fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" "answer-c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" "answer-8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" "answer-5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" "answer-2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" :answer/id #uuid "91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 41.7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" :answer/id #uuid "c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 42.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" :answer/id #uuid "8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 43.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer/id #uuid "5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 43.4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3" :answer/id #uuid "2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-165\pm 44.7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population. 

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x.
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$  are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} -  \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x},
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i,$ and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}).
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following: 

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as 

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize, 

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,$

- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1,$ and

- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0.$

In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the intercept parameter $\beta_0.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193892 :tutorial/content "Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{\widehat{\,\beta}_0}_{\:\: \textrm{point} \ \textrm{estimate}} \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}_{\textrm{standard} \ \,\:\: \textrm{error}}}^{\textrm{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0,$ given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{ \textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

where we have:

- $\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

- $S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2
$$

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by 

$$
(y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i).
$$

- The expression $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$ gives the sum of the squared residuals of our regression model.

- Even considering the entire population, the data points will not fall on a perfectly straight line. Thus, errors are present even in the "true" regression model. These errors have some (unknown) variance, which we'll denote as $\sigma^2.$

- It can be shown that the $\textrm{MSE}$ is an *unbiased* estimator of $\sigma^2.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193900 :tutorial/content "We'll now derive our expression for the confidence interval for our intercept parameter estimate $\widehat{\beta_0}.$

Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i).$

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Let's assume that our "global" regression line (i.e., the line that best fits the entire population) is given by

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

For each $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ let

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i,
$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and 

$$
\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2.$ The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/69/69135b6cdc4d34f5422da39bac5d15624d16f4817e91f282974507c711953796.png)

This means that each $y_i$ is a normally distributed random variable with

$$
y_i \sim N\left( \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i , \sigma^2\right).
$$

It can be shown that 

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0,
\qquad
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] =  \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right).
$$

We'll derive these results separately in a while. But for now, we'll simply state them.

Using these results, we can express the distribution of $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as

$$
\widehat{\beta}_0 \sim N\left(\beta_0, \: \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \right).
$$

We do not know $\sigma^2,$ the variance of the error terms. However, it can be shown that the mean squared error, given by

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2,
$$

is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2.$

Our estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_0$ is now given by

$$

$$

Finally, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$

$$

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}.
$$

Applying this formula with $n=4$ and $n=9,$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{4-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{3}, \\ {a}_{9} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{9-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $a_4 = 6$ and $a_9 = 192,$ we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{r}^{3}=6 \\ {a}_{1}{r}^{8}=192\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{r}^{8}}{{a}_{1}{r}^{3}} & =\frac{192}{6} \\ \frac{\cancel{\,{a}_{1}\,}{r}^{8}}{\cancel{\,{a}_{1}\,}{r}^{3}} & =\frac{192}{6} \\ \frac{{r}^{8}}{{r}^{3}} & =32 \\ {r}^{5} & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the common ratio satisfies $r^5 = 32.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147462 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7794f339-0fd4-50d9-a0ab-1ce4d82318cb" "question-a5c77383-51aa-56e3-a7b4-492c5c358798"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147226 :question/problem "Find the common ratio of the geometric sequence whose fourth term is $2$ and whose seventh term is $-686.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}.
$$

In this case, we're given $a_7 = -686$ and $a_4 = 2.$ Substituting $n=7$ and $m=4$ into the formula, we have

$$

$$

Finally, by solving the equation for $r,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =-343 \\ {r}^{3} & =(-7)^{3} \\ r & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147463 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e964bcbb-bd9b-5437-9046-a26f2773d2b6" "question-5abf554f-7e7b-567c-9a3f-c62e189188a5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147229 :question/problem "The third term of a geometric sequence is $80$ and its fifth term is $20.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive." :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

$r=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms ${a}_{m}$ and ${a}_{n},$ we use the formula

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}.
$$

In this case, we're given ${a}_{12}=-72$ and ${a}_{10}=-8.$ Substituting $n=12$ and $m=10$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{12-10} & =\frac{{a}_{12}}{{a}_{10}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{(-72)}{(-8)} \\ {r}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, solving the equation for $r$ and considering that $r$ is negative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2} & =(-3)^{2} \\ r & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f78565af-1ce0-5d78-bd24-bee276b6e56e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f78565af-1ce0-5d78-bd24-bee276b6e56e" :answer-field/id #uuid "f78565af-1ce0-5d78-bd24-bee276b6e56e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5" :answer/id #uuid "247506a5-a604-532e-ae42-730a93dd18f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148692 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a *positive* geometric sequence where the second term is $4$ and the fourth term is $64.$  How do we find the common ratio $r?$

This is a little trickier than before because we're not given two consecutive terms, but let's try to figure it out. First, let's denote

$$
a_2 = 4, \qquad a_4 = 64.
$$

The $n$th term of a geometric sequence is given by:

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}
$$

Applying this formula with $n=2$ and $n=4$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{2-1}={a}_{1}r \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{4-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using that $a_2 = 4$ and $a_4 = 64$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}r & =4 \\ {a}_{1}{r}^{3} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

So now, we have a system of equations to solve. To solve this system, we *divide* the *second* equation above by the *first* equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{r}^{3}}{{a}_{1}r} & =\frac{64}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{{a}_{1}}{r}^{3}}{\cancel{{a}_{1}}r} & =\frac{64}{4} \\ \frac{{r}^{3}}{r} & =16 \\ {r}^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r.$ Note that $16 = 4^2,$ and so we can solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since our sequence must be positive.

Therefore, the common ratio $r=4.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148693 :tutorial/content "Finding the common ratio by solving a system of equations is quite a lot of work. Is there an easier way?

Indeed there is. Given two terms of a geometric sequence $a_n$ and $a_m,$ the formula for $r$ is as follows:

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}
$$

Let's demonstrate how this works. Suppose that we have a geometric sequence whose second term is $3$ and whose fifth term is $192.$ What is the common ratio?

Here, we're given $a_5 = 192$ and $a_2 = 3.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=2$ into the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-2} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{192}{3} \\ {r}^{3} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r$ by noting that $64 = 4^3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =64 \\ {r}^{3} & ={4}^{3} \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So the common ratio is $r=4.$ 

When dealing with an equation that is **cubic** in $r$ (i.e., contains an $r^3$), then there is only one possible answer, unlike the squared case ($r^2$) where we have to pick from either positive or negative." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147713 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/id #uuid "5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60"] ["question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/math-academy-id "q-138860"] ["question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{({x}^{2}+2)(11{x}^{2}+24x-2)}{g(x)}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$"] ["question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}}{\sqrt[3]{3x+6}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6/3}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{2}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{2}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((3x+6)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+6)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2}\cdot 2x-\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3x+6}\cdot 3 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6}) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{4x(3x+6)-({x}^{2}+2)}{({x}^{2}+2)(3x+6)}) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{11{x}^{2}+24x-2}{({x}^{2}+2)(3x+6)}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)(11{x}^{2}+24x-2)}{\sqrt[3]{(3x-6)^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=\sqrt[3]{(3x-6)^{4}}.
$$"] ["question-5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-8c497ffd-4cca-50b5-a7fc-dc93d720ea25" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-5964ffcf-bc61-5cdb-8ce3-fe3d629e8c05" :question/math-academy-id "q-340513"] ["question-5964ffcf-bc61-5cdb-8ce3-fe3d629e8c05" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$"] ["question-5964ffcf-bc61-5cdb-8ce3-fe3d629e8c05" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi $-periodicity:

$$
f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $2\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

On the other hand, the point on the regression line that corresponds to $x=5$ has the $y$-coordinate $0.$ So, our estimated value of is $\overset{^}{y}=0.$

$$

$$"] ["question-855a07b7-e3c5-5f4d-b62e-d65fbbb7b6dd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-98f4db4e-2c19-5da3-9efd-62ed734fe2e6" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-1f3c0f66-15fe-5ce9-aae2-49226c3a0199"] [17592186177047 :tutorial/content "Given a dataset of paired numerical observations $(x,y)$ and the corresponding linear regression model $\widehat{y} =f(x),$ the **residual** for a particular observation $(x, y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-f(x) \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

We subtract the *estimated* value predicted by the model from the actual *observed* value.

To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature $x$ (measured in $^\circ \mathrm{F}$) and the resulting daily ice cream sales $y$ (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below. 

![](images/fc/fc149b8d911a7a9863df9cc25c635d6155accd676e83e335a65d9083596b779b.png)

Suppose the equation of the regression line is

$$
y= 2.5 x +165.
$$

Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates $\color{red}(82, 360)$ (shown in red on our graph). 

First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates ${\color{red}(82, 360)},$ our actual value is $y = {\color{red}360}.$

Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{y} & =2.5x+165 \\  & =2.5(82)+165 \\  & =370\end{aligned}
$$

 

![](images/38/3843c71b50251ae035378507ffb22cfade48dff8e1544d8e1317e4e6d611f7a1.png)

Finally, we compute the residual: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y} \\  & =360-370 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

     

The residual tells us that the linear model *overestimates* the true volume of ice cream sales by $\[math]10$ when the outside temperature is $82^\circ\,\textrm{F}.$"] [17592186177048 :tutorial/content "A **residual plot** displays the values of the independent variable along the horizontal axis and the residuals along the vertical axis.

![](images/62/6228578012fac7e42bedeb7ab7ad5fc9f42432aed8d5751b675df560bc867417.png)

If we calculate the numerical values for the residuals at each data point (from left to right), we get the following results:

-4, \quad 8, \quad -8, \quad 4

To compute our residual plot, we plot each $x$-value and its corresponding residual on some coordinate axes: 

![](images/ff/ff8e6da5489313f1f981c379505f9a72610dfd2a4b5dc0113685d647ba02a1f3.png)"] [17592186177051 :tutorial/content "![](images/ff/ff8e6da5489313f1f981c379505f9a72610dfd2a4b5dc0113685d647ba02a1f3.png)

We should be aware of the following interpretations for residual plots:

- Any point *above* the horizontal axis represents a *positive* residual. A positive residual means that the regression model *underestimates* the observed value for $y$ at this point.

- Any point *below* the horizontal axis represents a *negative* residual. A negative residual means that the regression model *overestimates* the observed value for $y$ at this point.

Residual plots can also be used to assess whether a trend line is a "good" fit for the corresponding data:

- If a linear trend line is a good fit for the data, the residuals should be scattered randomly above and below the horizontal axis and be relatively close to zero.

- In cases where the residuals show some clear pattern, this usually indicates that the data has no linear trend.

The residuals are scattered randomly about the horizontal axis in our last example. ["question-2abfd6a6-feff-503c-bea4-5ba5b90fc5a2" :question/problem "The function ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation $x{y}^{″}-(x+1){y}^{′}+y=0$ for $x>0.$ Use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation."] ["question-2abfd6a6-feff-503c-bea4-5ba5b90fc5a2" :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x({u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})-(x+1)({u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})+u{e}^{x} & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux)-{e}^{x}{u}^{′}(x+1)-{e}^{x}u(x+1)+{e}^{x}u & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux-{u}^{′}(x+1)-u(x+1)+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(2x-x-1)+u(x-x-1+1)) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x+w(x-1)=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}\,⟹\,u=-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}(-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=(1+x).
$$"] ["question-2abfd6a6-feff-503c-bea4-5ba5b90fc5a2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-f1e8ec1f-41ee-5320-b7b5-0129ea48c897" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-6a99613e-1f33-5aa3-a707-361661349677" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,-1,{e}^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }k \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\text{ }i-2yz\text{ }j-{y}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(1,-1,{e}^{2}) & =2{e}^{2}\text{ }i-2(-1)({e}^{2})\text{ }j-(-1)^{2}k \\  & =2{e}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{2}\,j-k \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2},2{e}^{2},-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,-1,{e}^{2})\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1,\,z-{e}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2{e}^{2},2{e}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1,\,z-{e}^{2}⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6a99613e-1f33-5aa3-a707-361661349677" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-69e14aac-1ab9-5ef1-86cb-e05f2514d2ec" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-af173c80-5734-52f5-887a-4f2d2e37a60e" :question/math-academy-id "q-37159"] ["question-af173c80-5734-52f5-887a-4f2d2e37a60e" :question/problem "$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$"] ["question-af173c80-5734-52f5-887a-4f2d2e37a60e" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-af173c80-5734-52f5-887a-4f2d2e37a60e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-79a8ed53-1004-51ec-854e-1bc8377232da" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,-8,-1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $2x+y-2z=-7.$"] ["question-39c46748-4786-53ad-a218-6f5fdd2db8c5" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=-3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z & =-7 \\ 2(1)+(-3)+7 & =2z \\ 6 & =2z \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,-3,3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-3,3⟩-⟨-2,-8,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,5,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨2,1,-2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|3\cdot 2+5\cdot 1+4\cdot (-2)|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|6+5-8|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\  & =\frac{|\,3\,|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-39c46748-4786-53ad-a218-6f5fdd2db8c5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b4a98275-e739-51cc-8112-6d634db0f987" :answer-field/id #uuid Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=-4,{u}_{23}=3,$ and ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{23}=-12.$"] ["question-39a7d310-9046-5578-9f8d-31308eeefed9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
D=|\begin{aligned}5 & -8 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -5 & 4\end{aligned}|.
$$

Now, to construct ${D}_{y}$, we replace the second column of the coefficient matrix by the right-hand side column of the given system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -7 & -3 \\ 1 & -10 & 4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8be0f924-0f3e-5631-9e67-77a4667752f3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5a66b44b-6b9e-5088-92dd-3e1f0889e8b3" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below. 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x+3y+z=1 \\ 6x-2y-z=-14 \\ 3x+y-z=1\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $27,$ then $z=$"] ["question-42ee0be6-4308-53bc-b367-0e542cac978e" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x+3y+1z=1 \\ 6x+(-2)y+(-1)z=-14 \\ 3x+1y+(-1)z=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by writing the determinant of the coefficients matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}|=27.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find ${D}_{z}$, we replace the third column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 & -14 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -14 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & -14 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-2+14)-3(6+42)+(6+6) \\  & =24-144+12 \\  & =-108.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying Cramer's rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}=\frac{-108}{27}=-4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-42ee0be6-4308-53bc-b367-0e542cac978e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b8fd5cb6-f113-5503-be05-ca917de23415" :answer-field/id #uuid system of equations below. 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}kx+2y-4z=-4 \\ x-2y+5z=-6 \\ 10x+y+2z=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that  $x=-\frac{20}{3}$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $12-9k,$ find the value of $k.$"] ["question-8259ae37-435b-52c3-a2f0-cf085e62a133" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}k & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 & 5 \\ 10 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=12-9k\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & -4 \\ -6 & -2 & 5 \\ 8 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-6 & 5 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(-4-5)-2(-12-40)-4(-6+16) \\  & =36+104-40 \\  & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\frac{100}{12-9k}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $x=-\frac{20}{3}.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{100}{12-9k} & =-\frac{20}{3} \\ 15 & =-12+9k \\ 9k & =27 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8259ae37-435b-52c3-a2f0-cf085e62a133" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-9df02a6a-4e09-5087-b781-68996219ec42" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Then Cramer's rule states that

$$

$$

is the unique solution of the system, where

![](images/dc/dcda1374b4582e7978133bbf3cea0375b40095d353573f826a3bac7f212dfc03.svg)"] [17592186121047 :tutorial/content "To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z=9 \\ 2y+3z=7 \\ -8x+y+6z=0\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z=9 \\ 0x+2y+3z=7 \\ -8x+1y+6z=0\end{aligned}
$$

We start finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ -8 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(12-3)-2(0+24)+(0+16) \\  & =36-48+16 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $D_x,$ $D_y,$ and $D_z.$

- To find $D_x,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *first* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =9(12-3)-2(42-0)+(7-0) \\  & =81-84+7 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *second* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=|\begin{aligned}4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \\ -8 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(42)-9(0+24)+(0+56) \\  & =168-216+56 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_z,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *third* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 7 \\ -8 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 7 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}|+9\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(-7)-2(0+56)+9(0+16) \\  & =-28-112+144 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to the system is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩ & =⟨\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},\frac{{D}_{y}}{D},\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4}{4},\frac{8}{4},\frac{4}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186119998 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0] ["activity-80dffb9b-6686-5250-93b4-d26b471b47b4" :activity/id #uuid "80dffb9b-6686-5250-93b4-d26b471b47b4"] :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }k \\  & =2y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+2{e}^{x}\text{ }j-{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,-1) & =2(1)e\text{ }i+2e\text{ }j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =2e\,i+2e\,j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =⟨2e,2e,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$

$f(x,y,z)=e-3.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}))j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2})k \\  & =(y{e}^{xy}-2x)i+(x{e}^{xy})j+(-4z)k \\ ∇f(1,1,-1) & =((1){e}^{(1)(1)}-2(1))\text{ }i+(1){e}^{(1)(1)}\text{ }j+(-4)(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =(e-2)\text{ }i+e\text{ }j+4\text{ }k \\  & =⟨e-2,\,e,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨e-2,\,e,\,4⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{a-b}{c}=\frac{(e-2)-e}{4}=-\frac{1}{2}.$"] ["question-d5913a4b-d974-52bc-82fc-74c4bb66f8ca" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}y+16 & =4\sqrt{x}+y. \\ {z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-16.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,-1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}y-4\sqrt{x}-y)\text{ }k \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\text{ }i+({z}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2zy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,-1,3) & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}\text{ }i+({3}^{2}-1)\text{ }j+2(3)(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =-\,i+8\text{ }j-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,8,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,-1,3)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y+1,\,z-3⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-1,8,-6⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y+1,\,z-3⟩ & =0 \\ -(x-4)+8(y+1)-6(z-3) & =0 \\ -x+8y-6z+30 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-138bcf11-9efc-57ee-ad7b-ef21818db0e7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-74e95cce-259a-58bc-a6dc-cf74c51c993b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-5cbfe710-aab6-5e49-b65f-e20759621640" :question/problem "![](images/ff/ff93274daa7f179f86343e59b7cf277c0e70555fdfdd3cce113c3cba149b08ac.png)

An airplane $A$ is flying horizontally at a constant height of $800\,\text{m}$ above the ground. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the airplane and a nearby radar station $R$ is decreasing at a rate of $0.05$ radians per second. What is the speed of the aircraft as a function of $\theta ?$"] ["question-5cbfe710-aab6-5e49-b65f-e20759621640" :question/worked-solution "![](images/29/29d06d071e6983d3487426b08d5a5548a611134dcf116674d199f6d3de03f246.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the airplane's altitude, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the radar station and the airplane. The quantity $y=800$ meters does not change with time because the airplane stays at a constant altitude.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{800}{x} \\ x & =800\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(800\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-800{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-0.05$ (negative because the angle is decreasing). Substituting these values into the above, we reach

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Converting the given information from degrees to radians, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $\theta ={45}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{180}^{∘}}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$

$$

Let $y$ denote the vertical distance from the drone's projection to the starting point, and $z$ be the distance between the drone and the starting point, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={60}^{∘},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ z & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=4\text{km}/\text{h}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot 4≈4.62
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the speed of the drone is approximately $4.62\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$"] ["question-847493a1-e66a-5ae4-9cf4-e1e68a84c19e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{40}{x} \\ x & =40\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(40\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-12\,\text{ft/s}$ (negative because the horizontal distance is decreasing). Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =(-40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{12}{40} & =({csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{12}{40}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{10}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{10}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{rad/s}.$"] ["question-70ef2d3a-cac0-51c8-b6cc-9ac0c81e8893" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-2573d8ba-3c24-5f3f-9b87-70aaa707f60f" :question/problem "The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $3.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?"] ["question-2573d8ba-3c24-5f3f-9b87-70aaa707f60f" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-2573d8ba-3c24-5f3f-9b87-70aaa707f60f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-80690941-9f30-50e8-8d51-0076ff14e552" :answer-field/id #uuid Consider the vector field $F=-3x\,i-2y\,j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*"] [17592186180043 :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/00/00a9df76d0be8ffd33b2ee968b57a21eb1e6947af6e94505313f163b584f5769.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =(-6)\cdot 2 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=-12.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(-3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-2)\cdot 4 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot (-12)+2\cdot (-8)=-40.
$$"] [17592186180043 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186177927 :answer-field/correct 17592186177928] ["activity-578b92bf-466f-5207-945a-0605d797aa62" :activity/id #uuid Moreover, it is a positive cubic because if we were to expand the parentheses, the coefficient of the $x^3$ term would be positive:

$$
\dfrac{1}{9}({\color{blue}{x}}-3)({\color{red}{x}}+2)(x+3) = \dfrac 1 9\cdot {\color{blue}{x}}\cdot {\color{red}{x}}\cdot x +\cdots = \dfrac 1 9 x^3+\cdots
$$

The equation is already in factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are $x=3,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=-3.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{9}(0-3)(0+2)(0+3) \\  & =\frac{(-3)(2)(3)}{9} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-3,-2,3$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=-2,$ as follows:

![](images/71/7164fec4ddfa7b68489775b7feef639b61846188fc603186fe115f492dec606d.png)"] [17592186115111 :question/problem "Given that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x)=x^3-x^2-4x+4,$ graph the curve $y=f(x).$"] [17592186115111 :question/worked-solution "We are told that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x),$ which means that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ So, to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by  $(x-2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 & -4 & 4 \\  &  & 2 & 2 & -4 \\  & 1 & 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-2)({x}^{2}+x-2) \\  & =(x-2)(x-1)(x+2),\end{aligned}
$$

so the other two roots of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=-2.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0-2)(0-1)(0+2) \\  & =(-2)(-1)(2) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}(x-1)(x+2)(x+3)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot x\cdot x\cdot x+⋯=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}+⋯
$$

The equation is already in factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are $x=1,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=-3.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}(0-1)(0+2)(0+3) \\  & =\frac{(-1)(2)(3)}{2} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an inverted $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-3,-2,1$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=-3,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{6}(0+3)(0-2)(0-3) \\  & =-\frac{(3)(-2)(-3)}{6} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-3,2,3$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=-3,$ as follows:

We are told that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by  $(x+2):$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & -1 & 5 & 2 & -24 \\  &  & 2 & -14 & 24 \\  & -1 & 7 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+2)(-{x}^{2}+7x-12) \\  & =-(x+2)({x}^{2}-7x+12) \\  & =-(x+2)(x-3)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to zero, we find that the roots of $f(x)$ are $x=-2,$ $x=3,$ and $x=4.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0+2)(0-3)(0-4) \\  & =-(2)(-3)(-4) \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an  $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-2,3,4$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=-24,$ as follows:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+1)(-{x}^{2}+x+6) \\  & =-(x+1)({x}^{2}-x-6) \\  & =-(x+1)(x+2)(x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to zero, we find that the roots of $f(x)$ are $x=-1,x=-2,$ and $x=3.$

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0+1)(0+2)(0-3) \\  & =-(1)(2)(-3) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}

cubic function $y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d$ (where $a >0$) has a characteristic inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape, with $y$-values ranging from $-\infty$ to $+\infty.$ This means that every such function has *at least* one real root and *at most* three distinct roots.

For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of $y = x^3-x.$ Then we set $y=0$ to find the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product rule, we get three distinct roots $x=0, -1, 1.$ 

So, we draw an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shaped graph that passes through these three roots, as follows:

![](images/ec/ec5e7195e9584059755c8462de65ddd9bba038f38b18d5fe301dc392e1cdc9b9.png)"] [17592186116520 :tutorial/content "The graph of any cubic function $y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d$ (where $a <0$)  has a characteristic ${\textsf{S}}$-shape, with $y$-values ranging from $+\infty$ to $-\infty.$ This means that every such function has *at least* one real root and *at most* three distinct roots. 

For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of $y = -x^3+4x.$ Then we set $y=0$ to find the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{3}+4x & =0 \\ -x({x}^{2}-4) & =0 \\ -x(x-2)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So by the zero-product rule, we get three distinct roots $x=0, -2, 2.$

A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${A}^{T}=A$

II. ${A}^{2}=A$

III. $A$ is an orthogonal projection matrix"] ["question-3561f664-6b98-59a1-983b-c026ed37b09d" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $Q$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if ${Q}^{2}=Q$ and ${Q}^{T}=Q.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${A}^{T}=A.$

- Statement II is false. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}20 & 10 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{20}{9} & \frac{10}{9} \\ \frac{10}{9} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false since not both statements I and II are true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-3561f664-6b98-59a1-983b-c026ed37b09d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-f95e685a-8719-5a28-8f48-34b22e58d837" a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,P=\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}{p}_{11} & {p}_{12} & {p}_{13} \\ {p}_{21} & {p}_{22} & {p}_{23} \\ {p}_{31} & {p}_{32} & {p}_{33}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that the vector $a$ above spans ${S}^{⊥},$ and that $P$ is the orthogonal projection matrix of ${R}^{3}$ onto the subspace $S$, what is the value of ${p}_{12}+{p}_{33}?$"] ["question-555dd099-33d6-5089-b5ce-f831f111dabe" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the orthogonal projection matrix onto ${S}^{⊥}=\text{Span}\{a\}.$

Using the formula for the orthogonal projection matrix

$$
{P}_{{S}^{⊥}}=a({a}^{T}\,a)^{-1}{a}^{T},
$$

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={6}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that ${P}_{S}+{P}_{{S}^{⊥}}=I.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S} & =I-{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${p}_{12}+{p}_{33}=1+2=3.$"] ["question-555dd099-33d6-5089-b5ce-f831f111dabe" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d228661a-466c-50ca-9003-6059a883594a" $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}=-2.6.

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{9,0.025}=2.262.
$$

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=2.262\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.78}{110}}≈0.2
