["question-9a0fa4ee-d860-5a97-91a9-24370dbc9085" :question/math-academy-id "q-159376"] ["question-9a0fa4ee-d860-5a97-91a9-24370dbc9085" :question/problem "Let $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.4+0.2x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $({x}_{1},{y}_{1}),\,…,\,({x}_{12},{y}_{12})$ of $n=12$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, the mean square error of the model is $0.7,$ and ${S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}=18.9,$ find a $95%$ confidence interval for the slope of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.228)=0.025,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $10$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is given by 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}.
$$

*"] ["question-9a0fa4ee-d860-5a97-91a9-24370dbc9085" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.4+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=2.4+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}=0.2.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.228)=0.025.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{10,0.025}=2.228.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=2.228\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7}{18.9}}≈0.4
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=0.2\pm 0.4
$$"] ["question-9a0fa4ee-d860-5a97-91a9-24370dbc9085" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3cfd90c1-e81f-5461-89ae-4d8978dbf8e2" :answer-field/id #uuid Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=28,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.007,$ find a $90%$ confidence interval for the slope of the regression line.

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=-4-0.1x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]}}.
$$

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

$$

$$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

["question-c2bc734f-9a4b-543f-ac01-84af782ea390" :question/math-academy-id "q-159518"] ["question-c2bc734f-9a4b-543f-ac01-84af782ea390" :question/problem "| **Height ($x$)** | **$67$** | **$70$** | The table above shows the heights, in inches, and corresponding shoe sizes of four randomly selected men. The corresponding linear regression line fitted using this sample is $\overset{^}{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x.$ 
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=71.5,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.338,$ find a $90%$ confidence interval for the slope of the regression line.  

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.92)=0.05,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the slope is given by* 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}.
$$"] ["question-c2bc734f-9a4b-543f-ac01-84af782ea390" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=-26.6+0.5x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}=0.5.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.92)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.05}=2.92.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(67-71.5)^{2}+(70-71.5)^{2}+(73-71.5)^{2}+(76-71.5)^{2} \\  & =20.25+2.25+2.25+20.25 \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=2.92\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.338}{45}}≈0.3
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=0.5\pm 0.3
$$"] ["question-c2bc734f-9a4b-543f-ac01-84af782ea390" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-086dbd14-306d-5d79-b710-e38344655d09" :answer-field/id #uuid random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population. 

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x.
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$  are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} -  \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x},
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i,$ and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}).
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following: 

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as 

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize, 

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,$

- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1,$ and

- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0.$

In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the slope parameter $\beta_1.$"] [17592186173229 :tutorial/content "Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the slope $\beta_1$ of our model can be written as

$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by 

$$

$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

$$

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})\overset{―}{y} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\overset{―}{x} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}n\overset{―}{x} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\overset{―}{y}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x}){y}_{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using our result for $S_{xy},$ we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{{\beta }_{1}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{{S}_{xx}}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
k_i = \dfrac{ x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}.
$$

The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{1}}] & =\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}\text{E}[{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}({\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\beta }_{0}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}+{\beta }_{1}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & ={\beta }_{0}\cdot 0+{\beta }_{1}\cdot 1 \\  & ={\beta }_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{^}{{\beta }_{1}}] & =\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{y}_{i}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }^{2} \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}\cdot {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{k}_{i}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{{S}_{xx}}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "$$
{x}_{1}=9,\,{x}_{2}=-8,\,{x}_{3}=-1,\,{x}_{4}=4,\,{x}_{5}=2
$$

Given the values ${x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4},\,{x}_{5}$ above, we have

${\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}=$ {{field-1}}."] ["question-f030361e-8a29-5e63-bca8-4e28e1ba5da0" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}$ equals ${x}_{i}$ when ${x}_{i}>0$ and equals $0$ otherwise. Thus, the sum 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}
$$

adds up only the positive values.

We evaluate the indicator function for each ${x}_{i}:$

- $1[{x}_{1}>0]=1[9>0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{2}>0]=1[-8>0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{3}>0]=1[-1>0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{4}>0]=1[4>0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{5}>0]=1[2>0]=1$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i} & =1\cdot 9+0\cdot (-8)+0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 4+1\cdot 2 \\  & =9+0+0+4+2 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f030361e-8a29-5e63-bca8-4e28e1ba5da0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a" :answer-field/id #uuid "034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a"] ["answer-156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59" :answer/id #uuid "156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59"] ["answer-156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59" :answer/value "15"] ["answer-field-034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a" :answer-field/correct "answer-156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59"] ["answer-field-034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a" :answer-field/choices "answer-156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59"] ["question-f030361e-8a29-5e63-bca8-4e28e1ba5da0" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a"] [17592186166969 :knowledge-point/questions "question-f030361e-8a29-5e63-bca8-4e28e1ba5da0"] ["question-e3d61585-203e-5ae2-ba7d-32b154b3cecc" :question/id #uuid "e3d61585-203e-5ae2-ba7d-32b154b3cecc"] ["question-e3d61585-203e-5ae2-ba7d-32b154b3cecc" :question/math-academy-id "q-347438"] ["question-e3d61585-203e-5ae2-ba7d-32b154b3cecc" :question/problem "$$

$$

Given the values ${x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4},\,{x}_{5}$ above, we have

${\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot (2{x}_{i})+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 1=$ {{field-1}}."] ["question-e3d61585-203e-5ae2-ba7d-32b154b3cecc" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot (2{x}_{i})+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 1$ equals $2{x}_{i}$ when ${x}_{i}\ge 0$ and equals $1$ when ${x}_{i}<0.$ Thus, the sum

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot (2{x}_{i})+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 1
$$

adds $2{x}_{i}$ for nonnegative values and $1$ for negative values.

We evaluate the indicator function for each ${x}_{i}:$

- $1[{x}_{1}\ge 0]=1[-6\ge 0]=0,$ $1[{x}_{1}<0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{2}\ge 0]=1[-1\ge 0]=0,$ $1[{x}_{2}<0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{3}\ge 0]=1[0\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{3}<0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{4}\ge 0]=1[4\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{4}<0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{5}\ge 0]=1[7\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{5}<0]=0$

Therefore,

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches and reflections, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches and reflections, followed by vertical translations.

To get $y=-3f(4x),$ we could apply the following steps: 

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}3):$ Stretch $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{4}$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(4x).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}4):$ Stretch $y=f(4x)$ by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=3f(4x).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}2):$ Reflect $y=3f(4x)$ across the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=-3f(4x).
$$

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

$\,$ $(\text{T}3)\to (\text{T}4)\to (\text{T}2).$"] ["question-1f3c3035-69e9-5d03-a0fc-4433cacd4260" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] The diagram above shows the function $y=f(x).$ Which of the following gives the graph of $y=-f(-2x)?$"] ["question-689e7bfc-91b5-5578-9523-c9029e296a11" :question/worked-solution "To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches and reflections, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches and reflections, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=f(-(2x))
$$

To plot $y=-f(-(2x)),$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(2x).$

![](images/7d/7d76ce80b4212d0cb6cd8b64c424492dd46cad3819ce3cba17bab22c4df115f5.png)

- Then, reflect the result across the $y$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(-2x).$

![](images/de/ded37839584d99725ab44ebfb4e60e05ea162da6a3845817aa96f6904d67146a.png)

- Finally, reflect the result across the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=-f(-2x).$

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches and reflections, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches and reflections, followed by vertical translations.

To plot $y=-f(x-2)-4,$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Translate it by $2$ units to the right to get the graph of $y=f(x-2).$

![](images/48/482f1dc55995a299b21894c0ec191c0f8fb8213038cdc5f80da1e77a0d64af4e.png)

- Then, reflect the result across the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=-f(x-2).$

![](images/a2/a2832ebdf82e2a7bfddccf24fd598758e1ce86fc0726f9c128503574b09fcd0b.png)

- Finally, translate it down by $4$ units to get the graph of $y=-f(x-2)-4.$

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}x).$

- Then, translate the result by $2$ units to the right to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-2)).$

![](images/ab/ab1f210741e01139618dc2fa1347cf1591cb90ca4f67906b89ebc7df29d77f32.png)

- Finally, reflect the result across the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=-f(\frac{1}{2}(x-2)).$

curve $y= f(x),$ there are two types of reflections we can apply to it:

1\. Reflection across the $y$-axis. This is a transformation of the form 

  $$
  y=f(-x).
  $$

2\. Reflection across the $x$-axis. This is a transformation of the form 

  $$
  y=-f(x).
  $$

For example, let's consider the function $y=f(x)$ below. 

![](images/69/6931216dd63985631394e3f3f2fe59246ddd810ecce5af0f0c7ad18b8634133b.png)

The graph of $y=f(-x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the $y$-axis, and it looks as follows:

![](images/e2/e2274a68c25ed14ba93410fe87d672f85b839b7214b30e80d34a3ae28f47ef03.png)

 

The graph of $y=-f(x)$ is a reflection of $y=f(x)$ in the $x$-axis, and it looks as follows:

![](images/ee/eee560bdd17899d55cdaea35204e9963ae9f0148f0ef897173e6250a3eb874b3.png)

  

We can also combine reflections with other graph transformations. Let's see how."] [17592186157496 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0] [17592186128857 :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as

$$
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)}  f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integrals, we see that the domain of integration $R = R_1\cup R_2,$ where $R_1$ and $R_2$ are type I regions, is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{1} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 1,\,\,x-1\le z\le {y}^{2}\}, \\ {R}_{2} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,y\le x\le 1,\,\,x-1\le z\le {y}^{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\int_a^b \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{x-1}^{y^2} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/c8/c8bfd933472e1944f63b1295bda7fc324311ea2ca2ada3636e9f5ab82e4e5fc5.png)

The region $D$ consists of two type II regions in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D =
\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq y \leq 0, \quad y^2 \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
\:\cup\:
\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad y \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the lower boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=y^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad

$$

$$

$$

$$

Notice that the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$

$$

and the top boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $z=z(y),$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,⟹\,z={e}^{y}.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le z\le {e}^{y}\},

![](images/c9/c94cfc38872dfe0673e112e09feec7781ab4f247f08932d1d8ecd167b4a99d32.png)

The elements $1,2,3,4,5,8$ are in either $X$ or $Y,$ or both. Therefore, the union of $X$ and $Y$ is

$$

$$"] [17592186157084 :question/problem "Given the sets $X = \{2, 5, 7, 8\},$ $Y = \{1, 3, 5\},$ and $Z = \{2, 4, 6, 8\},$ find $X \cup Y,$ $Y \cup Z,$ and $Z \cup X.$"] [17592186157084 :question/worked-solution "The union $X \cup Y$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $X$ or $Y,$ or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}X\cup Y & =\{2,5,7,8\}\cup \{1,3,5\} \\  & =\{1,2,3,5,7,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

The union $Y \cup Z$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $Y$ or $Z,$ or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Y\cup Z & =\{1,3,5\}\cup \{2,4,6,8\} \\  & =\{1,2,3,4,5,6,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$

The union $Z \cup X$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $Z$ or $X,$ or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Z\cup X & =\{2,4,6,8\}\cup \{2,5,7,8\} \\  & =\{2,4,5,6,7,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186157085 :question/problem "Let $A$ and $B$ be the set of all multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ and the set of all multiples of $6$ that are greater than $0,$ respectively. What is $A \cup B?$"] [17592186157085 :question/worked-solution "The multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
A = \{ 4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32, 36 \ldots \}.
$$

Likewise, multiples of $6$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
B = \{ 6,12,18,24,30,36,\ldots \}.
$$

Now, $A \cup B$ is the *union* of $A$ and $B,$ which means that we want to find the elements that are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cup B & =\{4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,…\}\cup \{6,12,18,24,30,36,…\} \\  & =\{4,6,8,12,16,18,20,24,28,30,32,36,…\}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186233058 :question/problem "![](images/1f/1f3d0b514bc4ec701b6ac755b82cec7246a7a819400108e1733759eb0a2fec86.png)

:question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be the set of all non-negative integer powers of $3$ and the set of all multiples of $4$ greater than $0,$ respectively. What is $X\cup Y?$"] ["question-b7be71bb-2a94-5959-b6e1-bd279930afab" :question/worked-solution "The non-negative integer powers of $3$ are

$$
X=\{1,3,9,27,…\}.
$$

Likewise, multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
Y=\{4,8,12,16,20,24,…\}.
$$

Now, $X\cup Y$ is the *union* of $X$ and $Y,$ which means that we want to find the elements that are in either $X$ or $Y,$ or both. In other words, $X\cup Y$ denotes the set of natural numbers that are either powers of $3$ or multiples of  $4.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}X\cup Y & =\{1,3,9,27,…\}\cup \{4,8,12,16,20,24,…\} \\  & =\{1,3,4,8,9,12,16,20,24,27,…\}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b7be71bb-2a94-5959-b6e1-bd279930afab" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a097d8b4-61d7-5c24-b4fc-50630068161e" :answer-field/id #uuid Notice that ![](images/a7/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) belongs to both ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) and ![](images/65/65ada9c919fe5c4bee19fb4cafff28ed46a36bf6fc90b4cecf70e0fa02386ce0.svg) but we list it only once in ![](images/bb/bbb285be6a3e138649aa4a514c34823a6b39d094dca3427eb34eb4a326854fcf.svg) In a set, each distinct element is written only once."] [17592186158478 :tutorial/content "Although Venn diagrams can be useful to visualize unions, we do not have to draw a Venn diagram every time we wish to compute a union.

For example, let's again consider the sets $A = \{ a,b,c \}$ and $B = \{ b, d, e \}.$ This time, we will compute the union $A \cup B$ without using a Venn diagram. We just need to find all the elements that are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

So, we will start with the elements of $A,$ and then go through the elements of $B$ to look for any elements that we do not already have. Remember that we are looking for elements that we do *not* already have in $A.$

- For the element $b \in B,$ we have $b \in A. \quad \color{red}\times$

- For the element $d \in B,$ we have $d \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- For the element $e \in B,$ we have $e \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

So, to get the union, we need to take the elements of $A$ and also include $d$ and $e.$

Therefore, the union of $A$ and $B$ is

$$
A \cup B = \{ a,b,c,d,e \}.
$$"] [17592186157483 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-8fe28743-a486-54a9-8fdd-bcbf858bcbbf" :question/id #uuid "8fe28743-a486-54a9-8fdd-bcbf858bcbbf"] ["question-8fe28743-a486-54a9-8fdd-bcbf858bcbbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-139035"] ["question-8fe28743-a486-54a9-8fdd-bcbf858bcbbf" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2{e}^{t/2},\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡3].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis."] ["question-8fe28743-a486-54a9-8fdd-bcbf858bcbbf" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t/2})={e}^{t/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t/2})}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{t}(1+{e}^{t})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t/2}\cdot {e}^{t/2}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{e}^{t}.$ Then, $\text{d}u={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi \cdot {\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}({4}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}(8-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}(4-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8fe28743-a486-54a9-8fdd-bcbf858bcbbf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c5e8aa5a-ac76-5fe7-8cbb-d1e2111d6174" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{5} & = \\ 3\cdot y\cdot \sqrt{5} & = \\ 3y\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-09d71431-cc0e-5153-8350-c0a86eafb77b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-391f389b-05b6-594c-95d0-cca64d0e6b52" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

:question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{20{n}^{5}}.$"] ["question-f380d0a4-2ab4-5ffd-9f65-88568a9b06d4" :question/worked-solution "We first write $20{n}^{5}$ as the product $4{n}^{4}\cdot 5n$ which contains a perfect square $(4{n}^{4}).$ Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{20{n}^{5}} & = \\ \sqrt{4{n}^{4}\cdot 5n} & = \\ \sqrt{(2{n}^{2})^{2}\cdot 5n} & = \\ \sqrt{(2{n}^{2})^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5n} & = \\ |2{n}^{2}|\cdot \sqrt{5n} & = \\ |2|\cdot |{n}^{2}|\cdot \sqrt{5n} & = \\ 2\cdot |{n}^{2}|\cdot \sqrt{5n}\end{aligned}
$$

A squared number is always positive or zero, and the absolute value of any positive (or zero) number is itself, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |{n}^{2}|\cdot \sqrt{5n} & = \\ 2\cdot {n}^{2}\cdot \sqrt{5n} & = \\ 2{n}^{2}\sqrt{5n}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f380d0a4-2ab4-5ffd-9f65-88568a9b06d4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5f773159-8463-5e37-81f8-8746b86bfcf3" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-e6203f86-9cf0-5174-84bf-8575e36ffa78" :question/math-academy-id "q-127310"] ["question-e6203f86-9cf0-5174-84bf-8575e36ffa78" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{2y}+4x,\,{x}^{7}-{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 0,-1\le y\le 0.$"] ["question-e6203f86-9cf0-5174-84bf-8575e36ffa78" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/09/09acd3df62b333bdaeb7553599507d4dbad7412ef2770b00e8fc8855b38a774e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{2y}+4x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}-{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,dy \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e6203f86-9cf0-5174-84bf-8575e36ffa78" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-64fabadb-f80e-5526-b940-02e3d7342ff0" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

$$

*"] ["question-851fa16f-b92a-5672-9bbf-979f258829aa" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=5+0.4x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{{{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{⏟}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=5+0.4x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=5.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(T>3.355)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{8,0.005}=3.355.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=3.355\cdot \sqrt{3.7\cdot (\frac{1}{10}+\frac{{4.3}^{2}}{330})}≈2.5
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$

$$"] ["question-851fa16f-b92a-5672-9bbf-979f258829aa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-caf088fc-e014-5a09-8ceb-3ba512fc68e7" :answer-field/id #uuid The table above shows the heights, in inches, and corresponding shoe sizes of four randomly selected men. The corresponding linear regression line fitted using this sample is $\overset{^}{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x.$ 
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=71.5,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.338,$ find a $90%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.  

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.920)=0.05,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is* 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}.
$$"] ["question-69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=-26.6+0.5x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=-26.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.920)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.05}=2.920.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(67-71.5)^{2}+(70-71.5)^{2}+(73-71.5)^{2}+(76-71.5)^{2} \\  & =20.25+2.25+2.25+20.25 \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.920\cdot \sqrt{0.338\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{71.5}^{2}}{45})}≈18.1
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=-26.6\pm 18.1
$$"] ["question-69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5f3ed31d-762f-57be-a238-32e2c1426527" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

The table above shows the ages, in years, and the number of hours each of four randomly selected adults slept last night. The corresponding linear regression line fitted using this sample is $\overset{^}{\,y}=0.6+0.2x.$
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=38,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.0125,$ find an $80%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line. 

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>1.886)=0.1,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is* 

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}.
$$"] ["question-4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\overset{^}{\,y}={\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{1}x=0.6+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overset{\text{margin of error}}{\overset{⏞}{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\overset{^}{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\overset{^}{\,y}=0.6+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}=0.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $80%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.8=0.2\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.1.
$$

We are given that $P(T>1.886)=0.1.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.1}=1.886.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(34-38)^{2}+(36-38)^{2}+(40-38)^{2}+(42-38)^{2} \\  & =16+4+4+16 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=1.886\cdot \sqrt{0.0125\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{38}^{2}}{40})}≈1.3
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\overset{^}{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=0.6\pm 1.3
$$"] ["question-4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a"] [17592186192683 :knowledge-point/questions "question-8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57"] [17592186193891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population. 

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x.
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$  are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} -  \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x},
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i,$ and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}).
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following: 

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as 

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize, 

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,$

- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1,$ and

- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0.$

Note the following:

- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0,$ given by

$$

where we have:

- $\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.

- $S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

For each $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ let

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the common ratio satisfies $r^5 = 32.$"] [17592186147226 :question/problem "Find the common ratio of the geometric sequence whose fourth term is $2$ and whose seventh term is $-686.$"] [17592186147226 :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =-343 \\ {r}^{3} & =(-7)^{3} \\ r & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186147229 :question/problem "The third term of a geometric sequence is $80$ and its fifth term is $20.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive."] [17592186147229 :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

"To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms ${a}_{m}$ and ${a}_{n},$ we use the formula

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}.
$$

In this case, we're given ${a}_{5}=6$ and ${a}_{2}=48.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=2$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-2} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{6}{48} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by solving the equation for $r,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ {r}^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7794f339-0fd4-50d9-a0ab-1ce4d82318cb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1e4ad903-4e09-5e2b-9085-556ef9945de6" :answer-field/id #uuid This is a little trickier than before because we're not given two consecutive terms, but let's try to figure it out. First, let's denote

$$
a_2 = 4, \qquad a_4 = 64.
$$

The $n$th term of a geometric sequence is given by:

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}
$$

Applying this formula with $n=2$ and $n=4$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{2-1}={a}_{1}r \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{4-1}={a}_{1}{r}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using that $a_2 = 4$ and $a_4 = 64$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}r & =4 \\ {a}_{1}{r}^{3} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

So now, we have a system of equations to solve. To solve this system, we *divide* the *second* equation above by the *first* equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{r}^{3}}{{a}_{1}r} & =\frac{64}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{{a}_{1}}{r}^{3}}{\cancel{{a}_{1}}r} & =\frac{64}{4} \\ \frac{{r}^{3}}{r} & =16 \\ {r}^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r.$ Note that $16 = 4^2,$ and so we can solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since our sequence must be positive.

Therefore, the common ratio $r=4.$"] [17592186148693 :tutorial/content "Finding the common ratio by solving a system of equations is quite a lot of work. Is there an easier way?

Indeed there is. Given two terms of a geometric sequence $a_n$ and $a_m,$ the formula for $r$ is as follows:

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}
$$

Let's demonstrate how this works. Suppose that we have a geometric sequence whose second term is $3$ and whose fifth term is $192.$ What is the common ratio?

Here, we're given $a_5 = 192$ and $a_2 = 3.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=2$ into the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-2} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{192}{3} \\ {r}^{3} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r$ by noting that $64 = 4^3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3} & =64 \\ {r}^{3} & ={4}^{3} \\ r & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So the common ratio is $r=4.$

$$

the **residual** for a particular observation $(x, y)$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - f(x) \\
&= y - y^(^)
\end{aligned}
$$

We subtract the *estimated* value predicted by the model from the actual *observed* value.

To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature $x$ (measured in $^\circ \mathrm{F}$) and the resulting daily ice cream sales $y$ (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below.

![](images/fc/fc149b8d911a7a9863df9cc25c635d6155accd676e83e335a65d9083596b779b.png)

Suppose the equation of the regression line is

$$
y= 2.5 x +165
$$

Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates $\color{red}(82, 360)$ (shown in red on our graph).

First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates ${\color{red}(82, 360)}$, our actual value is

$$
y = {\color{red}360}
$$

Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^(^) &= 2.5x + 165 \\
&= 2.5(82) + 165 \\
&= 370
\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/38/3843c71b50251ae035378507ffb22cfade48dff8e1544d8e1317e4e6d611f7a1.png)

Finally, we compute the residual:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - y^(^) \\
&= 360 - 370 \\
&=-10
\end{aligned}
$$

The residual tells us that the linear model *overestimates* the true volume of ice cream sales by $\[math]10$ when the outside temperature is $82^\circ\,\textrm{F}$."] [17592186177048 :tutorial/content "A **residual plot** displays the values of the independent variable along the horizontal axis and the residuals along the vertical axis.

$$

First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z &=9 \\ 0x+2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+1y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ -8 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(12-3)-2(0+24)+(0+16) \\  & =36-48+16 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $D_x,$ $D_y,$ and $D_z.$

- To find $D_x,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *first* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =9(12-3)-2(42-0)+(7-0) \\  & =81-84+7 \\  & =4\end{aligned}

- To find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *second* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=|\begin{aligned}4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \\ -8 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(42)-9(0+24)+(0+56) \\  & =168-216+56 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_z,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *third* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 7 \\ -8 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 7 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}|+9\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(-7)-2(0+56)+9(0+16) \\  & =-28-112+144 \\  & =4\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and

$$

$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2$. The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i$, and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$

$$

This is a little trickier than before because we're not given two consecutive terms, but let's try to figure it out. First, let's denote

$$
a_2 = 4, \qquad a_4 = 64
$$

The $n$th term of a geometric sequence is given by:

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}
$$

Applying this formula with $n=2$ and $n=4$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{2} &= a_{1}r^{2 - 1} = a_{1}r \\
a_{4} &= a_{1}r^{4 - 1} = a_{1}r^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using that $a_2 = 4$ and $a_4 = 64$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1}r &= 4 \\
a_{1}r^{3} &= 64
\end{aligned}
$$

So now, we have a system of equations to solve. To solve this system, we *divide* the *second* equation above by the *first* equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a_{1}r^{3}}{a_{1}r} &= \frac{64}{4} \\
\frac{a_{1}r^{3}}{a_{1}r} &= \frac{64}{4} \\
\frac{r^{3}}{r} &= 16 \\
r^{2} &= 16
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r$. Note that $16 = 4^2$, and so we can solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{2} &= 16 \\
r^{2} &= 4^{2} \\
r &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since our sequence must be positive.

Therefore, the common ratio $r=4$."] [17592186148693 :tutorial/content "Finding the common ratio by solving a system of equations is quite a lot of work. Is there an easier way?

Indeed there is. Given two terms of a geometric sequence $a_n$ and $a_m$, the formula for $r$ is as follows:

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}
$$

Let's demonstrate how this works. Suppose that we have a geometric sequence whose second term is $3$ and whose fifth term is $192$. What is the common ratio?

Here, we're given $a_5 = 192$ and $a_2 = 3$. Substituting $n=5$ and $m=2$ into the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{5 - 2} &= \frac{a_{5}}{a_{2}} \\
r^{3} &= \frac{192}{3} \\
r^{3} &= 64
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve the above equation for $r$ by noting that $64 = 4^3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{3} &= 64 \\
r^{3} &= 4^{3} \\
r &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

So the common ratio is $r=4$.

When dealing with an equation that is **cubic** in $r$ (i.e., contains an $r^3$), then there is only one possible answer, unlike the squared case ($r^2$) where we have to pick from either positive or negative."]]}

:answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186533887}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Given that $y=\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

${y}^{′}=\frac{(x-2)^{4}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}[$
{{field-1}}$]$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-2)^{5})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)-({x}^{2}+3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)-({x}^{2}+3x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{x-2}-(2x+3) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x-2}-(2x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y[\frac{5}{x-2}-(2x+3)]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}[\frac{5}{x-2}-(2x+3)] \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{5}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}[\frac{5-(x-2)(2x+3)}{x-2}] \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{4}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}[5-(x-2)(2x+3)] \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{4}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}[5-(2{x}^{2}-x-6)] \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{4}}{{e}^{{x}^{2}+3x}}[11+x-2{x}^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186534079 :question/id #uuid "deb7ada4-14d9-5457-acd5-ef77477a4e36" :question/math-academy-id "q-138832" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71dd9228-4b05-54d9-aeb2-3bdabf89e0e9" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Quotient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f947482-c2c6-568d-82f0-29af6bfba254" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}+8{x}^{3}+x+5" :db/id 17592186533253} {:answer/id #uuid "3e350aae-2cd2-5f81-8e5d-74dec200744b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}^{4}+8{x}^{3}+x+5" :db/id 17592186533284} {:answer/id #uuid "67b07a11-17f0-5c4c-a4ca-8e59d532b7ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}+16{x}^{3}+x+5" :db/id 17592186533382} {:answer/id #uuid "89588797-26b1-5b42-8b21-2029da27dbba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}^{4}+16{x}^{3}+2x+8" :db/id 17592186533468} {:answer/id #uuid "b35826d5-c07d-51fb-931e-4b0d6ab4dd47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}+16{x}^{3}+2x+8" :db/id 17592186533574}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "67b07a11-17f0-5c4c-a4ca-8e59d532b7ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}+16{x}^{3}+x+5" :db/id 17592186533382} :answer-field/id #uuid "0d94c7c1-de0e-5fb5-af87-71126c21e380" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186533784}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{6}}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}g(x)}{(x+8)^{7}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{6}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{6}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{4}+2x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+8)^{6}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{4}+2x-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+2x-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =4{x}^{3}+2-6\cdot \frac{1}{x+8} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =4{x}^{3}+2-\frac{6}{x+8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(4{x}^{3}+2-\frac{6}{x+8})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{6}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{6}}(4{x}^{3}+2-\frac{6}{x+8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{6}}(\frac{(4{x}^{3}+2)(x+8)-6}{x+8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{7}}((4{x}^{3}+2)(x+8)-6) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}}{(x+8)^{7}}(4{x}^{4}+32{x}^{3}+2x+16-6) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{4}+2x}(2{x}^{4}+16{x}^{3}+x+5)}{(x+8)^{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=2{x}^{4}+16{x}^{3}+x+5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186534090 :question/id #uuid "f3859b1c-a23b-517a-bfe5-a836f749be10" :question/math-academy-id "q-138834" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71dd9228-4b05-54d9-aeb2-3bdabf89e0e9" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Quotient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "42e00fa1-2d53-53c2-91c2-dbaf97414222" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "17{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}+15" :db/id 17592186533296} {:answer/id #uuid "84e65e07-d407-5744-b09c-1d7419c5f733" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "15{x}^{2}-3{x}^{3}+15" :db/id 17592186533452} {:answer/id #uuid "949b2307-7470-54c1-a231-4a7923ae08c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "15{x}^{2}+3{x}^{3}+15" :db/id 17592186533499} {:answer/id #uuid "9f5538e4-cb5c-53d2-8282-324285197339" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "17{x}^{2}+3{x}^{3}+15" :db/id 17592186533525} {:answer/id #uuid "cffa59f6-f8b3-5069-84a6-83cd2e84beae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}+15" :db/id 17592186533646}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "42e00fa1-2d53-53c2-91c2-dbaf97414222" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "17{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}+15" :db/id 17592186533296} :answer-field/id #uuid "f81d8766-b273-5742-81e1-135f6f4971d0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186533963}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x-1}}{(1-3x)^{6}}g(x)+\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-3x)^{5}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-3x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot (2x)-5\cdot \frac{1}{1-3x}\cdot (-3) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{15}{1-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{15}{1-3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{15}{1-3x}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{15}{1-3x})+\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}(\frac{2{x}^{2}(1-3x)+15({x}^{2}+1)}{({x}^{2}+1)(1-3x)})+\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}(\frac{17{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}+15}{({x}^{2}+1)(1-3x)})+\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x-1}}{(1-3x)^{6}}(17{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}+15)+\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{x}}{(1-3x)^{5}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=17{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}+15.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064148 :question/id #uuid "e0cec84d-96cf-5fed-ba05-a5cfc57841a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9847"} :knowledge-point/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2}(g(x)-({x}^{2}+4)\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\sqrt{({x}^{2}+4)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3/2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3/2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{3/2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\cdot 2x-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}(\frac{6x-({x}^{2}+4)\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2({x}^{2}+4)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}(\frac{6x-({x}^{2}+4)\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(6x-({x}^{2}+4)\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\sqrt{({x}^{2}+4)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=6x.
$$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f947482-c2c6-568d-82f0-29af6bfba254" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{x}^{4}+8{x}^{3}+x+5" :db/id function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caef414d-4f2a-5504-9b92-39a03d2f3c8f" :step/math-academy-id "8850f22e-33ee-545a-8f5e-4dc37bda3b30" :step/math-academy-id 37038} {:db/id 17592186065210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

$$
y =  f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)},
$$

we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms: 

$$
\ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b
$$

 

For example, let's compute $y',$ where the function $y$ is given by

$$
y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-2x)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{1-2x}\cdot (-2)-3\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute our expression for $y,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(\frac{2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)}{(1-2x)(x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(-4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+8x-7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7)}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8cf6e625-669a-5fda-b756-e1ce091eaa93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6090 :tutorial/title "Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "2141558f-a6d2-515d-902a-620581d72401" :step/math-academy-id 37041 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065208}}] :activity/title "Further Logarithmic Differentiation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064435} {:db/id 17592186065206 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caef414d-4f2a-5504-9b92-39a03d2f3c8f" :step/math-academy-id 37035 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065207}} {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$

{:db/id 17592186166562 :question/id #uuid "5888d4ce-bc45-540b-afa0-901008abfcde" :question/math-academy-id "e-21787" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"}] :question/problem "Let $F(x) = \cos(2x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \in [0,\pi)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+\pi) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

II. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

III. $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $\pi$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+\pi)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in[0,\pi).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi$-periodicity:

$$
f(x+\pi)=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $\pi$-periodic, because for any $x\in\mathbb{R},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+\pi )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(x+\pi ))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+2\pi )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\pi$-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{\pi }{2})=F(\frac{\pi }{2})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=f(0)=F(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \neq f(x)$ for $x=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"."} {:db/id 17592186049091} {:db/id 17592186049353} {:db/id 17592186050172} {:db/id 17592186167264 :question/id #uuid "a8290119-5783-5de1-8f8a-4d7cbbad292c" :question/math-academy-id "q-338488" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8f77c573-2e4c-536e-af1e-09bf69080857" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186164763} {:answer/id #uuid "def9c8ed-19ee-58e5-969f-de9782068ef0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186164764} {:answer/id #uuid "37f67a97-5731-525d-8eea-9e2adde19ccb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186164765} {:answer/id #uuid "7a4cd2e6-0da4-5d24-b3e3-7bda7e4d5751" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186164766} {:answer/id #uuid "7ceba1a1-ec81-5071-86b8-40131cdb7eed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186164767}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "8f77c573-2e4c-536e-af1e-09bf69080857" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186164763} :answer-field/id #uuid "757753c4-07c4-5df7-886c-f4e557b69cad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186164762}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $F(x)=2x$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,3)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+2)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,3).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+6)=f((x+3)+3)=f(x+3)=f(x)\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=4.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4)=f(1+3)=f(1)=F(1)=2(1)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4)=2(4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=4.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2)=f(4)=f(1+3)=f(1)=F(1)=2(1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

while 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2)=F(2)=2(2)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+2)\ne f(2)$ for $x=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186167265 :question/id #uuid "97cef292-5a85-5947-928d-d07517a20540" :question/math-academy-id "q-338489"} {:db/id 17592186311951 :question/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- **II.** $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- **III.** $f(x)=f(x-2\pi )$ for all $x\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\pi ).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi $-periodicity: 

$$
f(x+\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{3\pi }{2})=f(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi )=f(\frac{\pi }{2})=F(\frac{\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{3\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =f((x-\pi )+\pi ) \\  & =f(x-\pi ) \\  & =f((x-2\pi )+\pi ) \\  & =f(x-2\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186314968 :question/id #uuid "68a9f1f0-e085-5ed7-bf4c-69fbdf0774fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-340510"} {:db/id 17592186315068
