$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{2x}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{2x}{y} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}

$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=-x+7y$ and $v(x,y)=3x-y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =7 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 7 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3-7\cdot 1 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}xy \\ \frac{x}{y}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

 
Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y} \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2v}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "96a24d2f-6bfd-5bae-b385-4ad5b9f4b243"} {:db/id 17592186527250 :step/content {:db/id 17592186527136 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1da512ca-3f7f-55fa-ba92-0e0c6f6c21be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-v" :db/id 17592186526563} {:answer/id #uuid "3f9f7694-d0a1-5a9c-8f7b-8ada526129f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{u}{3v}" :db/id 17592186526627} {:answer/id #uuid "a0e1f31b-7a73-5f60-aa37-ebb1960532b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{v}{u}" :db/id 17592186526815} {:answer/id #uuid "c4ff2ce6-b380-5ab9-9fa2-41399e5c2bf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3v}" :db/id 17592186526881} {:answer/id #uuid "cabf98b2-4e8b-519a-86a9-7f344c20fcb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3v" :db/id 17592186526892}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186526881} :answer-field/id #uuid "3aa3cd04-7b64-5645-9bfe-bb149f8d1b73" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186527040}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "216ab53f-9c7f-5387-ad09-67452d907209" :question/math-academy-id "q-160572" :question/problem "Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+3{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u-2v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "631c1ffc-cc2d-54ee-9534-d0fd945d1a0f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186527250}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 17592186129892 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130327 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to compute the tangent plane to the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$ 

As an example, consider the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2 +y^2+z.
$$

 

Suppose that we wish to find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=  (1,1, 2).$ 

Evaluating $f$ at the point $(1,1,2),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = (1)^2 +(1)^2+2 = 4.
$$

 

So, the equation of our level surface is

$$
x^2 +y^2+z = 4.
$$

Now, to find the equation of the tangent plane to this surface at $(1,1,2),$ we can use the following result:

  *Given a hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ and a point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)$ that lies in the domain of $f$, the gradient $\nabla \! f (\mathbf x_0)$ is normal to the tangent plane of the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k$ at the point $\mathbf x_0$*. 

![](images/11/1140e80fbb2efd684311cb7625e5b0be361d6fb951036253f57b9e51234de3ee.png)

       

We can now find the equation of the tangent plane to our level surface.

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $\mathbf x_0 = (1,1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}\,i+{f}_{y}\,j+{f}_{z}\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(1,1,2) & =2(1)\text{ }i+2(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =2\text{ }i+2\text{ }j+k \\  & =⟨2,\,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally,  we write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\nabla f(1,1,2) \cdot \langle x-1, \: y-1, \: z-2 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\langle 2,\:2,\:1\rangle\cdot \langle x-1, y-1, z-2\rangle &= 0\[3pt]
      2(x-1)+ 2(y-1) + (z-2) & =0\
      2x +2y +z -6&=0   
}

17592186130327 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to compute the tangent plane to the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$ 

As an example, consider the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2 +y^2+z.
$$

 

Suppose that we wish to find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=  (1,1, 2).$ 

Evaluating $f$ at the point $(1,1,2),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = (1)^2 +(1)^2+2 = 4.
$$

 

So, the equation of our level surface is

$$
x^2 +y^2+z = 4.
$$

Now, to find the equation of the tangent plane to this surface at $(1,1,2),$ we can use the following result:

  *Given a hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ and a point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)$ that lies in the domain of $f$, the gradient $\nabla \! f (\mathbf x_0)$ is normal to the tangent plane of the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k$ at the point $\mathbf x_0$*. 

![](images/11/1140e80fbb2efd684311cb7625e5b0be361d6fb951036253f57b9e51234de3ee.png)

       

We can now find the equation of the tangent plane to our level surface.

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $\mathbf x_0 = (1,1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}\,i+{f}_{y}\,j+{f}_{z}\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(1,1,2) & =2(1)\text{ }i+2(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =2\text{ }i+2\text{ }j+k \\  & =⟨2,\,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally,  we write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\nabla f(1,1,2) \cdot \langle x-1, \: y-1, \: z-2 \rangle & = 0 \[3pt]
\langle 2,\:2,\:1\rangle\cdot \langle x-1, y-1, z-2\rangle &= 0\[3pt]
      2(x-1)+ 2(y-1) + (z-2) & =0\
      2x +2y +z -6&=0   
}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f7db883-9d6e-5a67-97d4-20274467a1e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2500 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "13f10d0e-ddd7-5833-b73f-b3f00ff7016a" :step/math-academy-id 11201 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129893}} {:db/id 17592186130327 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to compute the tangent plane to the level surface $f (x, y, z) = k,$ where $k$ is a constant, at some point $\mathbf x_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0).$

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a1c45efd-b454-595e-a933-aae318d15f95" :question/math-academy-id "q-102700" :question/problem "Given the function $f(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-{e}^{z}\text{ }j-y{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,2,1) & =\frac{2}{1}\text{ }i-{e}^{1}\text{ }j-(2){e}^{1}k \\  & =2\,i-e\,j-2ek \\  & =⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7ecf0ade-c143-56c2-83e7-b60005d8d75d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494028}} {:db/id 17592186494027 :step/content {:db/id 17592186237932 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d8438dc-a715-5c0c-aab2-6e47f02ae119" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x-y+2z-10=0" :db/id 17592186236008} {:answer/id #uuid "85b07a3f-7374-5a9c-b7c1-947842c86d0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+3y+z+12=0" :db/id 17592186236650} {:answer/id #uuid "94a5b114-54d1-55a1-b257-cc17cc5b9faf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y+5z-12=0" :db/id 17592186236759} {:answer/id #uuid "b02e51c4-263c-5a4d-80f9-9315bea2d383" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+4y-3z+15=0" :db/id 17592186236937} {:answer/id #uuid "c93bc415-579e-5faf-ba97-c8c120703f69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+4y+5z-18=0" :db/id 17592186237093}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186237093} :answer-field/id #uuid "86e7ba58-6e3b-5d46-8ec2-848013d679c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186237620}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a47eb1cf-14ab-540e-8110-7aec36247dcb" :question/math-academy-id "q-102711" :question/problem "Consider the surface $xy{z}^{2}=6-z.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(1,1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =(y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i+4j+5\,k \\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8542cb45-fe3e-585c-beae-8f3803d3fd88"} {:db/id 17592186494028 :step/content {:db/id 17592186366815 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "193c9497-7ea6-5a1d-b9f5-a009ce93ca23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x-y+12z-24=0" :db/id 17592186366817} {:answer/id #uuid "f29eacee-8051-57cb-aee4-51b137c18ee1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x-y+z+12=0" :db/id 17592186366818} {:answer/id #uuid "710265a2-6141-5b27-8548-bda3797d8905" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-2y-5z+11=0" :db/id 17592186366819} {:answer/id #uuid "d24d01c2-6eb5-5662-b203-5deae9c0dd73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6x-3y-4z+24=0" :db/id 17592186366820} {:answer/id #uuid "8c31a377-21c2-5c10-92eb-4e6439b5d5dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4z+13=0" :db/id 17592186366821}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186366817} :answer-field/id #uuid "ac4c269d-3ccc-505a-8b3b-1f9e614487fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186366816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "baefe5d5-6705-561e-af37-627a61278732" :question/math-academy-id "q-102704" :question/problem "Given the function $f(x,y,z)=6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes  through the point where $(x,y,z)=(\frac{1}{2},3,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b8b241c5-9ed0-5065-b6d8-8a3dd561fd54" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494023}} {:db/id 17592186494072 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129596 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13a034a0-40db-53e2-8743-0500f64927fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,1,-e⟩\cdot ⟨x-e,\,y-e,\,z-1⟩=0" :db/id 17592186493426} {:answer/id #uuid "4d8e49ba-c572-585b-9000-22f731c9e31c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩=0" :db/id 17592186493516} {:answer/id #uuid "7fd70068-b6fc-58b5-a8fd-0b6d0f6cdc1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,1,-e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩=0" :db/id 17592186493590} {:answer/id #uuid "a4259989-16f4-5162-93ea-522cff1adbaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,1,e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩=0" :db/id 17592186493652} {:answer/id #uuid "b48376c2-fa7d-5ea7-a3f5-9c2f64a3454e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y+1,\,z+e⟩=0" :db/id 17592186493683}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493516} :answer-field/id #uuid "675858d2-09f1-5094-a85f-2db7923cff6f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186127057}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "39528896-10e8-5126-bdec-f26e9bdcc487" :question/math-academy-id "q-36334" :question/problem "Given the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}-z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,e).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =(y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i+4j+5\,k \\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8542cb45-fe3e-585c-beae-8f3803d3fd88"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d8438dc-a715-5c0c-aab2-6e47f02ae119" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$

$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$

$\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$ 

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by
![](images/d9/d9388f46f84cc0c6b1d7e5cf43ee973085366ae4f44cfe74515c59bfc1994662.svg)

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and ![](images/f9/f99f37621c20057077eb7c6e23690a45159cfe1b665c6b88b4a604f8687728bf.svg) Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "827e9581-9fde-5941-ad91-2c364796e5b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3217 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "910841a1-0516-546a-8aac-f188c965b763" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186125822 :tutorial/content "We've seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B}.\end{aligned}
$$

In expanded form, the formula looks as follows:
![](images/89/890f34433211786e2cb8aa71057de40bdf3b12678c2bbb5a79ef5e680555937f.svg)

Also, remember that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}
	\quad\textrm{and}\quad
	P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cfffdf8e-9e9f-5304-8249-54a094cc7c11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4435 :tutorial/title "The Change-of-Basis Formula in Expanded Form"} :step/id #uuid "4c4259ae-ebd7-5d31-ae41-72156cefc066" :step/math-academy-id 27272 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125362}} {:db/id 17592186125667 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125708 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Now, suppose we would like to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ 

- We first need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 \mathbf{c}_1+x_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/58/58010a2a5206e3fc27e3d924de70cf32dcc92c3578bdb2821ace7278fbb223cf.svg)

- Similarly, we need to find $y_1$ and $y_2$ such that 

$$
y_1 \mathbf{c}_1+y_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/68/68788aa3e388c5cba14662a947c1b7afaacb95f611c256d11a7a6d7614c352b9.svg)

We can solve both systems using Gaussian elimination. However, we can do that simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](images/4b/4b00a4cbd7831f6da6acd06a087d5453bd455a89eb81f6b3036b1b572bb064d1.svg)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get a matrix of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & {x}_{1} & {y}_{1} \\ 0 & 1 & {x}_{2} & {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where the required coefficients will be stored in the columns on the right-hand side." :tutorial/id #uuid "d42ee304-2e1f-5cc2-b334-65d083ea7323" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13287 :tutorial/title "Using Gaussian Elimination to Find the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis"} :step/id #uuid "184b8c31-de1a-5e34-ad87-2f626c830182" :step/math-academy-id 462199 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125498}}] :activity/title "Changing a Basis Using the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124710} {:db/id 17592186125361 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125768 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$ 

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by
![](images/d9/d9388f46f84cc0c6b1d7e5cf43ee973085366ae4f44cfe74515c59bfc1994662.svg)

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and ![](images/f9/f99f37621c20057077eb7c6e23690a45159cfe1b665c6b88b4a604f8687728bf.svg) Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "827e9581-9fde-5941-ad91-2c364796e5b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3217 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "910841a1-0516-546a-8aac-f188c965b763" :step/math-academy-id 17537 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125500}} {:db/id 17592186125768 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & \frac{5}{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

B=\{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\},\,C=\{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\},\,[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given above. Find $[x]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b02f895b-b4b9-567f-99da-8866008266c1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486517}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "277d51c6-ba77-5bde-a9da-6f2d8333899a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cd3d1f8f-1ec9-5277-bd94-fc774bb919de" :question/math-academy-id "q-113595" :question/problem "The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ to $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 5-5\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 \\ -3 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e7ff6d11-7ab8-5df7-ab96-cc2f9b5a933c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486482}} {:db/id 17592186486510 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125036 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7b3fc777-c87e-5494-9361-753fc99b8a92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417145} {:answer/id #uuid "af2e1656-5790-518b-ae95-17ddec42b6bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417157} {:answer/id #uuid "c820d187-6507-5a27-8119-ca85d381bd74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417165} {:answer/id #uuid "d1949552-5c2a-51ed-85be-630d9f8df6a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417166} {:answer/id #uuid "fc368894-a420-5e78-a8ce-445dfc038e7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417173}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186417166} :answer-field/id #uuid "77968fba-758e-5c47-b717-abe8d60fbc59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186417179}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "618e1711-d591-5872-b815-9d14ad33b674" :question/math-academy-id "q-37160" :question/problem "$$

we know one solution to a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, we can use the **reduction of order method** to find a second solution to the equation. 

It works like this: if we know that some function $y_1(t)$ is a solution, then we let $y_2(t) = u(t) y_1(t)$ for some unknown function $u(t),$ and we write down a differential equation in terms of $u.$ Solving this equation, and then computing $y_2,$ gives us our second solution.

For example, suppose we're given that $y_1(t) = \sin{4t}$ is a solution to the equation

$$
y'' + 16y = 0.
$$

Let's use the reduction of order method to find a second solution $y_2(t).$

According to the reduction of order method, we let $y_{2} = u(t)\sin{4t}$ for some unknown function $u(t).$ Then, we write the differential equation in terms of $u.$ To do that, we first differentiate with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =u\operatorname{sin}4t \\ {y}_{2}^{'} & ={u}^{'}\operatorname{sin}4t+4u\operatorname{cos}4t \\ {y}_{2}^{''} & ={u}^{''}\operatorname{sin}4t+8{u}^{'}\operatorname{cos}4t-16u\operatorname{sin}4t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{''}+16y & =0 \\ ({u}^{''}\operatorname{sin}4t+8{u}^{'}\operatorname{cos}4t-16u\operatorname{sin}4t)+16u\operatorname{sin}4t & =0 \\ {u}^{''}\operatorname{sin}4t+8{u}^{'}\operatorname{cos}4t & =0 \\ {u}^{''} & =-8{u}^{'}\operatorname{cot}4t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $w = u'.$ Then our equation becomes a first-order equation,

$$
w' = -8w\cot{4t}.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w = c_1 \csc^2{4t}.
$$

Now, since $w = u',$ we have

$$
u' = c_1 \csc^2{4t} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u = -\dfrac{c_1}{4}\cot{4t} + c_2.
$$

Therefore, our expression for $y_2(t) = u \sin{4t}$ becomes

$$
y_2(t) = \sin{4t}\left( -\dfrac{c_1}{4}\cot{4t} + c_2 \right).
$$

We can choose any values for $c_1$ and $c_2$ to yield a second solution. For example, if we set $c_1 = -4$ and $c_2 = 0,$ then we get

$$
y_2(t) = \sin{4t}\left( \cot{4t} \right) = \cos{4t}.
$$

When selecting our constants $c_1$ and $c_2,$ we should try to get a solution that is "different" from the first. We will define precisely what we mean by "different" soon, but loosely speaking we should aim for a $y_2(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- None of the terms is a constant multiple of the first solution (here, we accomplished this by choosing $c_2=0$).

- The remaining terms are as simple as possible (here, we accomplished this by choosing $c_1=-4$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "af7458ab-92f7-5672-99ff-ffe77fdeeed1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4086 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4a6adb1a-163b-5824-9043-b2e7539b66f3" :step/math-academy-id 24522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125474}}] :activity/title "Reduction of Order" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124719} {:db/id 17592186125476 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125812 :tutorial/content "If we know one solution to a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, we can use the **reduction of order method** to find a second solution to the equation.

satisfied by $u(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=u(x){y}_{1}(x)=ux.

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=ux$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}x+u \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′})+5x({u}^{′}x+u)-5ux & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{x}^{3}+2{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+5{u}^{′}{x}^{2}+5ux-5ux & =0 \\ {u}^{″}{x}^{3}+7{u}^{′}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({u}^{″}x+7{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ee0e41e-0081-57b1-b63e-73976c761c93" :step/next {:db/id 17592186427173}} {:db/id 17592186427175 :step/content {:db/id 17592186427172 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17b214ce-ab5e-5f5c-a969-dbab5f241399" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x{u}^{″}+4{u}^{′}=0" :db/id 17592186427146} {:answer/id #uuid "935207a8-801a-5dc5-9425-a3cd78674d34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x{u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}=0" :db/id 17592186427150} {:answer/id #uuid "97c83eab-28ad-55eb-91f3-21e77e24722a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{″}-2x{u}^{′}=0" :db/id 17592186427151} {:answer/id #uuid "c6393b4b-5ac6-54cd-828e-f2c5d96b68e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}{u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}=0" :db/id 17592186427156} {:answer/id #uuid "cb3901fc-4414-5f50-8377-cc29adff3e54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{″}+4x{u}^{′}=0" :db/id 17592186427158}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427150} :answer-field/id #uuid "47dbd607-90bc-550b-8e0e-ad2915edaeb9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427166}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "879a358b-954a-58b1-b6bd-64affbba8f30" :question/math-academy-id "q-102795" :question/problem "The function ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{-1}$ is a solution to the equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4x{y}^{′}+2y=0$ for $x>0.$ If ${y}_{2}=u(x){y}_{1}(x)$ is a second solution of the equation, then which of the following equations must be satisfied by $u(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=u(x){y}_{1}(x)=u{x}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u{x}^{-1}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{x}^{-1}-u{x}^{-2} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{x}^{-1}-2{u}^{′}{x}^{-2}+2u{x}^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}({u}^{″}{x}^{-1}-2{u}^{′}{x}^{-2}+2u{x}^{-3})+4x({u}^{′}{x}^{-1}-u{x}^{-2})+2u{x}^{-1} & =0 \\ {u}^{″}x-2{u}^{′}+2u{x}^{-1}+4{u}^{′}-4u{x}^{-1}+2u{x}^{-1} & =0 \\ {u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
x{u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}=0.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "90e390d3-2285-5647-8dee-72ff1477f1a3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186427177}} {:db/id 17592186427176 :step/content {:db/id 17592186427169 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5624fee0-ac6c-5a27-a00d-a533ce8462a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-x}" :db/id 17592186427149} {:answer/id #uuid "c66f0cef-0e9d-5e23-a546-875b0af82f5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}" :db/id 17592186427157} {:answer/id #uuid "cb87e4e8-0d55-5f56-909c-77cfc9ff1845" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{x}" :db/id 17592186427159} {:answer/id #uuid "e92d5e88-cebd-5955-be19-3ce4ea54b887" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)=x" :db/id 17592186427161} {:answer/id #uuid "fc51c4e7-1541-5022-aa97-d43e54b6050a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}" :db/id 17592186427164}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427149} :answer-field/id #uuid "50d2223c-c444-5eb2-b0e0-62ae52349f8f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0006acdb-45b3-5900-8e6e-eb4bda5a2c89" :question/math-academy-id "q-64893" :question/problem "Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation." :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}={e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u) \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u)-{e}^{x}(u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u-u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}+2w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}\,⟹\,u=-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}{e}^{-2x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$

${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-6y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation." :question/worked-solution "According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{3x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{3x}+6{u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+9u{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({u}^{″}{e}^{3x}+6{u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+9u{e}^{3x})-({u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x})-6u{e}^{3x} & =0 \\ {e}^{3x}({u}^{″}+6{u}^{′}+9u-{u}^{′}-3u-6u) & =0 \\ {e}^{3x}({u}^{″}+5{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{3x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}+5{u}^{′}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}+5w=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}{e}^{-5x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}{e}^{-5x}\,⟹\,u=-\frac{{c}_{1}}{5}{e}^{-5x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{3x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}(-\frac{{c}_{1}}{5}{e}^{-5x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-5$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}\cdot {e}^{-5x}={e}^{-2x}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e444fcb5-e5b0-58fa-a276-f1b31f0b5d06"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5624fee0-ac6c-5a27-a00d-a533ce8462a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value and the plane $\Pi$ that is given by the equation 

$$
(\mathbf{r}-\langle 2 , 3 , 1 \rangle ) \cdot \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle = 0.
$$

 

First, note that $\mathbf{n} = \langle 4 , 4 , 2 \rangle$ is a vector that's normal to the plane.

![](images/7b/7b2dfcd87c1f5e4e2c2b1a0b9a7f73899772e33e1020465b2b38d1b2de29a66c.png)

Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(2,3,1)$. Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,1⟩-⟨3,0,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,3,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The shortest distance $d$ from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane, as shown below.

![](images/26/26e494eef47db4dba3ac36dfa96c7e9a9d191321b22bb82874f3e74bbd7116ef.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 4+3\cdot 4+3\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4+12+6|}{\sqrt{16+16+4}} \\  & =\frac{|14|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is $\dfrac{7}{3}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "224c4104-9097-5a92-9c37-5d0fe22171a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3261 by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-2$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+2y+2z & =8 \\ -1(-2)+2(1)+2z & =8 \\ 2z & =4 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-2,1,2)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-2,1,2⟩-⟨-2,3,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-1,2,2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|0\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot 2+8\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|0-4+16|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\  & =\frac{|12|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{12}{3} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-3y+6z & =16 \\ -2(-2)-3(0)+6z & =16 \\ 6z & =12 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-2,0,2)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-2,0,2⟩-⟨5,3,7⟩ \\  & =⟨-7,-3,-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-7)\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot (-3)+(-5)\cdot 6|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(6)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|14+9-30|}{\sqrt{4+9+36}} \\  & =\frac{|-7|}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{7}{7} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+2y+z & =6 \\ -2(1)+2(1)+z & =6 \\ z & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,1,6)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,6⟩-⟨-1,4,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-2,2,1⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|2\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2+11\cdot 1|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4-6+11|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}} \\  & =\frac{|1|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}

So, we get the point $Q(-1,1,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,0,1)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,0,1⟩-⟨-1,3,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨6,2,3⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|2\cdot 6+(-3)\cdot 2+5\cdot 3|}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|12-6+15|}{\sqrt{36+4+9}} \\  & =\frac{|21|}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{21}{7} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

involves writing a matrix $A$ as a product of two matrices $L$ and $U,$ where

- ![](images/2e/2e6c0b6fdaf90e3a3e23ed91ffe09cb360bb39325b9a630f1b7219b3188a25db.svg) is a *unit lower triangular matrix* (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- ![](images/0c/0c5d7337e47a53dfa5bdce8c6f4a96bb1e52ef6054349011a6cc38f29701cc61.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](images/22/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as 

![](images/d4/d4c92b2e8252619f9a1511d166be884b9a2bdb4311eea8e408e8fe75eed6f36c.svg)

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}}\cdot A \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{L}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ($R_j:=R_j+k R_i$ where $i < j$), and

- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed." :tutorial/id #uuid "5f8c6994-f448-5679-8d2e-5591b86c2a97" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3178 "a83c5862-ce81-57be-a501-0eb1330527bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-32681" :question/problem "Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-5{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$" :question/worked-solution "Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-5)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Cramer's Rule"}] :question/problem "Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below. Find $z.$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+3z &=-1 \\ 4x-2z &=1 \\ 3x+y-z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1x-1y+3z &=-1 \\ 4x+0y-2z &=1 \\ 3x+1y-1z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(0-(-2))+(-4+6)+3(4-0) \\  & =2+2+12 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficient in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"}] :question/problem "Let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below. Given that $x = 2,$ find the value of $k.$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z &=-1 \\ kx+3y-2z &=1 \\ 3x-y+2z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ k & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}k & -2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}k & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(6-2)-2(2k+6)-(-k-9) \\  & =4-4k-12+k+9 \\  & =1-3k\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x = \dfrac{D_x}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(6-2)-2(2+6)-(-1-9) \\  & =-4-16+10 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
x = \dfrac{D_x}{D} = \dfrac{-10}{1-3k}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $x=2.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-10}{1-3k} & =2 \\ -10 & =2-6k \\ 6k & =12 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120458 :question/id #uuid "d9b84023-6745-5aae-a304-bc4f9a263b31" :question/math-academy-id "q-43113"} {:db/id 17592186120459 :question/id #uuid "c8205961-c58e-5aea-a7e2-15eb2dd17972" :question/math-academy-id "q-43115" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fff04a-2bbe-5b26-ad65-edbd694ba9be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=2" :db/id 17592186416276} {:answer/id #uuid "7fe85483-816c-510e-9fd1-dd20c0b4191b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=-10" :db/id 17592186416284} {:answer/id #uuid "b4d8e391-d9ee-52da-94f1-37df36eceaa0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=5" :db/id 17592186416289} {:answer/id #uuid "c108d1a2-60fc-5674-aa0a-d546a2379dfd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=-8" :db/id 17592186416291} {:answer/id #uuid "ee89842c-a371-5c4d-bdf4-656e2b69eca7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=4" :db/id 17592186416295}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186416289} :answer-field/id #uuid "432aa278-91b8-5c39-89e2-129966c0aa56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186416297}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-3z &=7 \\ kx-4y+z &=-19 \\ x-y-4z &=4.\end{aligned}\right.

Given that  $z=-2$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $7k+23,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -3 \\ k & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}|=7k+23\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $z$ is given by $z=\frac{{D}_{z}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 7 \\ k & -4 & -19 \\ 1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-4 & -19 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}k & -19 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|+7\cdot |\begin{aligned}k & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-16-19)-(4k+19)+7(-k+4) \\  & =-70-4k-19-7k+28 \\  & =-61-11k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z=\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}=\frac{-61-11k}{7k+23}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $z=-2.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-61-11k}{7k+23} & =-2 \\ -61-11k & =-14k-46 \\ 3k & =15 \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272007 :question/id #uuid "b99085c9-ade3-5f37-a123-f7c001cf1137" :question/math-academy-id "q-140042"} {:db/id 17592186272008 :question/id #uuid "254e5808-cdaa-58f1-bc6f-06ea580b1b72" :question/math-academy-id "q-140043" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119791 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7263e25b-117e-528c-b2ad-2624f325da35" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Coefficient in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "178aa29c-c731-5575-b789-a031a7794737" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=9" :db/id 17592186269463} {:answer/id #uuid "32d6fe63-36e7-505d-b5ca-f8377d01d86a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=2" :db/id 17592186269733} {:answer/id #uuid "44193ff7-7933-5662-b23c-3e02bf36d32b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=1" :db/id 17592186269885} {:answer/id #uuid "9261b35a-1876-58e0-8b49-edd341555666" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=11" :db/id 17592186270549} {:answer/id #uuid "9a5e86f2-180e-58a4-a5c7-b73059c1110a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-4" :db/id 17592186270628}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "44193ff7-7933-5662-b23c-3e02bf36d32b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=1" :db/id 17592186269885} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2a02390-118a-5af6-b56f-a5456ae3d683" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186271885}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}6 & 5 & -2 \\ 4 & -5 & k \\ -2 & 10 & -5\end{aligned}|=160-70k\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}2 & 5 & -3 \\ 1 & -5 & k \\ -2 & 10 & -5\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-5 & k \\ 10 & -5\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & k \\ -2 & -5\end{aligned}|+(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(25-10k)-5(-5+2k)-3(10-10) \\  & =50-20k+25-10k+0 \\  & =75-30k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\frac{75-30k}{160-70k}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $x=\frac{1}{2}.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{75-30k}{160-70k} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ 2(75-30k) & =160-70k \\ 150-60k & =160-70k \\ 10k & =10 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186329680 :question/id #uuid "3eb8876e-4ac9-5db4-b3d5-66592db8b271" :question/math-academy-id "q-42684"} {:db/id 17592186329711 :question/id #uuid "53b9ad58-1c7d-58bd-abc1-d7698480a379" :question/math-academy-id "q-43111" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119791 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7263e25b-117e-528c-b2ad-2624f325da35" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Coefficient in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2241ec88-5356-5893-b69f-c9e4fd87c09c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=1" :db/id 17592186327230} {:answer/id #uuid "5da23a4c-faa7-5c6b-ac22-922696b59bba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-6" :db/id 17592186327759} {:answer/id #uuid "6f623b61-ca7e-5718-ac2b-2a0d442c6767" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-3" :db/id 17592186327898} {:answer/id #uuid "79ecd735-7b77-5ecc-a27c-75997ff676f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=4" :db/id 17592186327979} {:answer/id #uuid "c349a9f6-3ed5-56ea-bf87-5daf2f2c94bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=5" :db/id 17592186328641}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "5da23a4c-faa7-5c6b-ac22-922696b59bba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-6" :db/id 17592186327759} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1b47b03-47bb-5bf2-8a6d-aefaac24352a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186329523}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}5 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 & k \\ 2 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=97-21k\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $z$ is given by $z=\frac{{D}_{z}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}5 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 9\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}|-(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =5(36+3)+3(9+2)+(3-8) \\  & =195+33-5 \\  & =223.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z=\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}=\frac{223}{97-21k}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $z=1.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{223}{97-21k} & =1 \\ 223 & =97-21k \\ 21k & =-126 \\ k & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342061 :question/id #uuid "209a5a36-a432-55a5-bdf5-16c608d27113" :question/math-academy-id "q-73694"} {:db/id 17592186342062 :question/id #uuid "0e7d5f36-83df-59b5-b06e-da52c530f2e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-73697" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119791 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7263e25b-117e-528c-b2ad-2624f325da35" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Coefficient in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bb35856-1ec7-5c49-be2d-613b5999c247" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=4" :db/id 17592186339230} {:answer/id #uuid "429b7481-cf7c-5542-94eb-469ef9bc5c9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-3" :db/id 17592186339711} {:answer/id #uuid "58e38b5a-b8c9-5bf8-b5d2-e9e50b751d74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=3" :db/id 17592186339937} {:answer/id #uuid "8bf0a6b8-772c-56ce-9f67-a8b0a1030b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-4" :db/id 17592186340382} {:answer/id #uuid "efae4617-4d98-5b47-bcb8-8b5baad301dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-2" :db/id 17592186341241}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "0bb35856-1ec7-5c49-be2d-613b5999c247" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=4" :db/id 17592186339230} :answer-field/id #uuid "55a02894-8a7c-5f56-b37a-283aa26f6bcc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186341535}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

Given that $x=-4$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $15,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}|=15\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ k & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| & =-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ k & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ k & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(0-8)+(0-2k)+5(0-3k) \\  & =8-2k-15k \\  & =8-17k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\frac{8-17k}{15}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $x=-4.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8-17k}{15} & =-4 \\ 8-17k & =-60 \\ -17k & =-68 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342063 :question/id #uuid "606431ba-b0b3-579d-ac68-261fcff208d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-73698" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119791 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7263e25b-117e-528c-b2ad-2624f325da35" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Coefficient in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "182535ed-2c40-52e5-a8ea-da439ad71f39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=7" :db/id 17592186339342} {:answer/id #uuid "563ceb4e-01d8-5269-8c7c-88ade9717ce6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=2" :db/id 17592186339917} {:answer/id #uuid "614904de-89a3-53dc-9397-708ec20a06c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=3" :db/id 17592186339996} {:answer/id #uuid "91c1ca7c-7293-5998-9217-cd635329657e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-3" :db/id 17592186340435} {:answer/id #uuid "efca7b9b-1e72-54b4-a19e-5558ceb49120" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=-7" :db/id 17592186341242}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "182535ed-2c40-52e5-a8ea-da439ad71f39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "k=7" :db/id 17592186339342} :answer-field/id #uuid "032e2cd1-cc94-513a-bc74-a43cdbbabe51" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186341389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be the unique solution of the system of equations below.

Given that $y=-5$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $1,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=1\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y=\frac{{D}_{y}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=|\begin{aligned}2 & k & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|-k\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-1-0)-k(1-0)+2(2-0) \\  & =-2-k+4 \\  & =2-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
y=\frac{{D}_{y}}{D}=\frac{2-k}{1}=2-k.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $y=-5.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-k & =-5 \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186416302 :question/id #uuid "22790615-5765-50ce-b96c-1d82231be30c" :question/math-academy-id "q-42668" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0520e7af-36b0-5ef0-9563-eb7367b7cb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186416272} {:answer/id #uuid "3675aea5-a0c8-57f7-93a0-b11b85ed8248" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=3" :db/id 17592186416278} {:answer/id #uuid "49e9c67b-3d28-59fc-80d1-1d4cc0713555" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=-1" :db/id 17592186416280} {:answer/id #uuid "81135cf6-e842-57e1-aef8-392ad77737ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=-2" :db/id 17592186416286} {:answer/id #uuid "e67665d0-ea97-55a9-9c9d-1d7010759bbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k=-\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186416294}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186416280} :answer-field/id #uuid "4a46aaec-c335-5f1e-884c-19d1799ece0c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186416298}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ be a unique solution of the system of equations below. 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+y+z &=-4 \\ y-2z &=2 \\ 3x+2y+kz &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Given that  $y=6$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $7+4k,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & k\end{aligned}|=7+4k\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y=\frac{{D}_{y}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=|\begin{aligned}4 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 & k\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & k\end{aligned}|-(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 3 & k\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(2k+2)+4(0+6)+(0-6) \\  & =8k+8+24-6 \\  & =26+8k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
y=\frac{{D}_{y}}{D}=\frac{26+8k}{7+4k}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $y=6.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=-1 \\ x+5y+3z &=k \\ 7x-3y-z &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Given that $z=-3$ and that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is equal to $-16,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's write the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 7 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|=-16\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $z$ is given by $z=\frac{{D}_{z}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & k \\ 7 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & k \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & k \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 7 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-(4-7k)-(-3-35) \\  & =-4+7k+38 \\  & =7k+34.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z=\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}=\frac{7k+34}{-16}.
$$

From the problem statement, we know that $z=-3.$ So, we can solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7k+34}{-16} & =-3 \\ 7k+34 & =48 \\ 7k & =14 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186119852 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119667 :question/id #uuid "33693f3b-713f-5ffc-bd4e-27ad7a1e0c7c" :question/math-academy-id "e-6172"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b9c2dc67-95ca-52f2-a292-32891000b76a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048146} {:db/id 17592186050129}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120441 :question/id #uuid "b69dc5d3-fe00-5843-9b79-6c2a6e202607" :question/math-academy-id "q-42625"} {:db/id 17592186120443 :question/id #uuid "0f2938e3-2c86-58a3-8014-2fd96089eb1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-42681"} {:db/id 17592186271992 :question/id #uuid "c6ebb206-cdb6-551e-a660-6c517ea901a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-139985"} {:db/id 17592186342059 :question/id #uuid "dceddfaf-57df-5ca9-a79f-af2de59df96b" :question/math-academy-id "q-73686"} {:db/id 17592186392515 :question/id #uuid "8e9092a7-94c4-59d4-8639-d2ed92a81148" :question/math-academy-id "q-42693"} {:db/id 17592186393348 :question/id #uuid "dfde2756-df99-506c-8f8b-640eb254c853" :question/math-academy-id "q-73688"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Parts of Cramer's Rule"} {:db/id 17592186119667 :question/id #uuid "33693f3b-713f-5ffc-bd4e-27ad7a1e0c7c" :question/math-academy-id "e-6172" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119852 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b9c2dc67-95ca-52f2-a292-32891000b76a" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Parts of Cramer's Rule"}] :question/problem "Consider the system of equations

[{:db/id 17592186120648 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121026 :tutorial/content "Cramer's rule applies to square systems of linear equations with any number of variables. In this lesson, we will practice applying Cramer's rule to solve $3 \times 3$ systems of equations.

Suppose we have a square system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y+{a}_{13}z &={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y+{a}_{23}z &={b}_{2} \\ {a}_{31}x+{a}_{32}y+{a}_{33}z &={b}_{3},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $|\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & {a}_{13} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & {a}_{23} \\ {a}_{31} & {a}_{32} & {a}_{33}\end{aligned}|$. 
Then Cramer's rule states that

$$
\left< x,y,z \right> = \left\langle  \dfrac{D_x}{D}, \dfrac{D_y}{D}, \dfrac{D_z}{D} \right\rangle
$$

is the unique solution of the system, where

$$
|\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & {a}_{12} & {a}_{13} \\ {b}_{2} & {a}_{22} & {a}_{23} \\ {b}_{3} & {a}_{32} & {a}_{33}\end{aligned}|
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f245bf99-3b45-5a27-9aca-aaee391628ed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3079 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "620dc976-5ed3-54d8-a37a-7483259c65bb" :step/math-academy-id 16705 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120706}} {:db/id 17592186120649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119789 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119600 :question/id #uuid "41a8466d-8bc6-5811-a557-e5a4e840f51c" :question/math-academy-id "e-4577"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71c540ac-3cb5-5e0e-9b7b-5e2ccf1615c5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120440} {:db/id 17592186120442} {:db/id 17592186271993} {:db/id 17592186271995} {:db/id 17592186329710} {:db/id 17592186329712} {:db/id 17592186342060} {:db/id 17592186416303} {:db/id 17592186416304}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving for an Unknown in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"} :step/id #uuid "c34a23fc-50c9-5fb1-b89d-0a53b98720ed" :step/math-academy-id 16707 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120651}} {:db/id 17592186120651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119791 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119602 :question/id #uuid "e1eb00d6-77fe-5110-8095-a54e63981c09" :question/math-academy-id "e-4579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7263e25b-117e-528c-b2ad-2624f325da35" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120458} {:db/id 17592186120459} {:db/id 17592186272007} {:db/id 17592186272008} {:db/id 17592186329680} {:db/id 17592186329711} {:db/id 17592186342061} {:db/id 17592186342062} {:db/id 17592186342063} {:db/id 17592186416302} {:db/id 17592186416305}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving for a Coefficient in a 3x3 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule"} :step/id #uuid "bd4aa514-64cb-5bde-8bf4-8e5364299dc3" :step/math-academy-id 16711} {:db/id 17592186120706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121047 :tutorial/content "To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z &=9 \\ 2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z &=9 \\ 0x+2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+1y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ -8 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(12-3)-2(0+24)+(0+16) \\  & =36-48+16 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $D_x,$ $D_y,$ and $D_z.$

- To find $D_x,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *first* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$

$$

- To find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *second* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$

In this lesson, we will practice applying Cramer's rule to solve $3 \times 3$ systems of equations.

Suppose we have a square system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y+{a}_{13}z &={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y+{a}_{23}z &={b}_{2} \\ {a}_{31}x+{a}_{32}y+{a}_{33}z &={b}_{3},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $|\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & {a}_{13} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & {a}_{23} \\ {a}_{31} & {a}_{32} & {a}_{33}\end{aligned}|$. 
Then Cramer's rule states that

$$
\left< x,y,z \right> = \left\langle  \dfrac{D_x}{D}, \dfrac{D_y}{D}, \dfrac{D_z}{D} \right\rangle
$$

is the unique solution of the system, where

$$
|\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & {a}_{12} & {a}_{13} \\ {b}_{2} & {a}_{22} & {a}_{23} \\ {b}_{3} & {a}_{32} & {a}_{33}\end{aligned}|
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f245bf99-3b45-5a27-9aca-aaee391628ed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3079 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "620dc976-5ed3-54d8-a37a-7483259c65bb" :step/math-academy-id 16705 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120706}} {:db/id 17592186121026 :tutorial/content "Cramer's rule applies to square systems of linear equations with any number of variables. where $|\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & {a}_{13} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & {a}_{23} \\ {a}_{31} & {a}_{32} & {a}_{33}\end{aligned}|$. 
Then Cramer's rule states that

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f245bf99-3b45-5a27-9aca-aaee391628ed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3079 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186120706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121047 :tutorial/content "To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z &=9 \\ 2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
