the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3a8e9986-4b85-5793-91b8-d47f73b67205" :step/math-academy-id 54038} {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form

quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "14546d02-e8ca-5bbd-82f2-37c20dd8c152" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414675}} {:db/id 17592186414675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "310e7c10-e8a2-5719-93d8-e4b398b84456"} {:db/id 17592186414676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389629 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33fcc9d7-da26-566b-892f-8ca0dccbf100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389631} {:answer/id #uuid "a86affbe-00af-5daa-9d5d-d6b4c732cb8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389632} {:answer/id #uuid "da2b263a-4cb7-517f-88b9-8ca97ec6707e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389633} {:answer/id #uuid "b5f8b750-04ea-55ad-b825-30a6ece0925e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389634} {:answer/id #uuid "0ceac102-859c-568b-8eb7-f0592356b505" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389635}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389631} :answer-field/id #uuid "205f15e5-0108-5b4a-888b-1b37b338482c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8daa1f82-58aa-5738-bbe7-9b509869abcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-170411" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$"} :step/id #uuid "5eb99804-d9c9-598f-850b-ee8266ef1130" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414674}} {:db/id 17592186414677 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198562 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1512bf0f-a0b6-5737-8456-15bf7348d13a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414668} {:answer/id #uuid "189d044b-20ef-594f-9050-30d36ea1c805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414669} {:answer/id #uuid "3cba96ef-b9b9-582c-9ce3-fb19b45e7859" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414670} {:answer/id #uuid "b75669b6-5915-5577-8d99-85ede9b169dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414671} {:answer/id #uuid "e53e0f0c-01ad-5114-93c5-0442b0a0663a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414668} :answer-field/id #uuid "72e392f4-71c8-5797-8085-77f0d25ff7b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414673}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "48e09a9b-efe0-5a6d-96f4-c82dbcd33806" :question/math-academy-id "q-138095" :question/problem "The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $3.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20.

$$

$$

$$

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

$$

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$"} :step/id #uuid "3bf30ed1-f62d-5db0-95c3-bae2ee7a2121" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442118}} {:db/id 17592186442117 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7b55ab94-44ca-5e5f-8316-aab35be9951d"} {:db/id 17592186514542 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.

$$

$$

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "7b55ab94-44ca-5e5f-8316-aab35be9951d"} {:db/id 17592186514542 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$

$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

 Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

 

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

 This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

 the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

 we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

 

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$

$$

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8a01626c-0fe4-5c01-be55-c9b98f53762d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186551391}} {:db/id 17592186048308 :topic/difficulty 1.0036629092514608 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428619 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :db/id 17592186415100}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨3t,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t\in [0,1],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(1) & =⟨3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(3,1).$

{:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F,$ defined as

$$
F(x,y)=\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the curve $y={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)$ for $x\in [0,1].$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

First, we define $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as follows:

$$
F(x,y)={{\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\,i+{{\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\,j.
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-\frac{2xy}{(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-f(0,0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{1}^{2}+{ln}^{2}⁡2)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{ln}^{2}⁡2)-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{ln}^{2}⁡2).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134566 :question/id #uuid "ff7ad628-63c0-5640-b2d2-82a36608b04e" :question/math-academy-id "q-98995"} {:db/id 17592186240918 :question/id #uuid $$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ Since we're given that $F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,0⟩, \\ r(2\pi ) & =⟨4{\pi }^{2}+1,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0)$ and $(4{\pi }^{2}+1,2\pi ).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(4{\pi }^{2}+1,2\pi )-f(1,0) \\  & ={e}^{4{\pi }^{2}+1}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -{e}^{1}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & ={e}^{4{\pi }^{2}+1}-e \\  & =e({e}^{4{\pi }^{2}}-1).\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ Since we're given that $F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={x}^{2}-y, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}-xy.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(2) & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4)-f(0,1) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}\cdot (3\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot {4}^{3}-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot 4)-(\frac{1}{3}\cdot {0}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot {1}^{3}-0\cdot 1) \\  & =9{ln}^{3}⁡2+\frac{64}{3}-12\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =9{ln}^{3}⁡2-12\operatorname{ln}⁡2+21.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240924 :question/id #uuid "86f7c787-e5df-5794-8bba-c906aa91522f" :question/math-academy-id "q-104739"} {:db/id 17592186240925 :question/id #uuid "7507d02e-e1da-50a2-9a9d-6236d6a7afae" :question/math-academy-id "q-104745" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16f31b92-c386-50b2-b977-d94225bcfbc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{\pi }+1" :db/id 17592186238253} {:answer/id #uuid "465fbdf4-7176-5e2a-afb9-7055988a9594" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{{\pi }^{2}-1}" :db/id 17592186238665} {:answer/id #uuid "54e54a33-5402-591a-ac33-570a9653db6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi {e}^{\pi -1}" :db/id 17592186238789} {:answer/id #uuid "796fc17c-d543-5b01-83ae-f85bfdb65ad5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186239102} {:answer/id #uuid "dfd66caa-a9be-51dd-a8aa-57947da3bed9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}+1" :db/id 17592186240013}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238789} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ed60cbe-d21d-5310-989e-903acd1a44f7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240533}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F,$ defined as

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).

$$
F(x,y)={{({e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\,i+{{(x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\,j.
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,\pi ].

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,\pi -1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,2⟩, \\ r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\frac{\pi }{2},e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(\frac{\pi }{2},e).$

$$

2110} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134760 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135084 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b].$ The fundamental theorem of calculus states that

$$
\int_a^b f'(x)\,\textrm d x = f(b) - f(a).
$$

A similar result, known as **the fundamental theorem for line integrals,** exists for line integrals of conservative vector fields. This theorem can be stated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={x}^{2}-y, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}-xy.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(2) & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
F(x,y)=({e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+(x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,j.

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the curve $y=x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

First, we define $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as follows:

$$
F(x,y)={{({e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\,i+{{(x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\,j.
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,\pi -1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(\pi ,\pi -1).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(\pi ,\pi -1)-f(0,1) \\  & =(\pi \cdot {e}^{\pi -1}+(\pi -1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0\cdot {e}^{1}+1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(\pi {e}^{\pi -1}+0)-0 \\  & =\pi {e}^{\pi -1}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "49fc4c7e-267c-5cf4-a795-e02e380cf712" :step/next {:db/id 17592186539101}} {:db/id 17592186539101 :step/content {:db/id 17592186259591 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5570ad04-a911-54fe-882f-cae6a0eccb35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16-{e}^{16}" :db/id 17592186257514} {:answer/id #uuid "69d52aa2-f5a3-518e-9e37-8487d0ca7564" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{4}+12" :db/id 17592186257719} {:answer/id #uuid "7bdee35c-5f2c-5453-8ea0-524f7e2d5558" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{16}-{e}^{2}+12" :db/id 17592186257879} {:answer/id #uuid "a641ae1f-fce3-54ae-b9d3-8c7c4dd0c256" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{16}+{e}^{4}-4" :db/id 17592186258233} {:answer/id #uuid "c1f247a0-2670-5ca0-8d3b-f9534636b266" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{16}+16" :db/id 17592186258482}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186257879} :answer-field/id #uuid "399493dc-69ea-5245-b7ef-1fc5d184a6d1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "33d927c3-e1a0-5a24-bd3b-65369e4fc02e" :question/math-academy-id "q-124030" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{e}^{xy}.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $\frac{x}{2}=\sqrt{y}$ for $y\in [1,4],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t},t⟩,\,t\in [1,4].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2,1⟩, \\ r(4) & =⟨4,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ to the origin. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $\text{rank}(T)=1$,  where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$
- **II.** $\text{Im}(T)$ contains no vectors of ${R}^{2}$
- **III.** $\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is the zero-subspace ${0},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=0
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. In our case, we have 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=0.
$$

- Statement II is false. The image of $T$ contains the vector zero vector $0=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186360751 :question/id #uuid "2667e6b9-8784-550d-a849-0ee298d78d90" :question/math-academy-id "q-97078"} {:db/id 17592186366052 :question/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "If the linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=-3x$ then, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $⟨1,3⟩$ belongs to the range of $T$

- **II.** $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$

- **III.** $\text{Im}(T)={0}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. 

- Statement I is false. 
Notice that the point $(1,3)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=-3x$ since $3\ne -3\cdot 1.$ Therefore, the vector $⟨1,3⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, 
since $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line passing through the origin, we have that the standard matrix $T$ is singular. Hence, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement III is false. 
For example,  the point $(1,-3)$ satisfies the equation  $y=-3x$ since $-3=-3\cdot 1.$ Therefore, the vector $⟨1,-3⟩\in \text{Im}(T).$ Thus, $\text{Im}(T)\ne {0}.$"} {:db/id 17592186366059 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=2x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $⟨2,1⟩\in \text{Im}(T)$
- **II.** $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$
- **III.** $\text{nullity}(T)=2$, where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1,
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The point $(2,1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=2x$ since $1\ne 2\cdot 2.$ Hence, 

$$
⟨2,1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).
$$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{nullity}(T)=1,$ we get 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186380615 :question/id #uuid "6d9c3015-ea78-542d-9de3-a1c266f8369d" :question/math-academy-id "q-111793"} {:db/id 17592186382648 :question/id :topic/math-academy-id 3645} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176932 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177088 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following linear transformation: 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2
$$

The image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Therefore, it can only be one of the following:  

- the whole of $\mathbb{R}^2,$

- a line through the origin, or

- a single point (vector), namely the origin $(0,0).$

Let's denote the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ by $T.$ It turns out that the dimension of the image of $\mathbf{T}$ depends on $\text{rank}(T)$ (or equivalently on $\text{nullity}(T)$ by the rank-nullity theorem). Indeed, we have the following:

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=2,$ then the two columns of $T$ are linearly independent. This means $T$ is invertible and therefore, $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) =  \mathbb{R}^2.$

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto  $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$
![](images/7d/7de193042587cb9362641cbb541477a5e4951e96d9e82f074fb0cc3a86a80d3a.svg)

![](images/88/88baa47cae14d4a43d59b366c13b3c29376678edef2fe34ff505a942ef6af986.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=1,$ then there is a nonzero vector that generates the image of $\mathbf{T}.$ In this case, the image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\Bbb R^2$. So, it is a line passing through the origin.

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=2x\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/49/4952615b0c4ddf85cc6d60483f8c0587093c67734a320cde913644fe8fdafb55.svg)
Notice that the points $(2,4)$ and $(1,2),$ defined by the columns of $T,$ lie on the line $y=2x.$

![](images/03/0322f183c16fe82515277d10cf27a93ae753f8eadf7eeb1db4d3c5e404480b09.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=0$ then,  according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that  $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in \Bbb R^2$. So, in this case, we have that
![](images/4a/4a0ce67cffc02e28edffb9efeedca2e21ffc7c0d8b72ccfa0566cb29f6679865.svg)
which maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\{(0,0)\},$ i.e., the set containing only the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$

{:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176160} {:db/id 17592186176932 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177088 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following linear transformation: 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2
$$

The image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Therefore, it can only be one of the following:  

- the whole of $\mathbb{R}^2,$

- a line through the origin, or

- a single point (vector), namely the origin $(0,0).$

Let's denote the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ by $T.$ It turns out that the dimension of the image of $\mathbf{T}$ depends on $\text{rank}(T)$ (or equivalently on $\text{nullity}(T)$ by the rank-nullity theorem). Indeed, we have the following:

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=2,$ then the two columns of $T$ are linearly independent. This means $T$ is invertible and therefore, $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) =  \mathbb{R}^2.$

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto  $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$
![](images/7d/7de193042587cb9362641cbb541477a5e4951e96d9e82f074fb0cc3a86a80d3a.svg)

![](images/88/88baa47cae14d4a43d59b366c13b3c29376678edef2fe34ff505a942ef6af986.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=1,$ then there is a nonzero vector that generates the image of $\mathbf{T}.$ In this case, the image of $\mathbf{T}$ is a one-dimensional subspace of $\Bbb R^2$. So, it is a line passing through the origin.

For example, the following transformation maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the line $y=2x\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/49/4952615b0c4ddf85cc6d60483f8c0587093c67734a320cde913644fe8fdafb55.svg)
Notice that the points $(2,4)$ and $(1,2),$ defined by the columns of $T,$ lie on the line $y=2x.$

![](images/03/0322f183c16fe82515277d10cf27a93ae753f8eadf7eeb1db4d3c5e404480b09.png)

- If $\textrm{rank}(T)=0$ then,  according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that  $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{0}$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in \Bbb R^2$. So, in this case, we have that
![](images/4a/4a0ce67cffc02e28edffb9efeedca2e21ffc7c0d8b72ccfa0566cb29f6679865.svg)
which maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\{(0,0)\},$ i.e., the set containing only the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$

$F(x,y)=3xy\,i-{x}^{2}\,j$ and the circle $C$ given by ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ If the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ is $n=x\,i+y\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

![](images/38/386f010932b5846e7f47a605a94a5b5d580bd35dbe37512b1583d15d29f3dc70.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(3xy\,i-{x}^{2}\,j)\cdot (xi+y\,j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}2{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $2{x}^{2}y.$"} {:db/id 17592186552470 :question/id #uuid "89cfc1e4-7ca7-548a-8985-27acedeb025d" :question/math-academy-id "q-127054" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179645 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9c8ca56-5ea8-547c-80ab-6b1f1347447e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for Flux"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ac0a72f-211e-5ee3-ae1a-cdee72cf08a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-y" :db/id 17592186551763} {:answer/id #uuid "2d182642-d007-5fcb-afa9-a8fa7ef431cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "xy" :db/id 17592186551773} {:answer/id #uuid "5e5d59b2-0373-5c0b-afdf-10bb5a2f8068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186551891} {:answer/id #uuid "728d6f69-9ad5-569f-bfa9-38eefd7f9277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-xy" :db/id 17592186551938} {:answer/id #uuid "74cf75dc-c6e4-5de4-a02f-72578e740790" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}^{2}y" :db/id 17592186551941}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "74cf75dc-c6e4-5de4-a02f-72578e740790" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}^{2}y" :db/id 17592186551941} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1dca841-c306-5d01-962c-2f2e21f3e369" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186552385}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/0d/0dd48f19e9940f1684c0cbb723e772384dda3d7429fc89c2c9dc528f7ebfe42c.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i-{x}^{2}y\,j$ and the square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ shown above. If the flux of $F$ across the side ${C}_{4}$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

In our case, we need to find an expression for the flux across only the part ${C}_{4}$ of the closed curve $C.$ Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $n=-j.$

:question/problem "![](images/5c/5c8aef7238da3bb5aed0fd2a458f6fd9bcd42884bbd350616e58e7a25b1f0fe2.png)

Consider the vector field $F=-2x\,i-2y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/87/878a9992405e5968a03a04d12f42aeb85bca52c07dc7081244b04011643a74bf.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-2x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=3\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-3}^{3}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =-6(3-(-3)) \\  & =(-6)\cdot 6 \\  & =-36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-36)=-144.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262661 :question/id #uuid "6ae07821-3e5f-5e7b-b438-d7c5726b59a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-126890"} {:db/id 17592186262724 :question/id #uuid "b8d84a8f-b961-5115-a51c-b62b1cb780d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-127190" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179646 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "349c29ae-5eb5-5454-a98f-c1adac3d7108" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across a Square Using Symmetry"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00b4648b-d247-5f92-9d2b-f244cac28ba2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186259878} {:answer/id #uuid "4b1a741e-d70d-5584-8f47-17f6fe12b753" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186260521} {:answer/id #uuid "59ab7c77-806c-599b-bff5-2271fa35fc54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186260640} {:answer/id #uuid "825a056c-6bef-533e-873b-b5c171a4706c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186261008} {:answer/id #uuid "ed84226c-f819-56cf-82e3-e3cbf03ace66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186261963}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "4b1a741e-d70d-5584-8f47-17f6fe12b753" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186260521} :answer-field/id #uuid "5d3d48da-ade1-5236-99b3-6c5eeeefbc63" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262283}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/ea/ea53225d28411f38006861d6c8dc46f8d3d1ea01b3bb6183954f68e7124c5682.png)

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/c4/c4e47604540f3cfb3f73af34b0d3eb64bb649e9a42004d22eccc2dd9007de4fb.png)

Consider the vector field $F=2x\,i+y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=16.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(2x\,i+y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 16+2\cdot 8=48.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180043 :question/id #uuid "99c9a666-1234-5907-897c-c576caf3c171" :question/math-academy-id "q-127205" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179647 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "446c5e28-00d3-5a17-ad90-0e66b5ec3a59" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across a Rectangle Using Two Symmetry Properties"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d0b425eb-22e7-5126-9c59-1b5123683fa7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-40" :db/id 17592186177928} {:answer/id #uuid "12c2cb4f-61be-53d6-a2c3-6683264b610e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-48" :db/id 17592186177929} {:answer/id #uuid "302cc11d-b1c7-5509-a279-663acfb5cc82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-20" :db/id 17592186177930} {:answer/id #uuid "307bb29b-0e2c-55ac-acbb-7cf8129ef5d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-32" :db/id 17592186177931} {:answer/id #uuid "3254ddc0-ccb7-5590-9971-d8a69bbb023a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186177932}] :answer-field/id #uuid "f52107b4-b94f-5cca-902b-99cbc154821a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186177927}] :question/problem "![](images/96/9610c7c482b561f4893b562bb6cf891136b30bea20c73fd56caa9a1a12a7a088.png)
