\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{4b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7f52acc-285e-5a90-8147-1ce492061ed5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415148}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e85101-f9b2-5d74-83c6-aabdd8fc2745" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & -28 & 9 \\ -28 & 56 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}14 & -28 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{14} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

 From the second row, we have

$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & -9 \\ -18 & 6 & 3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a-\frac{3b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-\frac{3b}{c}=-1-\frac{3(-2)}{1}=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8a36cb6a-17f3-5f3e-b938-a84d2ec531d8"} {:db/id 17592186500405 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326897 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06c8cf07-1252-5e91-b5c9-12f38c1f946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324034} {:answer/id #uuid "91384dd4-5bcc-5860-814c-f96556460493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325204} {:answer/id #uuid "93d14029-007f-54bd-9d2a-0c82c9066807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186325227} {:answer/id #uuid "a9f7e58b-5b63-5e1f-ae19-6232045969c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186325419} {:answer/id #uuid "b3759c15-e036-5c30-848d-c2b42024912f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324034} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314ea6d-cf55-58df-9abc-6434d47d5c83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "db567127-1e8b-50cb-a3d2-dc5e2ea462cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-40950" :question/problem "$$

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 \\ -24 & 96\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -32\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 & 8 \\ -24 & 96 & -32\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{1}=8.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "17af7b62-4246-55c9-9ac3-d56e9433bbe0"} {:db/id 17592186504729 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134333 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2563641c-3674-599a-bc9b-6a7ff8dc6db8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186324278} {:answer/id #uuid "3380e44e-eb6f-5319-9afd-04efe1186590" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186324383} {:answer/id #uuid "4a8960b7-70fe-5198-ad4d-9a451b90165c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186324576} {:answer/id #uuid "d91bf06c-7c91-517f-8dda-93fec52181f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325860} {:answer/id #uuid "f579c837-0e7b-5922-9481-0a119644e5dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186326131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325860} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6ad0704-99f4-509f-bb7d-ffd14144c5c5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326518}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "871a1be1-8f4a-5616-a788-c400e98cd9b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-40943" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 \\ -30 & 30\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 & 1 \\ -30 & 30 & -1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

#uuid "4cb13173-852b-58a2-8c1f-3d6511a05fac" :question/math-academy-id "q-136920" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,\,\begin{bmatrix}20 & 10 & a \\ 10 & 5 & 5 \\ c & 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}20 & 10 & 10 \\ 10 & 5 & 5 \\ 10 & 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=10+4+10=24.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ba011249-f521-57db-a1bf-2b091aa5de6e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538056}} {:db/id 17592186538043 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134374 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "195f5438-dbcb-5fdf-b558-bce11648bd92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324187} {:answer/id #uuid "34da3d3b-8b0d-5731-9512-7880150858c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324401} {:answer/id #uuid "acc58718-2cff-5c4d-a0a5-bc1a9d33067c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186325439} {:answer/id #uuid "cd585b41-d5de-5636-9761-c198aae3b03f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325751} {:answer/id #uuid "edef752f-66e7-582a-9d21-188b3b7ac00b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186326067}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325751} :answer-field/id #uuid "2c9ed528-04bf-5ec5-8933-3ee5c01fd349" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326296}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "00e4806c-b4ce-579d-8d0e-03b84320da38" :question/math-academy-id "q-41919" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $30a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 \\ -30 & 30\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 & 1 \\ -30 & 30 & -1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{30}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{30}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{30} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
30a+\frac{b}{c}=30\cdot \frac{1}{30}+\frac{1}{1}=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9d99bb3-bbe7-5cd2-986b-c2d9fa71e9d6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538042}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06a52bea-6ee1-5ba3-91a9-fa2c837b2777" :answer/type {:db/id #uuid "8e0db89b-f0c6-50f0-a4df-0e579944e4eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-137033" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}\,+\,{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a-4b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & -4 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-\frac{3}{2})+2{x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{3} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-4b+c=-2-4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+0=4.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c9b55ea0-c7ec-5e84-a315-6b02347bb893"} {:db/id 17592186172110 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171688 :question/id #uuid "416faff8-3422-5bb0-9062-571ccfb18093" :question/math-academy-id "e-10094"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a42fd5c8-9721-5bf4-a1d7-b4b752b09708" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048944} {:db/id 17592186050604}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172336 :question/id #uuid "91e7efeb-2080-5fcf-90b5-7519fc7fd2a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-143249"} {:db/id 17592186172360 :question/id #uuid "25698e55-2308-5356-a383-ee209257efc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-159411"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Slope Parameters"} {:db/id 17592186171688 :question/id #uuid "416faff8-3422-5bb0-9062-571ccfb18093" :question/math-academy-id "e-10094" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172110 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a42fd5c8-9721-5bf4-a1d7-b4b752b09708" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Slope Parameters"}] :question/problem "Let $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7 x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $(x_1,y_1), \: \ldots, \: (x_{8},y_{8})$ of $n=8$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, the mean square error of the model is $1.25$, and $S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2 = 42$, find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the slope of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $6$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for $\widehat{\,\beta}_1$ is given by $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}$.*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and
- $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that

$$
\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7 x
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the slope $\beta_1$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_1$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.
- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.
- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_1$, given by
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}$
where we have:$\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:
$\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$
where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:
$\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=1.6+0.7 x$, our point estimate is
$\widehat{\,\beta}_1 = 0.7$.
- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have
$\alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05$.
We are given that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05$. As a result,
$t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{6,0.05} = 1.943$.
Now, we can compute the margin of error:
$t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = 1.943 \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{1.25}{42}} \approx 0.3$
- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:
$\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = 0.7 \pm 0.3$"} {:db/id 17592186048944} {:db/id 17592186050604} {:db/id 17592186172336 :question/id #uuid "91e7efeb-2080-5fcf-90b5-7519fc7fd2a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-143249"} {:db/id 17592186172360 :question/id #uuid "25698e55-2308-5356-a383-ee209257efc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-159411"} {:db/id 17592186172120 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171696 :question/id #uuid "4d33f1a3-c51f-5a97-a498-def7a8364d81" :question/math-academy-id "e-11098"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "184883f1-85ea-5bd1-8ccd-88226f105da1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172337 :question/id #uuid "1ac4a55b-9276-584c-aabe-f3000169b367" :question/math-academy-id "q-143260"} {:db/id 17592186172372 :question/id #uuid "2d548f76-b08c-5cf0-ae75-59db6390b2b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-159571"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals in Context"} {:db/id 17592186171696 :question/id #uuid "4d33f1a3-c51f-5a97-a498-def7a8364d81" :question/math-academy-id "e-11098" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172120 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "184883f1-85ea-5bd1-8ccd-88226f105da1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals in Context"}] :question/problem "| **Hours ($x$)** | **$4$** | **$4.5$** | **$5.5$** | **$6$** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Grades ($y$)** | $62$ | $65$ | $77$ | $81$ |

The table above shows the number of hours each of four students spent studying for a biology exam and the grades they finally obtained on that exam. The corresponding fitted linear regression line using this sample is $\widehat{\,y} = 21.3 + 10x$.
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overline{x}=5$, and $\textrm{MSE}=1.375$, find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the slope of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 2.92) = 0.05$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the slope is given by*
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}$." :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and
- $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that

$$
\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x = 21.3 + 10x
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the slope $\beta_1$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_1$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.
- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.
- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_1$, given by
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}$
where we have:$\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:
$\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$
where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:
$\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y} = 21.3 + 10x$, our point estimate is
$\widehat{\,\beta}_1 = 10$.
- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have
$\alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05$.
We are given that $P(T > 2.92) = 0.05$. As a result,
$t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{2,0.05} = 2.92$.Computing $S_{xx}$, we get
$∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2}|= (4 - 5)^{2} + (4.5 - 5)^{2} + (5.5 - 5)^{2} + (6 - 5)^{2}; = 1 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 1; = 2.5$. Now, we can compute the margin of error:
$t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = 2.92 \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{1.375}{2.5}} \approx 2.2$
- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:
$\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = 10 \pm 2.2$"} {:db/id 17592186172337 :question/id #uuid "1ac4a55b-9276-584c-aabe-f3000169b367" :question/math-academy-id "q-143260" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172120 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "184883f1-85ea-5bd1-8ccd-88226f105da1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c93c89a1-098f-50a0-ac3a-08dc83a84320" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 0.8" :db/id 17592186168886} {:answer/id #uuid "fd8140f2-ef6b-5dd8-a2ff-decbe7e83052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 0.2" :db/id 17592186168887} {:answer/id #uuid "414e1bd2-3ced-5d49-bc43-dff07a90e6dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 1.2" :db/id 17592186168888} {:answer/id #uuid "4d80f3c6-82c6-521a-a2a2-b01992d77cc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 1.4" :db/id 17592186168889} {:answer/id #uuid "7dd0969e-f100-53ab-a342-238468fad53c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 0.6" :db/id 17592186168890}] :answer-field/id #uuid "10137e41-2459-5b06-b3a4-3230a1046efa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186168885}] :question/problem "| **Age ($x$)** | **$3$** | **$5$** | **$7$** | **$9$** |

[{:db/id 17592186173029 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173218 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population.

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$ are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x}
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i$, and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following:

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize,

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$,
- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1$, and
- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0$.

In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the slope parameter $\beta_1$." :tutorial/id #uuid "37635fea-c916-5aaa-8856-9d9f7edd8d50" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6279 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8fa03444-9380-5875-abf1-e75bbb767c7e" :step/math-academy-id 38065 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173050}} {:db/id 17592186173030 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172110 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171688 :question/id #uuid "416faff8-3422-5bb0-9062-571ccfb18093" :question/math-academy-id "e-10094"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a42fd5c8-9721-5bf4-a1d7-b4b752b09708" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048944} {:db/id 17592186050604}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172336} {:db/id 17592186172360}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Slope Parameters"} :step/id #uuid "48431442-8239-5535-a7a1-fb9068d1372d" :step/math-academy-id 38066 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173049}} {:db/id 17592186173048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173228 :tutorial/content "We'll now derive our expression for the confidence interval for our slope parameter estimate $\widehat{\beta_1}$.

Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$.

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Let's assume that our "global" regression line (i.e., the line that best fits the entire population) is given by

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

For each

$$
i=1,2,\ldots,n
$$

let

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i
$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and

$$
\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2$. The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/69/69135b6cdc4d34f5422da39bac5d15624d16f4817e91f282974507c711953796.png)

This means that each $y_i$ is a normally distributed random variable with

$$
y_i \sim N\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \sigma^2\right)
$$

It can be shown that

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_1}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

We'll derive these results separately in a while. But for now, we'll simply state them.

Using these results, we can express the distribution of $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as

$$
\widehat{\beta}_1 \sim N\left(\beta_1, \: \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} \right)
$$

We do not know $\sigma^2$, the variance of the error terms. However, it can be shown that the mean squared error, given by

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$.

Our estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_1$ is now given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}
$$

Since this is an *estimate* of the standard error, it can be shown that the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 -\beta_1}{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta_1}]}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

Finally, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the slope $\beta_1$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "beb8e9bf-ec60-55d5-8b18-154ccf17124a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6964 :tutorial/title "Deriving an Expression for the Confidence Interval"} :step/id #uuid "3e7ac509-670d-5307-9c8f-7ca79acc2ee7" :step/math-academy-id 42154 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173077}} {:db/id 17592186173049 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172120 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171696 :question/id #uuid "4d33f1a3-c51f-5a97-a498-def7a8364d81" :question/math-academy-id "e-11098"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "184883f1-85ea-5bd1-8ccd-88226f105da1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172337} {:db/id 17592186172372}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals in Context"} :step/id #uuid "6279ed73-ac15-54d7-b41e-828f02e67018" :step/math-academy-id 42155 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173048}} {:db/id 17592186173050 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173229 :tutorial/content "Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the slope $\beta_1$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_1$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed by fitting the data points from our sample.
- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.
- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_1$, given by
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}$
where we have:$\textrm{MSE}$ is the so-called **mean squared error** of the model, given by
$\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$,
where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:
$\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2$

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by
$(y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)$.
- The expression $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$ gives the sum of the squared residuals of our regression model.
- Even considering the entire population, the data points will not fall on a perfectly straight line. Thus, errors are present even in the "true" regression model. These errors have some (unknown) variance, which we'll denote as $\sigma^2$.
- It can be shown that the $\textrm{MSE}$ is an *unbiased* estimator of $\sigma^2$." :tutorial/id #uuid "7336a854-0d9f-5a8e-aaf1-b47ea3b4cff1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6966 :tutorial/title "Summary of the Key Result"} :step/id #uuid "2e953bfd-106c-5024-96ce-735fef10d8c0" :step/math-academy-id 42157 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173030}} {:db/id 17592186173077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173249 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we made use of the following results:

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_1}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i
$$

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)nx^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using our result for $S_{xy}$, we can write

$$
β_{1}^(^) = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}y_{i}
$$

where

$$
k_i = \dfrac{x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}
$$

The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0$
- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$
- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}$

Now, we compute the mean and variance of $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as follows:

- For the mean, we have

$$

$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$ are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x}
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i$, and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following:

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize,

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$,
- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1$, and
- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0$.

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_1$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed by fitting the data points from our sample.
- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.
- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_1$, given by
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}$
where we have:$\textrm{MSE}$ is the so-called **mean squared error** of the model, given by
$\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$,
where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:
$\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2$

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by
$(y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)$.
- The expression $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$ gives the sum of the squared residuals of our regression model.

Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$.

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Let's assume that our "global" regression line (i.e., the line that best fits the entire population) is given by

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

For each

$$
i=1,2,\ldots,n
$$

let

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i
$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and

$$
\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2$. The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/69/69135b6cdc4d34f5422da39bac5d15624d16f4817e91f282974507c711953796.png)

This means that each $y_i$ is a normally distributed random variable with

$$
y_i \sim N\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \sigma^2\right)
$$

It can be shown that

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_1}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

We'll derive these results separately in a while. But for now, we'll simply state them.

Using these results, we can express the distribution of $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as

$$
\widehat{\beta}_1 \sim N\left(\beta_1, \: \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} \right)
$$

We do not know $\sigma^2$, the variance of the error terms. However, it can be shown that the mean squared error, given by

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$.

Our estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_1$ is now given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}
$$

Since this is an *estimate* of the standard error, it can be shown that the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 -\beta_1}{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta_1}]}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

Finally, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the slope $\beta_1$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "beb8e9bf-ec60-55d5-8b18-154ccf17124a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6964 :tutorial/title "Deriving an Expression for the Confidence Interval"} :step/id #uuid "3e7ac509-670d-5307-9c8f-7ca79acc2ee7" :step/math-academy-id 42154 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173077}} {:db/id 17592186173228 :tutorial/content "We'll now derive our expression for the confidence interval for our slope parameter estimate $\widehat{\beta_1}$.

:topic/math-academy-id 3218} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167962 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168050 :tutorial/content "Recall that the indicator function $\mathbf{1}_A(x)$ of a set $A$ equals $1$ if $x \in A$ and $0$ if $x \notin A.$ 
![](images/c1/c12d2f59eb7eb9730fc7576bb426cff90a3cff4ac8577c3f212db8101197300b.svg)

In this lesson, we introduce a more general notation that allows us to write indicator functions for any condition, not just set membership.

The **Iverson bracket notation** $\mathbf{1}[P]$ takes a predicate $P$ and returns
![](images/4d/4dbe29e205fecf97bd7d4c0bfbf810c7336a6a50198fa35319e7ae8b0ac505c0.svg)

For example:

- $\mathbf{1}[3 > 2] = 1$ because $3 > 2$ is true.

- $\mathbf{1}[5 \leq 4] = 0$ because $5 \leq 4$ is false.

- $\mathbf{1}[7 \in \{2, 5, 7\}] = 1$ because $7$ is an element of $\{2, 5, 7\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "83dcb8a1-56ef-59d0-addc-dfaa18628695" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14816 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "691d9e29-1625-5c4d-8958-88262d0bc24b" :step/math-academy-id 610829 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167963}} {:db/id 17592186167963 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166967 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166577 :question/id #uuid "5ebf00aa-406d-5286-b4ae-0f0044ce9b4d" :question/math-academy-id "e-21905"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "144f097c-0080-5857-b992-8996f194ca22" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048808} {:db/id 17592186049002}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167299} {:db/id 17592186167300} {:db/id 17592186521461} {:db/id 17592186521476} {:db/id 17592186521478} {:db/id 17592186521512} {:db/id 17592186521540}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Indicator Functions to Check Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "9565a3bd-15ac-5aa0-88fe-2e6938ac1515" :step/math-academy-id 610830 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167964}} {:db/id 17592186167964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168059 :tutorial/content "The set-based notation from the previous lesson is a special case of Iverson bracket notation. Specifically,

$$
\mathbf{1}_A(x) = \mathbf{1}[x \in A].
$$

1. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f$. We first carry out horizontal stretches and reflections, followed by horizontal translations.

$$
y=-f(x+3)
$$

we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x)$.
- Translate it to the left by $3$ units $y=f(x+3)$.

- Then, reflect the result across the $x$- axis to get the graph of $y=-f(x+3)$.

- Apply transformation $(\textrm{T}1)$: Translate $y=-f(x-2)$ by $3$ units up to get the graph of $y=-f(x-2)+3$.

The triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over the region $R$ (shown above) can be expressed as the following repeated integral:

$$
\iiint\limits_R  f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\int_0^1\int_{\sqrt{z}}^1\int_0^{y^2-z} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z
$$

Rewrite this repeated integral by integrating first with respect to $x,$ then $z,$ and then $y.$" :question/worked-solution "From the given repeated integral, we see that $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: \sqrt{z} \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq y^2-z \big\}
$$

We wish to rewrite our triple integral as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\int_a^b\int_{v_1(y)}^{v_2(y)}\int_{u_1(y,z)}^{u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y
$$

Since both repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\int_a^b\int_{v_1(y)}^{v_2(y)}\int_0^{y^2-z} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/ec/ec195fe4aa1bec5221ec25a1921dfe36e78db34ad3e295fec541c1d05a85d60d.png)

The region $D$ is a type II region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: \sqrt{z} \leq y \leq 1 \big\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}z$ to $\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(y),$ is 

$$
y=\sqrt{z}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
z = y^2
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region $D$ is

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z\leq y^2 \big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/84/841f014cae7bb224b6f743a86583cb0a70a423d60176b2efd6482d155aa020bc.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}V
=

\int_0^1 \int_{0}^{y^2} \int_0^{y^2-z} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}x\:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048986} {:db/id 17592186050165} {:db/id 17592186050197} {:db/id 17592186050524} {:db/id 17592186129528 :question/id #uuid "318d728a-5f9a-5d33-846c-76ae520cec78" $$

$$

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{y}\le x\le 1},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/f4/f49af5da2e4f1f281700e16c4659fabfcd0b15661947ca985d38f208f8563877.png)

{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y
$$

Since both repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{1+y-z}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/8f/8fff232443e6da697862c2e85a9d3abfe0554b80c2fcbfa8c93de42b94a45691.png)

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{z}}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the bottom boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(y),$ is 

$$
y=\sqrt[3]{z}\,⟹\,z={y}^{3}
$$

and the top boundary of the region is

$$
z=1.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region $D$ is

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,{y}^{3}\le z\le 1},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/72/726ff420cae25c40f212714141a134fab84633cca7f49bdd268f0668d5248766.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{1}{\int }_{1+y-z}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.

:question/problem "By changing the order of integration, find the missing limits in the following repeated integral.

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{2y}-1}^{2-y/2}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{-1}^{p}{\int }_{0}^{(z+1)^{2}/2}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z+{\int }_{1}^{q}{\int }_{0}^{r}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z+{\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{{v}_{3}(z)}^{{v}_{4}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{3}(xy,z)}^{{u}_{4}(y,z)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,\sqrt{2y}-1\le z\le 2-\frac{y}{2},\,\,-2z\le x\le y+3}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{2y}-1}^{2-y/2}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z+{\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{{v}_{3}(z)}^{{v}_{4}(x)}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/a4/a4de9d9df51efcec67253a1c7118466f29459ffd5c9136c144d33500ec5557bc.png)

The region $D$ is a type I region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{2y}-1\le z\le 2-\frac{y}{2}}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we split $D$ into two type II regions.

![](images/18/18bb3e55f076e022176bb60df27d5665ed2d91d75d618969c04ce192378db922.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the lower region, written in the form $y=y(z),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=\frac{1}{2}(z+1)^{2}.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the upper region, written in the form $y=y(z),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=4-2z.$

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}={(y,z)\,:\,-1\le z\le 1,\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2}(z+1)^{2}}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}={(y,z)\,:\,1\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le 4-2z}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{(z+1)^{2}/2}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-2z}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129280 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128858 :question/id #uuid "72795f5f-0d15-52e1-bfd8-997ae8e20265" :question/math-academy-id "e-12404"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bbc25e04-f750-5d25-829a-ea061f010502" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129522 :question/id #uuid "9b2728e6-ec74-51e3-ae11-aa2ea4502e36" :question/math-academy-id "q-161557"} {:db/id 17592186129529 :question/id #uuid "c00cd44a-d34c-5f6e-aacf-b4ef475837d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-162253"} {:db/id 17592186281423 :question/id #uuid "871a8fcb-2fd3-5ed7-9580-a8fb144d6d26" :question/math-academy-id "q-162236"} {:db/id 17592186281429 :question/id #uuid "90d38ce0-881b-51da-a009-3b19a6113351" :question/math-academy-id "q-162250"} {:db/id 17592186281430 :question/id #uuid "716050fb-6be1-5474-89de-ead930408990" :question/math-academy-id "q-162251"} {:db/id 17592186281439 :question/id #uuid "0f6f33b6-ca94-5283-b578-c8f6fe4dfa5c" :question/math-academy-id "q-162325"} {:db/id 17592186281440 :question/id #uuid "55c78036-de48-5eea-9253-f540a61a0813" :question/math-academy-id "q-162330"} {:db/id 17592186281441 :question/id #uuid "63019a17-1ba4-5f61-b529-aa74e153abd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-162331"} {:db/id 17592186281443 :question/id #uuid "11b88039-dcd3-5fe3-9ad3-e8f58ab164bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-162334"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Triple Integrals by Changing the Projection Type"} {:db/id 17592186128858 :question/id #uuid "72795f5f-0d15-52e1-bfd8-997ae8e20265" :question/math-academy-id "e-12404" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186129280 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bbc25e04-f750-5d25-829a-ea061f010502" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Triple Integrals by Changing the Projection Type"}] :question/problem "Evaluate
$\displaystyle
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{y}^{1} \int_{0}^{y} 3e^{x^3} \: \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.$

*Hint: Change change the order of integration to $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} 3e^{x^3} \:\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: y \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq y \right\}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{0}^{y} 3e^{x^3} \:\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/bd/bdd856ef8a7940a009b7ee27d6614fdb8c042e6655c2316ce4db0633bfd04e9f.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad y \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $y = y(x),$ is

$$
x = y \qquad\Longrightarrow \qquad y = x
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y = 0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq x \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/1e/1e28e1cef9743da80d6fd2d38840810b12239d8546254c4d4cca767568f76a53.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{\int }_{0}^{y}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[z]_{0}^{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3y{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{e}^{{x}^{3}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129522 :question/id #uuid "9b2728e6-ec74-51e3-ae11-aa2ea4502e36" :question/math-academy-id "q-161557"} {:db/id 17592186129529 :question/id #uuid "c00cd44a-d34c-5f6e-aacf-b4ef475837d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-162253" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129280 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bbc25e04-f750-5d25-829a-ea061f010502" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Triple Integrals by Changing the Projection Type"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "562d0704-f8bb-56d1-ad51-2efebd134efa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e-1" :db/id 17592186279380} {:answer/id #uuid "65d6262f-31f6-5c6a-a73b-e3a7b55728a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186279520} {:answer/id #uuid "d301c278-fecb-50eb-a7b0-cf15bf32c993" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186280453} {:answer/id #uuid "d5144876-7c4f-5ef7-b912-312e36e6a5a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186280471} {:answer/id #uuid "f7eac3ef-b262-53cc-9f03-528d3cd26d5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186280764}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "d5144876-7c4f-5ef7-b912-312e36e6a5a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186280471} :answer-field/id #uuid "35b87413-958f-55b3-b6a9-0b06c650f7b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186280929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Evaluate
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{z}\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {e}^{z/x}}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $y,$ the $y$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](images/e8/e83c249a6abf9710a201462e16c646a11411dbcdbca46f34e9beb8d2db7a654b.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xz$-plane:

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\sqrt{z}\le x\le 1}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $z=z(x),$ is

$$
x=\sqrt{z}\,⟹\,z={x}^{2}
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
z=0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/7e/7e684766b85a214d1f1dd7845979052c532e11ecce74d0284b8fc379b5669957.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}[y]_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{z/x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{z/x}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{e}^{z/x}]_{z=0}^{z={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x{e}^{x}-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[(x-1){e}^{x}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-\frac{1}{2})-(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281423 :question/id #uuid "871a8fcb-2fd3-5ed7-9580-a8fb144d6d26" :question/math-academy-id "q-162236"} {:db/id 17592186281429 :question/id #uuid "90d38ce0-881b-51da-a009-3b19a6113351" :question/math-academy-id "q-162250" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129280 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bbc25e04-f750-5d25-829a-ea061f010502" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Triple Integrals by Changing the Projection Type"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e74a82f-4bd7-5c2f-8751-ac19f153eecf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{\pi }+2" :db/id 17592186278722} {:answer/id #uuid "90db29e8-ff5c-5044-9543-fee4992d484f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2e+1" :db/id 17592186279884} {:answer/id #uuid "98b9f9a0-15c1-5dd0-a2e6-9d749f3ab244" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186279942} {:answer/id #uuid "a8b2e64a-c3e7-5882-8acf-3672f33bf2ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{\pi /2}" :db/id 17592186280082} {:answer/id #uuid "bfd49d7b-3fa3-52dd-9351-bc6320abedca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e-1" :db/id 17592186280277}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "bfd49d7b-3fa3-52dd-9351-bc6320abedca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e-1" :db/id 17592186280277} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c737135-2cdd-59c3-a038-3b9c326dc776" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186280994}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Evaluate
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le z\le {e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/38/38eb7316b1ee5c947eee37a9cc10530ff08f793b7564cf0d88c6ce24e1239f9d.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y=0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/24/241abff7fae5d6ba3301d605ff4c4e62ff61e423515c7bc3a54b17b9aec525aa.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}[{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}[z]_{0}^{{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}[y]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi /2}-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}) \\  & =-(1-e) \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}

${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{arccos}⁡y}{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \operatorname{arccos}⁡y,\,\,0\le x\le 2}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/c5/c5f4ec9b9b12411f3057bc074a14a1f541c768c30d3a9746d7a0484b0491ad2e.png)

The region $D$ is type I region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le \operatorname{arccos}⁡y}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we write $D$ as a type II region.

Notice that the left boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y=0
$$

and the right boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $y=y(z),$ is

$$
z=\operatorname{arccos}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡z.
$$

Then, the type II representation of the region is

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{cos}⁡z},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/07/077fc8133673cd57aba570cca9a6e0f5f25aa742720948c46db2b9e1d05add69.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{arccos}⁡y}{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}[{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}y\,[x]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2z)\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[z+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2z]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281441 :question/id #uuid "63019a17-1ba4-5f61-b529-aa74e153abd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-162331"} {:db/id 17592186281443 :question/id #uuid "11b88039-dcd3-5fe3-9ad3-e8f58ab164bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-162334" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129280 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bbc25e04-f750-5d25-829a-ea061f010502" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Triple Integrals by Changing the Projection Type"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "48e2a033-443c-584c-a15f-eea6d9dae46d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4e" :db/id 17592186279242} {:answer/id #uuid "642f63b8-b430-5120-8afa-60337721d5a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\pi e+1" :db/id 17592186279503} {:answer/id #uuid "f1d73ed0-76b2-520e-9de6-dc0f038550ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi e}{3}" :db/id 17592186280698} {:answer/id #uuid "f5cf9286-3e28-5594-96ef-d23587fa7550" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\pi (e-2)}{3}" :db/id 17592186280744} {:answer/id #uuid "f899ec44-2bfd-5d46-ac07-d2e8f6a0ae6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186280775}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f5cf9286-3e28-5594-96ef-d23587fa7550" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\pi (e-2)}{3}" :db/id 17592186280744} :answer-field/id #uuid "06018cfb-ebc1-54fb-ba81-4655903daaf9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186280840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le z\le e,\,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡z\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{3}y}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}y}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/14/14c67512e143995cbfcfcf9e80c8d0975bbbc42368c97aa29956bd2d3f3454a8.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,1\le z\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡z\le y\le 1}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
z=1
$$

and the top boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $z=z(y),$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,⟹\,z={e}^{y}.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le z\le {e}^{y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d18470b45d21b4734187c1f639784a4e75924ed212e3fa4c7a214d19eaeb6022.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}y}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}y}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}y}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}{[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{3}y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}\frac{\pi }{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{y}}\text{d}z]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\pi }{3}[z]_{1}^{{e}^{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\pi }{3}({e}^{y}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}[{e}^{y}-y]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}(e-1-1+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi (e-2)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049016} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a8851999-6145-5384-9b2a-5c298247d5af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "p =-1, q =
