17592186130215 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130458 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the following repeated integral:

$$
\int_0^1\int_{x^2}^{1} \int_{0}^{1}\,\dfrac{e^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\textrm{d}z\, \textrm{d}y\, \textrm{d}x
$$

For this repeated integral, the integration domain is the type I region 

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\:  x^2 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

as illustrated below.

![](images/54/54bdc97100c19657d261f35123eec8a4d2d927f0d92073462ae6e9335aef0921.png)

The expression '$\,\textrm{d}z\, \textrm{d}y\, \textrm{d}x$' means we should integrate first with respect to $z,$ then with respect to $y,$ and lastly with respect to $x.$ Let's see what happens when we attempt to integrate in this order:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot [z]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot proceed any further because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of $\dfrac{e^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}.$

To resolve this issue, we first note that the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane is the type I plane region $D$ shown below.

![](images/5f/5f681a48038d51cdb592b265e7f482aa03fffb2d1235df02b38390083fe73f3a.png)

This region can also be represented as the type II plane region.

![](images/89/89836e63d7f184624334daef7c50239dc818324f24071118aa41a2a1ca5accb6.png)

Using set notation, $D$'s representation as a type II plane region is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq \sqrt{y} \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate this integral by keeping the inner integral the same and swapping the order of integration in the middle and outer integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate this integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}[z]_{0}^{1}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot [x]_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\frac{{e}^{y}}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{y}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =e-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note the following:

- In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute triple integrals by changing the representation of the projection $D$ of $R$ from a type I plane region to type II (and vice-versa).

- It's also possible to change the spatial (i.e., three-dimensional) representation of $R$ from type I to type II, type I to type III, type II to type III, etc. This is slightly more involved, so we'll leave that discussion for a separate lesson.

This is a geometric sequence with common ratio $r = \dfrac12.$ What is the behavior of this sequence as $n\to\infty?$

$$
a_1 = \dfrac32, \qquad a_2 = \dfrac34, \qquad a_3 = \dfrac38, \qquad a_4 = \dfrac{3}{16}, \qquad \ldots\,.
$$

![](images/8b/8b31b82126b56226a74aac5f3406d2d4ad5c85ec5c468e089acd028eba6c0469.png)

7, 8\}$, $Y = \{1, 3, 5\}$, and $Z = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$, find $X \cup Y$, $Y \cup Z$, and $Z \cup X$." :question/worked-solution "The union $X \cup Y$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $X$ or $Y$, or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
X∪Y &= {2, 5, 7, 8}∪{1, 3, 5} \\
&= {1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8}
\end{aligned}
$$

The union $Y \cup Z$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $Y$ or $Z$, or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y∪Z &= {1, 3, 5}∪{2, 4, 6, 8} \\
&= {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8}
\end{aligned}
$$

The union $Z \cup X$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $Z$ or $X$, or both. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z∪X &= {2, 4, 6, 8}∪{2, 5, 7, 8} \\
&= {2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157566 :question/id #uuid "0b31d4bf-a16e-5bc9-8d07-4f4f1dee7270" :question/math-academy-id "q-1219"} {:db/id 17592186157567 :question/id #uuid "7c210194-4f34-5c6f-af7f-c3f66eb89b06" :question/math-academy-id "q-1220"} {:db/id 17592186233059 :question/id #uuid "d225b6fc-9a5d-575c-b160-431e6d3f0348" :question/math-academy-id "q-102071"} {:db/id 17592186234421 :question/id #uuid "eb52dfa1-582a-5919-bcb1-54e17134a2a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-80423"} {:db/id 17592186157281 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157085 :question/id #uuid "6a3a434d-5fe4-53cd-ba34-4d10db5c85fe" :question/math-academy-id "e-7154"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "03cc876e-66d5-51af-ad8d-6c20bc599609" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157765 :question/id #uuid "00d13187-04b4-5974-9e1e-fe5bf0b64c43" :question/math-academy-id "q-36190"} {:db/id 17592186157788 :question/id #uuid "245baf95-d62b-57ce-8782-7644e8e59da6" :question/math-academy-id "q-80874"} {:db/id 17592186233063 :question/id #uuid "170296b9-c190-5827-9bae-43bfced8507f" :question/math-academy-id "q-102146"} {:db/id 17592186234433 :question/id #uuid "26c3bb06-29af-54da-a6db-d70352bbb70a" :question/math-academy-id "q-81562"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Unions of Sets Given Verbally"} {:db/id 17592186157085 :question/id #uuid "6a3a434d-5fe4-53cd-ba34-4d10db5c85fe" :question/math-academy-id "e-7154" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186157281 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "03cc876e-66d5-51af-ad8d-6c20bc599609" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Unions of Sets Given Verbally"}] :question/problem "Let $A$ and $B$ be the set of all multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ and the set of all multiples of $6$ that are greater than $0$, respectively. What is $A \cup B$?" :question/worked-solution "The multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
A = \{4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32, 36 \ldots \}
$$

Likewise, multiples of $6$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
B = \{6,12,18,24,30,36,\ldots \}
$$

Now, $A \cup B$ is the *union* of $A$ and $B$, which means that we want to find the elements that are in either $A$ or $B$, or both.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
A∪B &= {4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, …}∪{6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, …} \\
&= {4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28, 30, 32, 36, …}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157765 :question/id #uuid "00d13187-04b4-5974-9e1e-fe5bf0b64c43" :question/math-academy-id "q-36190"} {:db/id 17592186157788 :question/id #uuid "245baf95-d62b-57ce-8782-7644e8e59da6" :question/math-academy-id "q-80874"} {:db/id 17592186233063 :question/id #uuid "170296b9-c190-5827-9bae-43bfced8507f" :question/math-academy-id "q-102146"} {:db/id 17592186234433 :question/id #uuid "26c3bb06-29af-54da-a6db-d70352bbb70a" :question/math-academy-id "q-81562" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186157281 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "03cc876e-66d5-51af-ad8d-6c20bc599609" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Unions of Sets Given Verbally"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $A$ and $B$ be the set of all multiples of $4$ greater than $0$ and the set of all multiples of $5$ greater than $0,$ respectively. What is $A\cup B?$" :question/worked-solution "The multiples of $4$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
A={4,8,12,16,20,…}.
$$

Likewise, multiples of $5$ that are greater than $0$ are

$$
B={5,10,15,20,…}.
$$

Now, $A\cup B$ is the *union* of $A$ and $B,$ which means that we want to find the elements that are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both. In other words, $A\cup B$ denotes the set of natural numbers that are either multiple of $4$ or multiple of $5.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cup B & ={4,8,12,16,20,…}\cup {5,10,15,20,…} \\  & ={4,5,8,10,12,15,16,20,…}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157291 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157095 :question/id #uuid "3de58ae0-eb3a-5faf-a404-0347d64d4979" :question/math-academy-id "e-7171"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37248a2e-6deb-5b4c-af42-51c358f21110" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049065}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157804 :question/id #uuid "75b2bcd6-fce4-5c6c-b324-6f65fe9c4f30" :question/math-academy-id "q-81418"} {:db/id 17592186157805 :question/id #uuid "06215931-7dcb-5df8-841d-4242842ecdc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-81419"} {:db/id 17592186233058 :question/id #uuid "b2a78df4-f852-500a-b23e-2d5ff58187c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-102051"} {:db/id 17592186234432 :question/id #uuid "e2c958c5-b4c3-5056-8455-f0cd2a648bf2" :question/math-academy-id "q-81549"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Union of Sets Using a Venn Diagram"} {:db/id 17592186157095 :question/id #uuid "3de58ae0-eb3a-5faf-a404-0347d64d4979" :question/math-academy-id "e-7171" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186157291 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37248a2e-6deb-5b4c-af42-51c358f21110" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Union of Sets Using a Venn Diagram"}] :question/problem "![](images/dc/dcddc9ee6fe49965ea4f261fcb43c6f7ccd14193910e864b950745ef513e67a6.png)

For example, consider the sets

$$
A = \{a,b,c \}
$$

and

$$
B = \{b, d, e \}
$$

We can represent these sets using a Venn diagram, as follows:

![](images/83/8351db4817ac8b0d2991fe8ef09ee1f2583c84cb772114ef0614a0ef96c96389.png)

The union $A \cup B$ consists of all the elements that are in $A$ or $B$, or both. To represent $A \cup B$, we will shade in all the area that is contained within either $A$ or $B$, or both.

![](images/e9/e912fe53d530ac47245c916bd16f1758df487ded32da88abfab253ed1ee0cc63.png)

The elements $a,b,c,d,e$ are in either $A$ or $B$, or both. Therefore, the union of $A$ and $B$ is

$$
A \cup B = \{a,b,c,d,e \}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7d7d339f-bbdd-5e0c-9913-c3e6cdc13958" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4331 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cb58bb7c-83ec-5c28-97f8-f0bbb8d177aa" :step/math-academy-id 26362 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158124}} {:db/id 17592186158124 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157291 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157095 :question/id #uuid "3de58ae0-eb3a-5faf-a404-0347d64d4979" :question/math-academy-id "e-7171"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37248a2e-6deb-5b4c-af42-51c358f21110" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049065}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157804} {:db/id 17592186157805} {:db/id 17592186233058} {:db/id 17592186234432}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Union of Sets Using a Venn Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "dddb7100-0567-5656-8491-fb90b50c309a" :step/math-academy-id 26376 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158127}} {:db/id 17592186158127 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158478 :tutorial/content "Although Venn diagrams can be useful to visualize unions, we do not have to draw a Venn diagram every time we wish to compute a union.

For example, let's again consider the sets

$$
A = \{a,b,c \}
$$

and

$$
B = \{b, d, e \}
$$

This time, we will compute the union $A \cup B$ without using a Venn diagram. We just need to find all the elements that are in either $A$ or $B$, or both.

So, we will start with the elements of $A$, and then go through the elements of $B$ to look for any elements that we do not already have. Remember that we are looking for elements that we do *not* already have in $A$.

- For the element $b \in B$, we have $b \in A. \quad \color{red}\times$
- For the element $d \in B$, we have $d \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$
- For the element $e \in B$, we have $e \not \in A. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

So, to get the union, we need to take the elements of $A$ and also include $d$ and $e$.

Therefore, the union of $A$ and $B$ is

$$
A \cup B = \{a,b,c,d,e \}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "387bbd7c-3300-588c-9e61-54dda9490e81" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4338 :tutorial/title "Unions Without Venn Diagrams"} :step/id #uuid "1b8eae72-5bc4-59c4-9a2d-4ed1e29eec02" :step/math-academy-id 26380 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158109}}] :activity/title "The Union of Sets" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157483} {:db/id 17592186158115 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158472 :tutorial/content "The **union** of two sets $A$ and $B$, denoted $A \cup B$, is the set of all elements belonging to either $A$ or $B$, or both.

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t+1,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(t+1)\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(t+1)\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541085 :question/id #uuid "5b66c4d7-d9b1-5cb6-840d-18a9a3471ea0" :question/math-academy-id "q-138966"} {:db/id 17592186129319 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$

$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟹{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{16}\text{d}u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{3}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(27-1) \\  & =13\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186530465 :question/id #uuid "6528b016-7e7a-5f42-bb80-0fc7063586be" :question/math-academy-id "q-352031" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "961eb0d5-8253-50e6-a961-755f2db89486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi}{6}" :db/id 17592186529944}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186529944} :answer-field/id #uuid "a3f06b1d-08c6-50bc-8914-e903872c2d7d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186530333}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(t/2)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{csc}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}2\pi \,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[u]}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]=\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]}^{2}+{[\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)=1$ and ${sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1={tan}^{2}⁡(t)$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{tan}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot |\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-2\pi [\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-2\pi (\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =-2\pi \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =6\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{5}-2{t}^{3}-3t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0} \\  & =6\pi [0-(\frac{27}{6}-\frac{9}{2}-\frac{9}{2})] \\  & =6\pi \cdot \frac{27}{6} \\  & =27\pi .\end{aligned}

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=1$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t)={t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{({t}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot {t}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using direct integration we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-2)-(\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{22}{5}+\frac{4}{5}] \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{26}{5} \\  & =\frac{52\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2e8bc30-41c9-56c8-a5b2-e047a033dedb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\pi {\int "e80c9bca-b203-5866-835e-d0d29bbfdf22" :topic/math-academy-id 1995} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186130300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130449 :tutorial/content "Recall that when we rotate a curve by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, the area generated by this surface of revolution is given by

$$
S =  \int 2\pi y \, \textrm{d}s.
$$

Now suppose we have a parametrically defined curve: 

$$
x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t \in \left[t_1,t_2\right].
$$

In the case of a parametric curve, the arc length element $\textrm{d}s$ is given by

$$
\textrm{d}s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

As a result, we obtain the following formula for the surface area generated by rotating a parametrically defined curve about the $x$-axis:

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t
$$

 

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "36a57433-1c78-58b8-860c-0ea6e3471761" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6113 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c5c27e9e-03cb-5a93-8a56-bd33588960fe" :step/math-academy-id 618749 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130301}} {:db/id 17592186130301 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130466 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}, \qquad
t \in [0,\pi].
$$

If we rotate this curve by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we obtain a sphere of radius $1.$ 

![](images/d0/d0d323b764b70d3f2830d821636a9bc27b40e7f7e9f45df909c81dd279dc16e4.png)

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of our surface of revolution can be computed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi (-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-2\pi (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-2\pi (-1-1) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f849fe7f-670f-5a7f-8dc7-dbbd33a876f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7707 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "031d5fb3-1834-595b-8a36-577430a0f9a7" :step/math-academy-id 618750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130302}} {:db/id 17592186130302 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129318 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129073 :question/id #uuid "066f76be-83f6-52fd-ab3f-00786d18f64e" :question/math-academy-id "e-9866"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b02082a8-b56e-5478-859d-51db7273f765" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049272} {:db/id 17592186050860}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129487} {:db/id 17592186129493} {:db/id 17592186269195} {:db/id 17592186269202} {:db/id 17592186388599} {:db/id 17592186435123} {:db/id 17592186435125} {:db/id 17592186527172} {:db/id 17592186531587} {:db/id 17592186532670} {:db/id 17592186541085}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X"} :step/id #uuid "a6a3e1f3-c536-58d3-a81e-7966262884ce" :step/math-academy-id 618751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130303}} {:db/id 17592186130303 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130450 :tutorial/content "When we rotate a curve by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis, the area generated by this surface of revolution is given by

radians about the $x$-axis, the area generated by this surface of revolution is given by

$$
S =  \int 2\pi y \, \textrm{d}s.
$$

Now suppose we have a parametrically defined curve: 

$$
x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t \in \left[t_1,t_2\right].
$$

In the case of a parametric curve, the arc length element $\textrm{d}s$ is given by

$$
\textrm{d}s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

As a result, we obtain the following formula for the surface area generated by rotating a parametrically defined curve about the $x$-axis:

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "36a57433-1c78-58b8-860c-0ea6e3471761" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6113 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130301 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130466 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}, \qquad
t \in [0,\pi].
$$

If we rotate this curve by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we obtain a sphere of radius $1.$ 

![](images/d0/d0d323b764b70d3f2830d821636a9bc27b40e7f7e9f45df909c81dd279dc16e4.png)

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of our surface of revolution can be computed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi (-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-2\pi (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-2\pi (-1-1) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f849fe7f-670f-5a7f-8dc7-dbbd33a876f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7707 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "031d5fb3-1834-595b-8a36-577430a0f9a7" :step/math-academy-id 618750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130302}} {:db/id 17592186130466 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve defined by the parametric equations

$$"} :step/id #uuid "032c215a-e883-53c2-bdc0-c14d20b9401e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186530563}} {:db/id 17592186530550 :step/content {:db/id 17592186530454 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f3256b67-7e99-5826-a95a-b55a197e4d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13\pi" :db/id 17592186530184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186530184} :answer-field/id #uuid "12fa28de-d131-50b4-b0e1-7dd696b0e54f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186530230}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4f72f786-eb31-5b03-9051-ae70858e9f5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-352035" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4},\,t\in [0,\sqrt[4]{6}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟹{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{16}\text{d}u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{3}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(27-1) \\  & =13\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "08362200-3b6f-52bb-9fff-49cbac1aba34" :step/next {:db/id 17592186530555}} {:db/id 17592186530555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186530493 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c15a0040-721e-5583-80c4-6b4b6d161036" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi(2-\sqrt{3})" :db/id 17592186530062}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186530062} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b596d95-5abf-5a25-8619-bd46ab687c7e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186530300}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "95891d65-20e2-5732-9bd4-e52bbf49b5d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-352088" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2})),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(t/2)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{csc}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟹{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{16}\text{d}u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{3}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(27-1) \\  & =13\pi .\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(t/2)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{csc}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}2\pi \,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[u]}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]=\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]}^{2}+{[\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)=1$ and ${sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1={tan}^{2}⁡(t)$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{tan}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot |\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-2\pi [\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-2\pi (\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =-2\pi \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}

as

x=3{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-3t,\,t\in [-\sqrt{3},0].

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=-\sqrt{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=0.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t)=3{t}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\sqrt{{(6t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2}-3)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}-18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\sqrt{9({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\cdot 3\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)|{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{3}-3t)({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{5}-2{t}^{3}-3t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =6\pi {\int }_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0}({t}^{5}-2{t}^{3}-3t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{-\sqrt{3}}^{0} \\  & =6\pi [0-(\frac{27}{6}-\frac{9}{2}-\frac{9}{2})] \\  & =6\pi \cdot \frac{27}{6} \\  & =27\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "64958667-b549-5eb7-8561-a3974fe10b64" :step/next {:db/id 17592186532743}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4d11b877-fb53-589c-8eea-da397cb6e4c7" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-352091" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{3}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]=\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]}^{2}+{[\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)=1$ and ${sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1={tan}^{2}⁡(t)$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{tan}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot |\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-2\pi [\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-2\pi (\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =-2\pi \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "679ce636-9dcd-5b15-ab39-bb3b7ed24f1c"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e381238e-91d4-5561-a74f-947fada01bf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186532419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186532419} :answer-field/id #uuid "1a1dc858-f317-5a50-ac0a-63bd26d09cc3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186532505} {:answer/id #uuid "e381238e-91d4-5561-a74f-947fada01bf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186532419} {:db/id 17592186532747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186532703 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2dd285d1-cf9d-5646-a446-ce41bd2e2458" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{52\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186532024} {:answer/id #uuid "c01060b2-f26a-567b-a1dd-ba792972b5d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{32\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186532346} {:answer/id #uuid "ef41bf2a-c7d0-5536-922b-f7eb8c9ec0ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{40\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186532450} {:answer/id #uuid "f173cc96-34cf-5cea-9d45-09f0f19aa1e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{48\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186532455} {:answer/id #uuid "f9f80523-10c6-5bea-b36a-01b7f0de1f7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186532477}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186532024} :answer-field/id #uuid "d460285e-96c9-5656-88a1-24adf10022f6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186532593}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c339d0f2-af34-5938-bbf8-d47914ddf165" :question/math-academy-id "q-138967" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=1$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t)={t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{({t}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot {t}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using direct integration we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-2)-(\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{22}{5}+\frac{4}{5}] \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{26}{5} \\  & =\frac{52\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}

17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129751 :question/id #uuid "9ad6bc33-7c9a-5d03-8204-18b81f486eea" :question/math-academy-id "q-39669" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129269 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e290e8b2-7766-55ff-95da-99a3430b18e3" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a3dfa61-4983-5101-a590-b7cae3069606" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186324062} {:answer/id #uuid "5975b6e2-4d63-5522-bc15-85311b4304c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186324714} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d3c1d8-1ca4-5893-ae40-8a4995898733" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{16}" :db/id 17592186325383} {:answer/id #uuid "c5fd3b47-8f20-518a-a996-2dbd4fa2edc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{40}" :db/id 17592186325679} {:answer/id #uuid "fcb623d2-5638-5465-9671-82a386df23f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "40" :db/id 17592186326195}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c5fd3b47-8f20-518a-a996-2dbd4fa2edc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{40}" :db/id 17592186325679} :answer-field/id #uuid "5d44cd8a-7ab2-5c59-a740-4c19610ad44c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326377}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(12+6)-1(-4-0) \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}.\end{aligned}

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =3 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & z & y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(0+1) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281334 :question/id #uuid "256171d6-afaa-51cd-ae04-b8a4f7e24f09" :question/math-academy-id "q-161804"} {:db/id 17592186281335 :question/id #uuid "21d2a60a-f1f7-5e79-815f-2e9babe829a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161805" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d44b6cc-3a93-5117-a27f-6f280b9b11c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{u}" :db/id 17592186278862} {:answer/id #uuid "47b2751a-712d-5998-bd6d-e5e60e8c5b22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{v+w}{u}" :db/id 17592186279233} {:answer/id #uuid "7a98c4b3-ed46-5cfd-8a6c-e55f7a475d3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u(w-v)" :db/id 17592186279683} {:answer/id #uuid "9aa88b3c-e8a4-5165-97f7-0e1e8c3eec3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "uv" :db/id 17592186279962} {:answer/id #uuid "f792ff52-2762-5037-adc2-ea50c01f1006" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186280762}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278862} :answer-field/id #uuid "db389b2e-8734-58ef-b276-82b4a342763c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281214}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x \\ z-y \\ xy\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=x,\,v(x,y,z)=z-y,\,w(x,y,z)=xy.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ y & x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-x) \\  & =-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =-u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281336 :question/id #uuid "9bd3e29c-50b2-5640-b3fa-d0adf89e1fac" :question/math-academy-id "q-161806" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21988933-2fdd-5343-979b-14ba2f6e68d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{uvw}}" :db/id 17592186278894} {:answer/id #uuid "413d8651-c816-595c-bfd1-f51fa29900be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}" :db/id 17592186279172} {:answer/id #uuid "4e964f3b-c23d-5355-8277-f886ef034e49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{uvw}" :db/id 17592186279306} {:answer/id #uuid "7bc53c83-70d3-5bd8-adc4-31458e829c60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4uvw" :db/id 17592186279694} {:answer/id #uuid "8888de73-401c-58c0-8c74-d084f5008000" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{uvw}" :db/id 17592186279811}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279172} :answer-field/id #uuid "efb87408-7532-5806-bc11-5c1c98d338e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281337 :question/id #uuid "82aa7a5f-aede-5ec9-8984-8cdea4eb6f95" :question/math-academy-id "q-161807" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0626020c-ffd0-5d52-be60-af389fc83a02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(uvw)^{1/3}" :db/id 17592186278648} {:answer/id #uuid "57bde7fd-ba02-508b-9c77-edf62367e8ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}" :db/id 17592186279398} {:answer/id #uuid "84467733-f429-5feb-8388-07e2d51f176e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(uvw)^{3}" :db/id 17592186279778} {:answer/id #uuid "af416bf2-0b93-5782-b6de-1f1c2d402fc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(uvw)^{2/3}" :db/id 17592186280143} {:answer/id #uuid "c8f31297-6e1d-54c7-be43-6fdd25ab29fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{(uvw)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186280352}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279398} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bbffbbf-30e0-555b-b5e7-55199b3bfffb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280913}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186424181 :question/id #uuid "bbf87425-cede-5e7e-870f-278bd2b11904" :question/math-academy-id "q-161808" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ba467583-3a17-5baa-8344-2ff452a1d080" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{u}" :db/id 17592186424165} {:answer/id #uuid "bc7a65b8-5911-5995-890e-26eb26de2d86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{vw}" :db/id 17592186424166} {:answer/id #uuid "cda476b6-e024-5c13-a813-a0217e4446ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186424167} {:answer/id #uuid "ecf34300-0330-5f0e-9e12-24a74c4b83db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2u}{v-w}" :db/id 17592186424170} {:answer/id #uuid "fa885cf6-9f29-528c-8aeb-86e960fc0083" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{w}{v}" :db/id 17592186424172}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424165} :answer-field/id #uuid "f602c505-c9b2-58a6-873a-3101dc02439a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424177}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549253 :question/id #uuid "13892e3f-d765-51b3-b960-59a3b31629f7"} {:db/id 17592186549258 :question/id #uuid "28f499ce-a5b7-5f3f-90af-72bf76f6b98e"} {:db/id 17592186549263 {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}-v \\ {u}^{2}+v \\ {e}^{w}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186281338 :question/id #uuid "d47d2404-bd86-5706-ba43-4f015172617a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161809" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b1e167f-c36b-51bb-8f7d-1c5abfba9d3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the cylinder ${v}^{2}+{u}^{2}=1.$" :db/id 17592186278842} {:answer/id #uuid "398d98c4-80d9-5695-9ad1-7904a7156b87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the $uv-$plane." :db/id 17592186279097} {:answer/id #uuid "50abbce6-3f16-512e-a087-34dc285e7cbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the plane $v=u.$" :db/id 17592186279329} {:answer/id #uuid "cc12c5cd-4583-53a4-9f13-8cababa0d611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v={u}^{2}.$" :db/id 17592186280382} {:answer/id #uuid "de43abc5-071a-5046-a899-84beee7c637b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the $uw-$plane." :db/id 17592186280551}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279329} :answer-field/id #uuid "73950424-d736-5015-94bb-837d8bf513c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281040}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=uv,\,y(u,v,w)=u+v,\,z(u,v,w)=w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}v & u & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ v-u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+3w,\,y(u,v,w)=v+2w,\,z(u,v,w)={v}^{2}-u.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =3 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$

$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 3-4v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,y(u,v,w)=v-u,\,z(u,v,w)=uw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ w & 0 & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ w & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(u-0)+2(0-w) \\  & =u-2w.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ u-2w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
