A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=16,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-16I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}-16\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-12 & -6 \\ -6 & -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "42130988-8a9c-5c98-b57a-c5c217558433" :step/next {:db/id 17592186428018}} {:db/id 17592186428018 :step/content {:db/id 17592186428015 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "089ec07a-5e86-5e2c-9ee0-7a59f0e9ce6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}" :db/id 17592186428009} {:answer/id #uuid "7011776a-f74f-5038-88b7-bd75d4a9eff4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}" :db/id 17592186428010} {:answer/id #uuid "7450dd95-1930-5564-96d4-6c9e274f1579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186428011} {:answer/id #uuid "a9766852-3203-5031-bf4e-845ae1f644cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186428012} {:answer/id #uuid "da310c2d-2eb6-5830-855e-93aa19083cd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186428013}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186428010} :answer-field/id #uuid "01f21526-a5f6-5403-8d94-60d82378f21e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186428014}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "39a1a8bd-f69f-5f36-99bc-5bd95f9b782d" :question/math-academy-id "q-96238" :question/problem "$$

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-81I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-81I=\begin{bmatrix}73 & 24 \\ 24 & 9\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 24 \\ 24 & -72\end{bmatrix}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}|=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}.

$$

$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=8.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 4 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{9}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{36}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

$$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 4 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=8.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 4 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{9}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{36}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{32}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

$$

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$

$$

$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 4 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=8.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-81\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 4 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}65 & 4 \\ 4 & 80\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{9}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{36}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{32}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\end{bmatrix}

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-81[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -24 \\ -24 & -72\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}72 & -24 \\ -24 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-27 & -18 \\ -18 & -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12 & -18 \\ -18 & 27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{24}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{16}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{10}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}

A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 8 \\ 8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-9\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ba507f27-de8d-57b9-abc6-5d9ed7fc3ec1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520585}} {:db/id 17592186520618 :step/content {:db/id 17592186371290 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8816896f-cca6-5ce2-bf30-8d2b1f66e3f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186371292} {:answer/id #uuid "2e10c5b6-c997-5994-9093-7e45e10efbd5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186371293} {:answer/id #uuid "d4fea695-072e-5f95-902a-71d988e363cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186371294} {:answer/id #uuid "dcd9c1a8-ef05-5de9-af7d-a1baeb76d255" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}" :db/id 17592186371295} {:answer/id #uuid "5b42e903-5007-58dd-9a44-08bf6ca76aac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186371296}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186371292} :answer-field/id #uuid "8aac91f8-948d-551f-bd8b-56bc67976e79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186371291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fa5f61d9-1d7f-5da9-9527-e7cc3f414c94" :question/math-academy-id "q-95904" :question/problem "$$

$$

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=10.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=100.$ 

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}58 & 42 \\ 42 & 58\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-100I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-100I=\begin{bmatrix}58 & 42 \\ 42 & 58\end{bmatrix}-100\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-42 & 42 \\ 42 & -42\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-100I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|=|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|=\sqrt{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "eee3bc90-1ac6-5bfc-8f49-7bbeddbe8022" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520583}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of 2x2 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186519991} {:db/id 17592186520525 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162666 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "54deaa5d-b42c-582b-add4-d6575e45a079" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520120} {:answer/id #uuid "5adca1a5-04fa-5979-ab07-c4374ef39ef9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520132} {:answer/id #uuid "8584a18f-938b-5b11-9a92-aea06357491c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520185} {:answer/id #uuid "875c7469-79dd-5306-8869-1ae4d067e4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520190} {:answer/id #uuid "e5b0b4f8-5d8c-5df5-bcb5-6a41d1765e47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186520326}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520120} :answer-field/id #uuid "50d8446e-fd5b-543b-bc96-f048b71511a7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186161288}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1290450b-3f65-5ec4-8f81-47e7a7dc9fcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-95734" :question/problem "$$

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}72 & -24 \\ -24 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 8 \\ 8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{bmatrix}-9\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 \\ -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-64\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-27 & -18 \\ -18 & -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12 & -18 \\ -18 & 27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{24}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{16}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{10}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9110dbbf-595e-5932-adab-f257d78e5fbe"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2d3ea076-4d0b-50b5-af4f-ca0b0399c71f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}$

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨-x,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y+1,$ $\,x={e}^{y},$ and the line $y=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/72/728036ffc90e2476017b3102b6279f9c5900f0e7fc58536e76c9aa038eb04f02.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=-x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y+1\le x\le {e}^{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}+y-1)\,dy \\  & =-{[{e}^{y}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[(e+\frac{1}{2}-1)-1] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-e.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e5/e570374b37c116e32c3a7762b8cf09a28bdbb3e06b5e67e25837902a89bcd264.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x+\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y+\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553757 :question/id #uuid "391564c7-a751-5991-b788-dcbb08b27c2c"} {:db/id 17592186553764 :question/id #uuid "9f300428-dd28-5d22-81b0-c450650df73d"} {:db/id 17592186172100 Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4y-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4y-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-4xy-6{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[(-4(1)^{2}y-6(1)^{2}{y}^{2})-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-4y-6{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =[-2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2(1)^{2}-2(1)^{3})-(-2(-1)^{2}-2(-1)^{3}) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424523 :question/id #uuid "ef2a7e7d-9054-51ec-bb29-4e186ac65a15" :question/math-academy-id "q-127307"} {:db/id 17592186520740 :question/id #uuid "25491ab2-3faf-524d-80c3-eb7b98861b8b"} {:db/id 17592186541081 :question/id #uuid "512baac6-6af2-5983-be4f-040d5e0743f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-127327" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "42f7866a-874a-59e8-98df-e82497daf28c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186540642} {:answer/id #uuid "44289665-fb34-50eb-942c-684dbafac462" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186540644} {:answer/id #uuid "5d52696f-f66a-5483-9d31-ad3010ca9bf6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186540685} {:answer/id #uuid "675393a7-a22d-52c0-8122-89d84461848c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186540704} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1a18cf-57e7-594a-bab2-ece7b5646c56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186540734}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540734} :answer-field/id #uuid "dcc96fea-c51a-5b5e-9f54-45e9c86734fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186541040}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3},\,\sqrt[3]{x}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/fa/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}y+x)\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[((1)^{3}y+1)-((-1)^{3}y+(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+2)\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}+2y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =((2)^{2}+2(2))-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050534} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2153ce06-d6d5-5127-8a6c-97309bd972d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{\int {:db/id 17592186173012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

    

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5862 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form"} :step/id #uuid "e5c29654-0b83-51e0-a3d0-c6fbf08c8f2d" :step/math-academy-id 35877 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173010}} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!

To see how, we first recall that the flux of $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s= \oint\limits_C P\, \textrm{d}y -Q\, \textrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is closed and $\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Now, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have

$$

"b533c8b3-90f2-54ee-ae35-a98929d6ba6e" :step/math-academy-id 35837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173009}} {:db/id 17592186173012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

    

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

through $C$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1736de57-90cb-505e-97a3-07df8bb92125" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481473}} {:db/id 17592186481472 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262736 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a4a4e6e-8fd1-5522-991a-091f0cb886bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(6{y}^{2}+8x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186260102} {:answer/id #uuid "20290a0e-d346-5c30-942c-4f76e1fbd4e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+8x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186260151} {:answer/id #uuid "a3837ae4-763a-595f-890a-8cc4ef3801c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{3}(1+8x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186261299} {:answer/id #uuid "b8b24ec3-56ed-5096-95a0-c3abce767ce2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{3}(1+8x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186261495} {:answer/id #uuid "fa68bf59-8089-510b-855b-d18f12a481e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-1}^{1}6{y}^{2}(1+8x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186262064}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186261299} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e39b9c2-8ba1-5d6a-8730-4f02deaa62b2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262373}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "64b95036-f7c8-5305-8593-d176862393c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-127229" :question/problem "Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. $$
F(x,y)=⟨x+\sqrt{y},\,y+\sqrt{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e5/e570374b37c116e32c3a7762b8cf09a28bdbb3e06b5e67e25837902a89bcd264.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x+\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y+\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ec17ec80-3152-54be-96ed-dd7762345db6"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a2f6f5b-f063-50fd-a445-e5206861484d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int "512baac6-6af2-5983-be4f-040d5e0743f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-127327" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3},\,\sqrt[3]{x}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/fa/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}y+x)\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[((1)^{3}y+1)-((-1)^{3}y+(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+2)\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}+2y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =((2)^{2}+2(2))-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ffe0a3c1-5d07-5ea1-84fe-9437d4f004d0"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6730175f-e2ca-5f18-8300-20f526084f78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value 17592186192682 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7813df9e-9641-58a3-8537-e672e5fd079c" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Intercept Parameters"}] :question/problem "Let $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7 x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $(x_1,y_1), \: \ldots, \: (x_{8},y_{8})$ of $n=8$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overline{x}=2.4$, the mean square error of the model is $1.25$, and $S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2 = 42$, find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $6$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for $\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is given by $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{\textrm{MSE} \cdot \bigg(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}} \bigg)}$*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and
- $\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that

$$
\widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7x
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{\widehat{\,\beta}_0}_{\:\: \textrm{point} \ \textrm{estimate}} \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.
- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.
- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0$, given by
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{\textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}$
where we have:$\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:
$\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$
where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:
$\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=1.6+0.7x$, our point estimate is
$\widehat{\,\beta}_0 = 1.6$.
- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have
$\alpha=1-0.90=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05$.
We are given that $P(T > 1.943) = 0.05$. As a result,
$t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{6,0.05} = 1.943$.
Now, we can compute the margin of error:
$t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = 1.943 \cdot \sqrt{1.25 \cdot \bigg(\dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{2.4^2}{42} \bigg)} \approx 1.1$
- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:
$\widehat{\,\beta}_0 \: \pm \: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = 1.6 \pm 1.1$"} {:db/id 17592186192979 :question/id #uuid "68d56eaf-9e11-54bc-9fcb-5131b64bc995" :question/math-academy-id "q-143256" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186192682 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7813df9e-9641-58a3-8537-e672e5fd079c" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Intercept Parameters"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9c65fed1-27c9-5cfc-9048-2d116fad5f1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3.5 ± 2.8" :db/id 17592186189761} {:answer/id #uuid "b7842007-8121-5dd4-a02c-c92f2536f71b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 1.2" :db/id 17592186189762} {:answer/id #uuid "dc1201b7-f41e-5d52-a92b-aa861df718df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3.5 ± 3.0" :db/id 17592186189763} {:answer/id #uuid "f1a87739-c0db-5853-84a1-48a7c08ba98c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3.5 ± 1.2" :db/id 17592186189764} {:answer/id #uuid "4ebecaf8-b15e-5a58-abfe-4e33b137f1b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5 ± 2.5" :db/id 17592186189765}] :answer-field/id #uuid "2f9df6ed-4f2d-5912-b30b-a8d79df169ce" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186189760}] :question/problem "Let $y^(^) = β^(^)_{0} + β^(^)_{1}x = 3.5 + 5x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $(x_{1}, y_{1}), …, (x_{20}, y_{20})$ of $n = 20$ paired observations. where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=21.3 + 10x$, our point estimate is

:step/math-academy-id 38068 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193690}} {:db/id 17592186193676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population.

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$
y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x
$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$ are given by

$$
\widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x}
$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i$, and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following:

![](images/68/681a96293905841b417dd7ca9faa2631aedc5ad57e4f2d95fcd40089b9e83c6e.png)

Notice that we referred to $\widehat{\beta_0}$ and $\widehat{\beta_1}$ as *estimates*. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

The two lines are shown below.

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

To summarize,

- the regression equation $y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x$ is an estimate of the true regression equation $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$,
- $\widehat{\beta_1}$ is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter $\beta_1$, and
- $\widehat{\beta_0}$ is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter $\beta_0$.

In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the intercept parameter $\beta_0$." :tutorial/id #uuid "109cb2d6-433c-5ebc-8c14-b0db564dcee8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6965 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "140fd64b-240a-5128-bceb-5d2258cb5439" :step/math-academy-id 42156 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193677}} {:db/id 17592186193677 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193892 :tutorial/content "Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{\widehat{\,\beta}_0}_{\:\: \textrm{point} \ \textrm{estimate}} \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}_{\textrm{standard} \ \,\:\: \textrm{error}}}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$

Note the following:

- $\!\widehat{\,\beta}_0$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.
- $P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.
- $\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]$ is the standard error of $\widehat{\,\beta}_0$, given by
$\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,] = \sqrt{\textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}$
where we have:$\textrm{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:
$\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$
where $\widehat{\,y}_i$ is the estimate of $y_i$ given by our regression model.$S_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:
$\displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2$

The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

- Each data point in the sample has some *residual* (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point $(x_i,y_i)$ is given by
$(y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)$.
- The expression $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2$ gives the sum of the squared residuals of our regression model.
- Even considering the entire population, the data points will not fall on a perfectly straight line. Thus, errors are present even in the "true" regression model. These errors have some (unknown) variance, which we'll denote as $\sigma^2$.
- It can be shown that the $\textrm{MSE}$ is an *unbiased* estimator of $\sigma^2$." :tutorial/id #uuid "cc1aaf89-d357-53d7-8943-926609018212" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6967 :tutorial/title "Summary of the Key Result"} :step/id #uuid "ac2be2f7-e3fa-5b92-b417-ac33fa6ff9d7" :step/math-academy-id 42158 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193503}} {:db/id 17592186193678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193893 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we made use of the following results:

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] = \sigma^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)
$$

Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i
$$

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)nx^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we define $k_i$ as

$$
k_i = \dfrac{x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}
$$

The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0$
- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1$
- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}$

Now, recall that

$$
\widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x}
$$

We can rewrite our expression for $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
β_{0}^(^) &= y^(―) - β_{1}x^(―) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i} - \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}x^(―) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i} - (∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i})/(S_{xx})x^(―) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}y_{i}x^(―) \\
&= \frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i} - x^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}y_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

We're now in a position to compute $\textrm{E}[{\widehat{\beta_0}}]$ and $\textrm{Var}[{\widehat{\beta_0}}]$.

- For the mean, we have
$E[β_{0}^(^)]|= \frac{1}{n}E[∑_(i)y_{i}] - x^(―)E[∑_(i)k_{i}y_{i}]; = \frac{1}{n}∑_(i)E[y_{i}] - x^(―)∑_(i)E[k_{i}y_{i}]; = \frac{1}{n}∑_(i)(β_{0} + β_{1}x_{i}) - x^(―)∑_(i)k_{i}(β_{0} + β_{1}x_{i}); = \frac{1}{n}∑_(i)(β_{0} + β_{1}x_{i}) - x^(―)[β_{0}∑_(i)k_{i} + β_{1}∑_(i)k_{i}x_{i}]; = \frac{1}{n}∑_(i)(β_{0} + β_{1}x_{i}) - x^(―)[β_{0}∑_(i)k_{i}^{0} + β_{1}∑_(i)k_{i}x_{i}^{1}]; = \frac{1}{n}∑_(i)(β_{0} + β_{1}x_{i}) - x^(―)β_{1}; = \frac{β_{0}}{n}∑_(i)1 + \frac{β_{1}}{n}∑_(i)x_{i} - x^(―)β_{1}; = \frac{β_{0}}{n} \cdot n + x^(―)β_{1} - x^(―)β_{1}; = β_{0}$.
- For the variance, we have
$Var[β_{0}^(^)]|= \frac{1}{n^{2}}Var[∑_(i)y_{i}] + x^(―)^{2}Var[∑_(i)k_{i}y_{i}]; = \frac{1}{n^{2}}∑_(i)Var[y_{i}] + x^(―)^{2}∑_(i)k_{i}^{2}Var[y_{i}]; = \frac{1}{n^{2}}nσ^{2} + x^(―)^{2}∑_(i)k_{i}^{2}σ^{2}; = \frac{1}{n^{2}}nσ^{2} + x^(―)^{2}σ^{2}∑_(i)k_{i}^{2}; = \frac{1}{n}σ^{2} + x^(―)^{2}σ^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{S_{xx}}; = σ^{2}(\frac{1}{n} + (x^(―)^{2})/(S_{xx}))$.

So finally, we have

$$
\widehat{\beta_0} \sim N\left(\beta_0,\sigma^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e3cbadc-9a0c-5925-af3f-b47ca4a2ff80" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6968 :tutorial/title "Expectation and Variance of Intercept Parameter Estimates"} :step/id #uuid "2e9c0fd9-3132-5c7d-b2e2-2b04a2530995" :step/math-academy-id 42159} {:db/id 17592186193690 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193900 :tutorial/content "We'll now derive our expression for the confidence interval for our intercept parameter estimate $\widehat{\beta_0}$.

Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$.

$$
(x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)
$$

Let's assume that our "global" regression line (i.e., the line that best fits the entire population) is given by

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

For each

$$
i=1,2,\ldots,n
$$

let

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i
$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and

$$
\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2$. The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/69/69135b6cdc4d34f5422da39bac5d15624d16f4817e91f282974507c711953796.png)

This means that each $y_i$ is a normally distributed random variable with

$$
y_i \sim N\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \sigma^2\right)
$$

It can be shown that

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] = \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)
$$

We'll derive these results separately in a while. But for now, we'll simply state them.

Using these results, we can express the distribution of $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as

$$
\widehat{\beta}_0 \sim N\left(\beta_0, \: \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \right)
$$

We do not know $\sigma^2$, the variance of the error terms. However, it can be shown that the mean squared error, given by

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$.

Our estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_0$ is now given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \sqrt{\textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

Since this is an *estimate* of the standard error, it can be shown that the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_0 -\beta_0}{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta_0}]}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

Finally, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1aef59f3-040d-59b5-90f2-5f746d059c4a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7007 :tutorial/title "Deriving an Expression for the Confidence Interval"} :step/id #uuid "e07f8b0d-114e-5676-8692-12b109c4375f" :step/math-academy-id 42309 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193678}}] :activity/title "Confidence Intervals for Linear Regression Intercept Parameters" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186192927} {:db/id 17592186193676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population.

$$
i=1,2,\ldots,n
$$

let

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i
$$

where we assume that the error terms $\epsilon_i$ are I.I.D, and

$$
\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

for some unknown variance $\sigma^2$. The error terms and their distribution can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/69/69135b6cdc4d34f5422da39bac5d15624d16f4817e91f282974507c711953796.png)

This means that each $y_i$ is a normally distributed random variable with

$$
y_i \sim N\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \sigma^2\right)
$$

It can be shown that

$$
\textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \beta_0, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_0}] = \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)
$$

We'll derive these results separately in a while. But for now, we'll simply state them.

Using these results, we can express the distribution of $\widehat{\beta_0}$ as

$$
\widehat{\beta}_0 \sim N\left(\beta_0, \: \sigma^2\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \right)
$$

We do not know $\sigma^2$, the variance of the error terms. However, it can be shown that the mean squared error, given by

$$
\textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2
$$

is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$.

Our estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_0$ is now given by

$$
\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta}_0] = \sqrt{\textrm{MSE}\cdot\left(\dfrac1n+ \dfrac{\overline{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}
$$

Since this is an *estimate* of the standard error, it can be shown that the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_0 -\beta_0}{\textrm{SE}[\widehat{\beta_0}]}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

Finally, given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the intercept $\beta_0$ of our model can be written as

$$
\widehat{\,\beta}_0 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_0\,]}^{\textrm{margin of error}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1aef59f3-040d-59b5-90f2-5f746d059c4a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7007 :tutorial/title "Deriving an Expression for the Confidence Interval"} :step/id #uuid "e07f8b0d-114e-5676-8692-12b109c4375f" :step/math-academy-id 42309 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193678}} {:db/id 17592186193891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of $n$ of *paired* observations $(x_i,y_i)$ drawn from a population.

$$

Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

$$

$$

Our *estimates* for the **slope parameter** $\widehat{\beta_1}$ and **intercept parameter** $\widehat{\beta_0}$ are given by

$$

where $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ are the mean values of $x_i$ and $y_i$, and the quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by

$$

![](images/df/df08670fd3c4aff99e994692eff28a49a9ec47d4aa73185682e3e0e829e3d562.png)

Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i

We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y^(―) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i} - y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―)) \\

&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))y_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

:answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186511418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162042 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161836 :question/id #uuid "bba077a6-56c6-5137-b949-26fae1c98625" :question/math-academy-id "e-8633"} :knowledge-point/id </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186370697 :question/id #uuid "f5a19d61-895b-51bb-abe5-e33bbbd340f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-363836"} {:db/id 17592186381942 :question/id #uuid $$

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$  select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by:

|  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${u}_{1}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ |  |  |

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal.

Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to 

$$
{{field-3}}.
$$

Choosing ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by:

|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | {{field-5}} |  |  |
|  |  | ${x}_{3}$ |  |  |

that we can rewrite as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the two linearly independent solutions are already mutually orthogonal, we only need to normalize them. Hence, we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423863 :question/id #uuid "bd607d3f-88f1-5057-a261-73a39b9023d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-363834"} {:db/id 17592186430360 :question/id #uuid
